Since leaving the White House, Sacks has "maintained close ties with the president," according to the Guardian, and "in May, he successfully urged Trump to scrap an executive order that would've subjected AI models to government review."

extraction.body: President Trump on Sunday named Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as his new "AI czar," adding a different category of intelligence, the "artificial" kind, to the U.S. spy chief's portfolio. In a post on Truth Social , Trump said Clayton will lead a newly formed "Super Intelligence Force" alongside Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor. The group will report directly to Trump and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles. Its goal, Trump wrote, is "to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans." Clayton will keep his job as DNI, which oversees the nation's 18 intelligence agencies. Trump's announcement follows meeting last Tuesday at the White House where top AI executives signed what he called a " morally binding " agreement to police themselves in order to prevent their increasingly powerful models from going rogue and harming humanity . "There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation," the president said at the meeting. "This is going to be all for the good, and we're going to have it be nice and safe." Despite new polls showing that 86% of Americans want AI companies to meet independent safety standards even if doing so slows development — with 74% largely mistrusting the leaders of those companies — Trump insisted in recent days that federal regulations are unnecessary and that those who say otherwise are " Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers ." "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" he wrote on social media . Elsewhere, Trump has said that regulation would handicap the U.S. in its race to "win" AI. "Whoever wins AI ... that's the group that wins," Trump told the United Nations General Assembly last month . "We're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way." According to the Guardian , Trump's previous AI and crypto czar, billionaire tech investor David Sacks, consistently "counseled the president to give a soft touch to AI regulation, helping push executive orders and other measures aimed at loosening restrictions on the technology." Sacks also "maintains direct financial stakes in multiple AI companies," the paper reported, though he took steps to divest some of his holdings last year while serving in the administration. He stepped down in March. Will Clayton follow Sacks's lead? Or will he chart a new course? Here's what we know so far. Clayton, 60, is a registered independent with degrees from the University of Pennsylvania (engineering, law) and the University of Cambridge (economics). As a lawyer in private practice, he focused mostly on Wall Street: mergers and acquisitions, market offerings and regulatory proceedings. During Trump's first term, from 2017 to 2020, Clayton chaired the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. From March 2021 to April 2025, Clayton served as chair and "lead independent director" of the board of Apollo Global Management . (Apollo has owned a 90% majority stake in Yahoo since September 2021.) In late 2024, Trump nominated Clayton to serve as U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, his first prosecutorial job; Trump later appointed Clayton to serve in an acting capacity after New York Sen. Chuck Schumer blocked his appointment. Reports suggest Clayton was also considered for roles as secretary of the treasury, attorney general and director of the Central Intelligence Agency. In November 2025, Trump ordered the Department of Justice to investigate Democrats associated with Jeffrey Epstein, and U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi assigned Clayton to lead the probe . After former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard resigned in May 2026, Trump tapped Clayton to replace her. "He's very qualified," Democratic Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia said at the time . But Clayton sidestepped questions over who won the 2020 election during his July confirmation hearings, and he was confirmed without Democratic support. "I'm not an election denier," Clayton told the Senate. "He went through our processes, and Joe Biden became the president of the United States." During his DNI confirmation hearings, Clayton described AI as "a game changer ," warning that it represents "not only an opportunity but a threat." "We should just all recognize that," he continued. "When something is both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it." On Tuesday, Clayton attended Trump's White House meeting with top AI executives. Speaking afterward to CNBC, he used the president's new preferred term for AI — i.e., "superintelligence " — while pushing back against lawmakers who have called for regulating or pausing U.S. AI development. "Super intelligence is a national security issue, and that was something that was recognized yesterday by not just the industry leaders but everybody in the room," Clayton said. "But to, in some way, not try to drive forward inside the United States, with companies that are regulated in the United States ... to somehow say we should back away from this and let the rest of the world develop these models and implement these models? I don't think anybody in that room, and I don't think any American, should think that that's a good strategy." Asked to respond to criticism from Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts that Trump's current policy of letting AI companies police themselves will prove to be "a recipe for disaster," Clayton suggested that the U.S. government's existing regulatory framework could also help keep AI in check. "My response to the American people on that front is we have a Federal Trade Commission, we have a Department of Justice," Clayton said. "I know the leaders of both those organizations, and they're committed to protecting the American people in this regard." According to Trump's post, the Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the federal government's dealings with AI companies, infrastructure providers, consumers, public interest groups and religious organizations, CNN reported . Last month, Trump wrote on social media that he would "be announcing, in the near future, the AI 'Czar.' "Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" he added. In the same post, the president again dismissed concerns about AI safety as a "hoax" perpetrated by "Radical Left Democrats." He also wrote that going forward, his administration would not "in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," which he described as "the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet" — only "even larger and more impactful." "Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!" Trump explained. As for reining in "bad" actors, he wrote, "we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System." Clayton, it seems, will now be in charge of cherishing, helping and watching over the AI industry as it grows. He's "a good man," Trump told Axios when the outlet asked last week if Clayton was being considered for the job . "He's right here. That's a good idea." It's unclear what happened to a separate idea Trump floated last month, which he called "the AI Force." "I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force , which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term," Trump wrote in his September social media post about naming an AI czar. According to Axios , Trump's AI Force idea "caught advisers by surprise," setting off "a mad dash" within the administration "to imagine what AI Force would look like." When Sacks served as AI czar, he repeatedly persuaded the president and his administration to resist new AI restrictions, including state laws to limit AI . Since leaving the White House, Sacks has "maintained close ties with the president," according to the Guardian, and "in May, he successfully urged Trump to scrap an executive order that would've subjected AI models to government review." The Wall Street Journal recently reported the Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles were "caught off guard and unhappy" with Trump's decision after they "spent months negotiating to increase oversight of AI and had consulted a range of industry executives on the order." According to the Journal's sources, Wiles "told others that Sacks had persuaded Trump" to back down "in a last-minute call," leaving Bessent "worried that AI-led cyberattacks could wreak havoc on the nation's banking system." The convicted killer is in hospital in Tennessee after surviving two lethal injections, in a case that has raised many questions.

passages: Donald Trump on Sunday named Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence , to also serve as the new White House AI czar.
Trump had initially created the AI and cryptocurrency czar position when he returned to the White House in January 2025.
Trump previously floated Clayton’s name as a potential AI czar, telling Axios in September that Clayton was “a good man” and the prospect of appointing him was “a good idea”.
In a social media post on Sunday, Trump announced that Clayton would lead what the US president called “the Super Intelligence Force (SIF)”.
Musk said on his social media platform X that SI was “better” than AI – and that he was renaming his aerospace company’s AI unit from SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI.
Clayton, who leads the US’s 18 intelligence agencies , previously served as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and led the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term.
In September, Trump announced he was creating an “AI Force” and a czar to oversee the technology’s growth and monitor for “bad” development.
The announcement came after tech industry leaders warned that AI was developing too rapidly to control and that it could harm humans.

Trump’s post also said the SIF would “coordinate the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and super intelligence companies”.
But to address concerns, the president created an advisory committee in addition to the czar – whom he previously promised would be led by a “high IQ” individual.
Trump also recently met with AI industry leaders to discuss concerns.
Trump has insisted continued development is paramount to defeating China in the global AI race.

extraction.body: Clayton had said AI was a ‘gamechanger’ but also posed ‘a threat’ during his confirmation hearing Clayton had said AI was a ‘gamechanger’ but also posed ‘a threat’ during his confirmation hearing Donald Trump on Sunday named Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence , to also serve as the new White House AI czar. Clayton, who leads the US’s 18 intelligence agencies , previously served as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and led the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term. During his Senate confirmation hearing , Clayton said AI was a “gamechanger” but it also posed “a threat”. “When something’s both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it,” Clayton told lawmakers when asked about AI. CBS News was the first to report that Clayton would be appointed White House AI czar. In a social media post on Sunday, Trump announced that Clayton would lead what the US president called “the Super Intelligence Force (SIF)”. Trump’s post also said the SIF would “coordinate the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and super intelligence companies”. Among those reacting on Sunday to Trump’s invoking the term “super intelligence” was SpaceX chief Elon Musk . Musk said on his social media platform X that SI was “better” than AI – and that he was renaming his aerospace company’s AI unit from SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. Senator Mark Warner, a Virginia Democrat who is vice-chair of the Senate select committee on intelligence, cautiously welcomed the appointment of Clayton, while noting that “the administration has resisted meaningful safeguards without offering a serious alternative for addressing the national security risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems”. “I look forward to working with Director Clayton on ensuring the United States stays ahead of China and other adversaries, strengthening the security and resilience of our most advanced AI systems, and establishing rigorous testing and safeguards so that increasingly powerful systems remain secure, reliable, and under human control,” Warner added. In September, Trump announced he was creating an “AI Force” and a czar to oversee the technology’s growth and monitor for “bad” development. The announcement came after tech industry leaders warned that AI was developing too rapidly to control and that it could harm humans. The president has largely brushed aside concerns about AI development and the construction of datacenters, which power the technology. Trump has insisted continued development is paramount to defeating China in the global AI race. But to address concerns, the president created an advisory committee in addition to the czar – whom he previously promised would be led by a “high IQ” individual. Trump also recently met with AI industry leaders to discuss concerns. On Tuesday, Trump and six executives signed an AI accord at the White House, promising to create internal and external monitors to ensure the technology is used as intended and any safety issues are addressed. Trump had initially created the AI and cryptocurrency czar position when he returned to the White House in January 2025. David Sacks, the venture capitalist and tech businessman, served as the administration’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March 2026, when he reached his employment limit under his designation as a “special government employee”. Sacks still co-chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. Trump previously floated Clayton’s name as a potential AI czar, telling Axios in September that Clayton was “a good man” and the prospect of appointing him was “a good idea”.

Donald Trump on Sunday named Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence , to also serve as the new White House AI czar.
Clayton, who leads the US’s 18 intelligence agencies , previously served as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and led the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term.
During his Senate confirmation hearing , Clayton said AI was a “gamechanger” but it also posed “a threat”.
“When something’s both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it,” Clayton told lawmakers when asked about AI.
CBS News was the first to report that Clayton would be appointed White House AI czar.
In a social media post on Sunday, Trump announced that Clayton would lead what the US president called “the Super Intelligence Force (SIF)”.

Trump’s post also said the SIF would “coordinate the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and super intelligence companies”.

Among those reacting on Sunday to Trump’s invoking the term “super intelligence” was SpaceX chief Elon Musk . Musk said on his social media platform X that SI was “better” than AI – and that he was renaming his aerospace company’s AI unit from SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI.

Senator Mark Warner, a Virginia Democrat who is vice-chair of the Senate select committee on intelligence, cautiously welcomed the appointment of Clayton, while noting that “the administration has resisted meaningful safeguards without offering a serious alternative for addressing the national security risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems”.

“I look forward to working with Director Clayton on ensuring the United States stays ahead of China and other adversaries, strengthening the security and resilience of our most advanced AI systems, and establishing rigorous testing and safeguards so that increasingly powerful systems remain secure, reliable, and under human control,” Warner added.

In September, Trump announced he was creating an “AI Force” and a czar to oversee the technology’s growth and monitor for “bad” development. The announcement came after tech industry leaders warned that AI was developing too rapidly to control and that it could harm humans.
The president has largely brushed aside concerns about AI development and the construction of datacenters, which power the technology.
Trump has insisted continued development is paramount to defeating China in the global AI race.

But to address concerns, the president created an advisory committee in addition to the czar – whom he previously promised would be led by a “high IQ” individual. Trump also recently met with AI industry leaders to discuss concerns.

On Tuesday, Trump and six executives signed an AI accord at the White House, promising to create internal and external monitors to ensure the technology is used as intended and any safety issues are addressed.
Trump had initially created the AI and cryptocurrency czar position when he returned to the White House in January 2025.

David Sacks, the venture capitalist and tech businessman, served as the administration’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March 2026, when he reached his employment limit under his designation as a “special government employee”.
Sacks still co-chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.
Trump previously floated Clayton’s name as a potential AI czar, telling Axios in September that Clayton was “a good man” and the prospect of appointing him was “a good idea”.

Mariam Zuhaib/AP hide caption Director of national intelligence Jay Clayton is the new White House AI czar, President Trump said on Sunday. Trump wrote on Truth Social that Clayton will lead the White House's new "Super Intelligence Force," a group that will "ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence." Trump prefers the term "super intelligence" to "artificial intelligence." He said his "Super Intelligence Force" will "coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies." Before being confirmed earlier this year to lead national intelligence, Clayton was United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York, and chairman of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Trump's announcement follows various statements of alarm from tech leaders over risks in the rapid development of AI, including that it could go rogue. Trump has largely brushed aside the warnings and attempted to reframe concerns around AI. On Tuesday, Trump met with AI executives at the White House, and said afterwards that leaders of several artificial intelligence companies had signed a voluntary accord that will include internal and external reviews of their work. Meanwhile, the White House also launched a revamped government website this week, America.gov , which says it is sourced via artificial intelligence from "official government sources." In his social media post, Trump also named other members of his "Super Intelligence Force". He said it will include: Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor, and Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael. It is unclear what Clayton's appointment as AI czar means for the AI industry, as current artificial intelligence regulation by the U.S. government is limited. Congress has not passed federal law broadly regulating the use or development of AI. Some states, including California, have enacted measures about AI, including requiring entities to be transparent when it is used . During an interview with CNBC last month, Clayton called super intelligence a "national security issue." He also pushed back against calls for a "pause" in developing the technology, pointing out that other countries around the world are continuing to develop AI. "I don't think any American should think that that's a good strategy," he said. In December 2024, president-elect Trump announced he would appoint David Sacks, a Silicon Valley investor, as an AI and crypto czar , with a brief to advise the administration on policies surrounding AI. Earlier this year, Sacks stepped down from his role and became co-chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. He has backed AI leaders Sam Altman and Dario Amodei's warnings about the technology, and the idea of a "slow down" in AI development. Last month, Sacks wrote on social media that the tech leaders should "stop pretending you need anyone else's permission" to make such moves. passages: US President Donald Trump has appointed Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as the administration's AI czar, the Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday, citing an interview with Clayton.
Clayton, who was appointed intelligence chief in August, will lead a new White House panel tasked with reporting within 120 days on the risks and opportunities posed by AI, the newspaper said.

Clayton's panel will review AI-related risks and current government reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks and other incidents, and recommend ways to strengthen federal-response capabilities under existing authorities, the Journal said, citing the task force's charter.
Venture capitalist David Sacks held the AI czar role at the beginning of Trump's second term.
Trump has appeared to take a light touch toward AI regulation, arguing that excessive oversight could weaken competitiveness against China.
He said on Tuesday that he does not want to work with Chinese President Xi Jinping on governing AI technology.

Clayton, who was appointed intelligence chief in August, will lead a new White House panel tasked with reporting within 120 days on the risks and opportunities posed by AI, the newspaper said. "The president asked that a group be put together," which the administration refers to as the "Super Intelligence Force," to ensure the US remains a leader in advanced AI while protecting Americans' interests, Clayton told the Journal, adding that "the risk of not being first is high." The safety of AI has become a major issue in recent weeks, with some researchers warning that people building the technology believe it could kill humans within a decade. Several Democratic and Republican lawmakers have responded with alarm and calls for more action. Trump has appeared to take a light touch toward AI regulation, arguing that excessive oversight could weaken competitiveness against China. He said on Tuesday that he does not want to work with Chinese President Xi Jinping on governing AI technology. Clayton's panel will review AI-related risks and current government reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks and other incidents, and recommend ways to strengthen federal-response capabilities under existing authorities, the Journal said, citing the task force's charter. This is the second time Trump has named an adviser to oversee AI-related decisions across the administration. Venture capitalist David Sacks held the AI czar role at the beginning of Trump's second term. The task force's vice chairs will be Emil Michael, Scott Kupor and Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, while members will include Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, according to the report. External advisers will also include Sacks and former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, the Journal said. coreStoryFacts.text: President Trump on Sunday named Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as his new "AI czar," adding a different category of intelligence, the "artificial" kind, to the U.S. spy chief's portfolio.

Since leaving the White House, Sacks has "maintained close ties with the president," according to the Guardian, and "in May, he successfully urged Trump to scrap an executive order that would've subjected AI models to government review."
Clayton, 60, is a registered independent with degrees from the University of Pennsylvania (engineering, law) and the University of Cambridge (economics).
As a lawyer in private practice, he focused mostly on Wall Street: mergers and acquisitions, market offerings and regulatory proceedings.

From March 2021 to April 2025, Clayton served as chair and "lead independent director" of the board of Apollo Global Management . (Apollo has owned a 90% majority stake in Yahoo since September 2021.)

In a post on Truth Social , Trump said Clayton will lead a newly formed "Super Intelligence Force" alongside Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor.
The group will report directly to Trump and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.

Its goal, Trump wrote, is "to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans."

Despite new polls showing that 86% of Americans want AI companies to meet independent safety standards even if doing so slows development — with 74% largely mistrusting the leaders of those companies — Trump insisted in recent days that federal regulations are unnecessary and that those who say otherwise are " Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers ."
But Clayton sidestepped questions over who won the 2020 election during his July confirmation hearings, and he was confirmed without Democratic support.
In late 2024, Trump nominated Clayton to serve as U.S.

On Tuesday, Clayton attended Trump's White House meeting with top AI executives.
Speaking afterward to CNBC, he used the president's new preferred term for AI — i.e., "superintelligence " — while pushing back against lawmakers who have called for regulating or pausing U.S.
"I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force , which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term," Trump wrote in his September social media post about naming an AI czar.
Asked to respond to criticism from Democratic Sen.
Clayton, it seems, will now be in charge of cherishing, helping and watching over the AI industry as it grows.
He's "a good man," Trump told Axios when the outlet asked last week if Clayton was being considered for the job .
According to Axios , Trump's AI Force idea "caught advisers by surprise," setting off "a mad dash" within the administration "to imagine what AI Force would look like."
"Whoever wins AI ... that's the group that wins," Trump told the United Nations General Assembly last month .
"We're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way."
As for reining in "bad" actors, he wrote, "we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System."

In the same post, the president again dismissed concerns about AI safety as a "hoax" perpetrated by "Radical Left Democrats." He also wrote that going forward, his administration would not "in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," which he described as "the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet" — only "even larger and more impactful."

The group will report directly to Trump and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles. Its goal, Trump wrote, is "to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans." Clayton will keep his job as DNI, which oversees the nation's 18 intelligence agencies. Trump's announcement follows meeting last Tuesday at the White House where top AI executives signed what he called a " morally binding " agreement to police themselves in order to prevent their increasingly powerful models from going rogue and harming humanity . "There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation," the president said at the meeting. "This is going to be all for the good, and we're going to have it be nice and safe." Despite new polls showing that 86% of Americans want AI companies to meet independent safety standards even if doing so slows development — with 74% largely mistrusting the leaders of those companies — Trump insisted in recent days that federal regulations are unnecessary and that those who say otherwise are " Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers ." "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" he wrote on social media . Elsewhere, Trump has said that regulation would handicap the U.S. in its race to "win" AI. "Whoever wins AI ... that's the group that wins," Trump told the United Nations General Assembly last month . "We're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way." According to the Guardian , Trump's previous AI and crypto czar, billionaire tech investor David Sacks, consistently "counseled the president to give a soft touch to AI regulation, helping push executive orders and other measures aimed at loosening restrictions on the technology." Sacks also "maintains direct financial stakes in multiple AI companies," the paper reported, though he took steps to divest some of his holdings last year while serving in the administration. Clayton, 60, is a registered independent with degrees from the University of Pennsylvania (engineering, law) and the University of Cambridge (economics). As a lawyer in private practice, he focused mostly on Wall Street: mergers and acquisitions, market offerings and regulatory proceedings. From March 2021 to April 2025, Clayton served as chair and "lead independent director" of the board of Apollo Global Management . (Apollo has owned a 90% majority stake in Yahoo since September 2021.) In late 2024, Trump nominated Clayton to serve as U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, his first prosecutorial job; Trump later appointed Clayton to serve in an acting capacity after New York Sen. Chuck Schumer blocked his appointment. Reports suggest Clayton was also considered for roles as secretary of the treasury, attorney general and director of the Central Intelligence Agency. In November 2025, Trump ordered the Department of Justice to investigate Democrats associated with Jeffrey Epstein, and U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi assigned Clayton to lead the probe . After former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard resigned in May 2026, Trump tapped Clayton to replace her. "He's very qualified," Democratic Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia said at the time . But Clayton sidestepped questions over who won the 2020 election during his July confirmation hearings, and he was confirmed without Democratic support. "I'm not an election denier," Clayton told the Senate. "He went through our processes, and Joe Biden became the president of the United States." During his DNI confirmation hearings, Clayton described AI as "a game changer ," warning that it represents "not only an opportunity but a threat." "We should just all recognize that," he continued. "When something is both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it." On Tuesday, Clayton attended Trump's White House meeting with top AI executives. Speaking afterward to CNBC, he used the president's new preferred term for AI — i.e., "superintelligence " — while pushing back against lawmakers who have called for regulating or pausing U.S. AI development. "Super intelligence is a national security issue, and that was something that was recognized yesterday by not just the industry leaders but everybody in the room," Clayton said. "But to, in some way, not try to drive forward inside the United States, with companies that are regulated in the United States ... to somehow say we should back away from this and let the rest of the world develop these models and implement these models? I don't think anybody in that room, and I don't think any American, should think that that's a good strategy." Asked to respond to criticism from Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts that Trump's current policy of letting AI companies police themselves will prove to be "a recipe for disaster," Clayton suggested that the U.S. government's existing regulatory framework could also help keep AI in check. "My response to the American people on that front is we have a Federal Trade Commission, we have a Department of Justice," Clayton said. "I know the leaders of both those organizations, and they're committed to protecting the American people in this regard." According to Trump's post, the Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the federal government's dealings with AI companies, infrastructure providers, consumers, public interest groups and religious organizations, CNN reported . Last month, Trump wrote on social media that he would "be announcing, in the near future, the AI 'Czar.' "Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" he added. Its goal, Trump wrote, is "to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans."
Clayton will keep his job as DNI, which oversees the nation's 18 intelligence agencies.

Trump's announcement follows meeting last Tuesday at the White House where top AI executives signed what he called a " morally binding " agreement to police themselves in order to prevent their increasingly powerful models from going rogue and harming humanity .
"There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation," the president said at the meeting. "This is going to be all for the good, and we're going to have it be nice and safe."

Despite new polls showing that 86% of Americans want AI companies to meet independent safety standards even if doing so slows development — with 74% largely mistrusting the leaders of those companies — Trump insisted in recent days that federal regulations are unnecessary and that those who say otherwise are " Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers ."

"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" he wrote on social media . Elsewhere, Trump has said that regulation would handicap the U.S. in its race to "win" AI.

"Whoever wins AI ... that's the group that wins," Trump told the United Nations General Assembly last month . "We're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way."

According to the Guardian , Trump's previous AI and crypto czar, billionaire tech investor David Sacks, consistently "counseled the president to give a soft touch to AI regulation, helping push executive orders and other measures aimed at loosening restrictions on the technology." Sacks also "maintains direct financial stakes in multiple AI companies," the paper reported, though he took steps to divest some of his holdings last year while serving in the administration. He stepped down in March.
Will Clayton follow Sacks's lead? Or will he chart a new course? Here's what we know so far.

Clayton, 60, is a registered independent with degrees from the University of Pennsylvania (engineering, law) and the University of Cambridge (economics). As a lawyer in private practice, he focused mostly on Wall Street: mergers and acquisitions, market offerings and regulatory proceedings. During Trump's first term, from 2017 to 2020, Clayton chaired the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. From March 2021 to April 2025, Clayton served as chair and "lead independent director" of the board of Apollo Global Management . (Apollo has owned a 90% majority stake in Yahoo since September 2021.)

In late 2024, Trump nominated Clayton to serve as U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, his first prosecutorial job; Trump later appointed Clayton to serve in an acting capacity after New York Sen. Chuck Schumer blocked his appointment. Reports suggest Clayton was also considered for roles as secretary of the treasury, attorney general and director of the Central Intelligence Agency. In November 2025, Trump ordered the Department of Justice to investigate Democrats associated with Jeffrey Epstein, and U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi assigned Clayton to lead the probe .

After former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard resigned in May 2026, Trump tapped Clayton to replace her. "He's very qualified," Democratic Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia said at the time . But Clayton sidestepped questions over who won the 2020 election during his July confirmation hearings, and he was confirmed without Democratic support.
"I'm not an election denier," Clayton told the Senate. "He went through our processes, and Joe Biden became the president of the United States."
During his DNI confirmation hearings, Clayton described AI as "a game changer ," warning that it represents "not only an opportunity but a threat."
"We should just all recognize that," he continued. "When something is both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it."

On Tuesday, Clayton attended Trump's White House meeting with top AI executives. Speaking afterward to CNBC, he used the president's new preferred term for AI — i.e., "superintelligence " — while pushing back against lawmakers who have called for regulating or pausing U.S. AI development.

"Super intelligence is a national security issue, and that was something that was recognized yesterday by not just the industry leaders but everybody in the room," Clayton said. "But to, in some way, not try to drive forward inside the United States, with companies that are regulated in the United States ... to somehow say we should back away from this and let the rest of the world develop these models and implement these models? I don't think anybody in that room, and I don't think any American, should think that that's a good strategy."

Asked to respond to criticism from Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts that Trump's current policy of letting AI companies police themselves will prove to be "a recipe for disaster," Clayton suggested that the U.S. government's existing regulatory framework could also help keep AI in check.

"My response to the American people on that front is we have a Federal Trade Commission, we have a Department of Justice," Clayton said. "I know the leaders of both those organizations, and they're committed to protecting the American people in this regard."

According to Trump's post, the Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the federal government's dealings with AI companies, infrastructure providers, consumers, public interest groups and religious organizations, CNN reported .
Last month, Trump wrote on social media that he would "be announcing, in the near future, the AI 'Czar.'
"Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" he added.

In the same post, the president again dismissed concerns about AI safety as a "hoax" perpetrated by "Radical Left Democrats." He also wrote that going forward, his administration would not "in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," which he described as "the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet" — only "even larger and more impactful."

"Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!" Trump explained. As for reining in "bad" actors, he wrote, "we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System."

Clayton, it seems, will now be in charge of cherishing, helping and watching over the AI industry as it grows. He's "a good man," Trump told Axios when the outlet asked last week if Clayton was being considered for the job . "He's right here. That's a good idea."
It's unclear what happened to a separate idea Trump floated last month, which he called "the AI Force."
"I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force , which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term," Trump wrote in his September social media post about naming an AI czar.
According to Axios , Trump's AI Force idea "caught advisers by surprise," setting off "a mad dash" within the administration "to imagine what AI Force would look like."

When Sacks served as AI czar, he repeatedly persuaded the president and his administration to resist new AI restrictions, including state laws to limit AI . Since leaving the White House, Sacks has "maintained close ties with the president," according to the Guardian, and "in May, he successfully urged Trump to scrap an executive order that would've subjected AI models to government review."

The Wall Street Journal recently reported the Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles were "caught off guard and unhappy" with Trump's decision after they "spent months negotiating to increase oversight of AI and had consulted a range of industry executives on the order." According to the Journal's sources, Wiles "told others that Sacks had persuaded Trump" to back down "in a last-minute call," leaving Bessent "worried that AI-led cyberattacks could wreak havoc on the nation's banking system."

"The president asked that a group be put together," which the administration refers to as the "Super Intelligence Force," to ensure the US remains a leader in advanced AI while protecting Americans' interests, Clayton told the Journal, adding that "the risk of not being first is high." The safety of AI has become a major issue in recent weeks, with some researchers warning that people building the technology believe it could kill humans within a decade. Several Democratic and Republican lawmakers have responded with alarm and calls for more action. Trump has appeared to take a light touch toward AI regulation, arguing that excessive oversight could weaken competitiveness against China. He said on Tuesday that he does not want to work with Chinese President Xi Jinping on governing AI technology. Clayton's panel will review AI-related risks and current government reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks and other incidents, and recommend ways to strengthen federal-response capabilities under existing authorities, the Journal said, citing the task force's charter. This is the second time Trump has named an adviser to oversee AI-related decisions across the administration. Venture capitalist David Sacks held the AI czar role at the beginning of Trump's second term. The task force's vice chairs will be Emil Michael, Scott Kupor and Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, while members will include Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, according to the report. External advisers will also include Sacks and former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, the Journal said. President Trump said Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor, and Emil Michael, undersecretary of war for research and engineering, will lead the task force. The task force is expected to coordinate the government’s engagement with various stakeholders in a growing debate over the risks of AI, including consumers, public interest groups, tech companies, and infrastructure providers. “The Super Intelligence Force is tasked with coordinating the effort of the Federal Government to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” President Trump wrote on Truth Social. sources.title: Trump launches Super Intelligence Force to keep U.S. leading AI, names top officials
passages: President Donald Trump announced a new Super Intelligence Force (SIF) on Sunday and has already picked members who will lead the charge on AI in America.

"We’re going to be signing a document today at about 5 o’clock, renaming artificial intelligence, because it’s not artificial, we all agree on that," Trump said, "we're going to be renaming it super intelligence." Trump's full embrace of the use of artificial intelligence comes as Democrats have called for a halt to further developing the technology over fears it will put Americans out of work or at a disadvantage.
Trump made the announcement on Truth Social this morning, describing that the task force was created in response to his White House Accord on Super Intelligence that he hosted the previous week.

The site is designed to help citizens access federal information and services, such as filling out passport applications online and enrolling in Medicaid. 'Anyone who has used Grok or Gemini or ChatGPT will understand instantly how to use America.gov,' Trump said at an event unveiling the new website.

White House officials have stressed the importance of AI pushing ahead despite those concerns, explaining that American technologists must lead the AI boom to prevent China or other rivals from dominating the space.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump announced a new Super Intelligence Force (SIF) on Sunday and has already picked members who will lead the charge on AI in America. According to Trump, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will lead the task force alongside Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission, Andrew Ferguson, Pentagon Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael and the Director of the Office of Personnel Management, Scott Kupor. The task force is in charge of coordinating the government's engagement with religious organizations, superintelligence providers, consumers and AI companies. Trump said SIF will ensure that America continues to lead the world on AI, which he says, "is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans.' The team, which is led by Clayton, will report to Trump and the White House Chief of Staff, Susie Wiles. Trump made the announcement on Truth Social this morning, describing that the task force was created in response to his White House Accord on Super Intelligence that he hosted the previous week. The president summoned the world's most powerful tech executives to the White House on Tuesday, where he announced that he would be renaming artificial intelligence to super intelligence in all further government communications. "We’re going to be signing a document today at about 5 o’clock, renaming artificial intelligence, because it’s not artificial, we all agree on that," Trump said, "we're going to be renaming it super intelligence." Trump's full embrace of the use of artificial intelligence comes as Democrats have called for a halt to further developing the technology over fears it will put Americans out of work or at a disadvantage. White House officials have stressed the importance of AI pushing ahead despite those concerns, explaining that American technologists must lead the AI boom to prevent China or other rivals from dominating the space. Earlier the same day, the administration rolled out an AI-powered website, America.gov. The site is designed to help citizens access federal information and services, such as filling out passport applications online and enrolling in Medicaid. 'Anyone who has used Grok or Gemini or ChatGPT will understand instantly how to use America.gov,' Trump said at an event unveiling the new website.

sources.title: Trump calls for ‘tremendous self-regulation’ as AI execs sign ‘morally binding’ pact at White House - New York Post
passages: WASHINGTON — President Trump called for “tremendous self-regulation” of artificial intelligence Tuesday at a White House lunch with tech billionaires — where they agreed to a “morally binding” set of principles for the technology.
At the meal, Trump and six of the CEOs signed a one-page document titled the “White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities.”
Amodei, who dined with Trump on Sunday night, this month called for a deliberate slowdown of AI — after doomsday warnings from his former employee Jacob Coxon sparked Democratic calls for regulation.
“The biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it really is a form of protection… I think it’s morally binding.”

Trump fended off questions about polling showing 71% of Americans think the feds are doing too little to regulate AI and about Microsoft founder Bill Gates’ claim Sunday that AI could cause “a billion deaths” if mismanaged.
Trump said there was nothing to fear because the firms would be “policing each other” and “if something goes wrong, their companies are at stake.”
“It’s almost like a constitution in a way,” Trump told a stunned pack of reporters crowded around him and the group of businessmen on the driveway.
The leaders of Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI and XAI signed alongside Trump.
Huang, whom Trump called a “very handsome guy,” said that AI was essential to economic growth and had created about a million jobs in the US.
Trump said the “extremely friendly” lunch, whose bigwigs included Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Palantir CEO Alex Karp, featured “a lot of commonality.”
“I think the technology has very real risks,” Amodei told reporters alongside Trump outside the West Wing.
“We’re leading, and we’re going to keep it that way,” Trump declared.

The tech giants in attendance included Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su, who joined the head table as Trump hosted Xi for a state dinner last week, venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Broadcom CEO Hock Tan and Exiger CEO Brandon Daniels.

WASHINGTON — President Trump called for “tremendous self-regulation” of artificial intelligence Tuesday at a White House lunch with tech billionaires — where they agreed to a “morally binding” set of principles for the technology. Trump hosted nearly two dozen business titans in the East Room before surprising journalists by walking his guests onto the driveway outside the West Wing for a 33-minute impromptu press conference. “There’s a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation,” Trump said during the lunch as he sat between Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang on his right and XAI’s Elon Musk and Google’s Sundar Pichai to his left. “We automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that. But the self-regulation is very important.” At the meal, Trump and six of the CEOs signed a one-page document titled the “White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities.” “It’s almost like a constitution in a way,” Trump told a stunned pack of reporters crowded around him and the group of businessmen on the driveway. “The biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it really is a form of protection… I think it’s morally binding.” The leaders of Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI and XAI signed alongside Trump. The accord commits the firms to “four layers” of safeguards, including establishing internal controls to monitor risks to “cybersecurity, biosecurity, and chemical threats, and to ensure that its models do not hack or access technical systems in unintended ways.” Companies will then designate internal teams to track compliance. External auditors will conduct independent reviews, with a committee of each company’s board of directors in charge of “ensur[ing] any issues identified are remediated.” The six companies “will meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems,” the document says, adding, “Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations.” Zuckerberg said the agreement would yield “multiple layers of auditing and controls, starting with internal risk review, external auditors and evaluators, and agreeing that we’re going to have all of our boards of directors independently review the reports that come from the auditors.” “The idea isn’t that this is the only thing that we will ever do. It is that this is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to,” Zuckerberg said. Huang, whom Trump called a “very handsome guy,” said that AI was essential to economic growth and had created about a million jobs in the US. “There’s no conflict between innovation, technology, and safety,” Huang said. “You see behind me just an incredible number of leaders in our industry moving together as one, and we’re going to advance this technology that is so consequential to humanity, so consequential to the future prosperity of our nation. We’re going to do it responsibly and safely.” Pichai, jokingly introduced by the president as a “monster,” said “we are signing up to a set of processes and controls, like we do in other areas like financial controls.” Trump fended off questions about polling showing 71% of Americans think the feds are doing too little to regulate AI and about Microsoft founder Bill Gates’ claim Sunday that AI could cause “a billion deaths” if mismanaged. Trump said there was nothing to fear because the firms would be “policing each other” and “if something goes wrong, their companies are at stake.” Trump said that if he learned of catastrophic threats, “I’d come out here, I’d hold a news conference, and I’d let the world know about it.” Trump hosted the unusual driveway press conference shortly before signing orders renaming the technology as “super intelligence ” — a term he pushed last week at the United Nations and during meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The new terminology will be used in official communications, but there’s no guarantee of wider adoption. Trump said the “extremely friendly” lunch, whose bigwigs included Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Palantir CEO Alex Karp, featured “a lot of commonality.” Amodei, who dined with Trump on Sunday night, this month called for a deliberate slowdown of AI — after doomsday warnings from his former employee Jacob Coxon sparked Democratic calls for regulation. “I think the technology has very real risks,” Amodei told reporters alongside Trump outside the West Wing. The president basked in the presence of the famous tech pioneers — many of whom were invited to his inauguration last year, despite some of the cohort censoring and deplatforming him following the 2021 Capitol riot. “These are the greatest, the most brilliant people probably in the world,” he said. “The job they’ve done is unbelievable. We have a very big lead, and we’re going to keep our lead, and it’s a very positive thing. It’s an amazing industry.” “We’re leading, and we’re going to keep it that way,” Trump declared. “It’s not artificial. We all agree on that, and we’re going to be renaming it super intelligence, officially renaming it.” Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more. Trump also said that AI companies would make more of an effort to win over reluctant neighbors of massive new data centers springing up around the country. “They’re going to do things for the community that will be really financially beneficial and otherwise beneficial,” he said. “The one thing that we all have in common is we love our country, and we love the world, and we want to make sure it’s a safe place. And what we’re talking about today will make it a better place and a much safer place.” The tech giants in attendance included Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su, who joined the head table as Trump hosted Xi for a state dinner last week, venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Broadcom CEO Hock Tan and Exiger CEO Brandon Daniels.

WASHINGTON — President Trump called for “tremendous self-regulation” of artificial intelligence Tuesday at a White House lunch with tech billionaires — where they agreed to a “morally binding” set of principles for the technology.
Trump hosted nearly two dozen business titans in the East Room before surprising journalists by walking his guests onto the driveway outside the West Wing for a 33-minute impromptu press conference.

“There’s a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation,” Trump said during the lunch as he sat between Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang on his right and XAI’s Elon Musk and Google’s Sundar Pichai to his left.
“We automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that. But the self-regulation is very important.”
At the meal, Trump and six of the CEOs signed a one-page document titled the “White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities.”
“It’s almost like a constitution in a way,” Trump told a stunned pack of reporters crowded around him and the group of businessmen on the driveway.
“The biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it really is a form of protection… I think it’s morally binding.”
The leaders of Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI and XAI signed alongside Trump.

The accord commits the firms to “four layers” of safeguards, including establishing internal controls to monitor risks to “cybersecurity, biosecurity, and chemical threats, and to ensure that its models do not hack or access technical systems in unintended ways.”

Companies will then designate internal teams to track compliance. External auditors will conduct independent reviews, with a committee of each company’s board of directors in charge of “ensur[ing] any issues identified are remediated.”

The six companies “will meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems,” the document says, adding, “Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations.”

Zuckerberg said the agreement would yield “multiple layers of auditing and controls, starting with internal risk review, external auditors and evaluators, and agreeing that we’re going to have all of our boards of directors independently review the reports that come from the auditors.”
“The idea isn’t that this is the only thing that we will ever do. It is that this is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to,” Zuckerberg said.
Huang, whom Trump called a “very handsome guy,” said that AI was essential to economic growth and had created about a million jobs in the US.
“There’s no conflict between innovation, technology, and safety,” Huang said.

“You see behind me just an incredible number of leaders in our industry moving together as one, and we’re going to advance this technology that is so consequential to humanity, so consequential to the future prosperity of our nation. We’re going to do it responsibly and safely.”
Pichai, jokingly introduced by the president as a “monster,” said “we are signing up to a set of processes and controls, like we do in other areas like financial controls.”

Trump fended off questions about polling showing 71% of Americans think the feds are doing too little to regulate AI and about Microsoft founder Bill Gates’ claim Sunday that AI could cause “a billion deaths” if mismanaged.
Trump said there was nothing to fear because the firms would be “policing each other” and “if something goes wrong, their companies are at stake.”
Trump said that if he learned of catastrophic threats, “I’d come out here, I’d hold a news conference, and I’d let the world know about it.”

Trump hosted the unusual driveway press conference shortly before signing orders renaming the technology as “super intelligence ” — a term he pushed last week at the United Nations and during meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
The new terminology will be used in official communications, but there’s no guarantee of wider adoption.
Trump said the “extremely friendly” lunch, whose bigwigs included Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Palantir CEO Alex Karp, featured “a lot of commonality.”
Amodei, who dined with Trump on Sunday night, this month called for a deliberate slowdown of AI — after doomsday warnings from his former employee Jacob Coxon sparked Democratic calls for regulation.
“I think the technology has very real risks,” Amodei told reporters alongside Trump outside the West Wing.

The president basked in the presence of the famous tech pioneers — many of whom were invited to his inauguration last year, despite some of the cohort censoring and deplatforming him following the 2021 Capitol riot.
“These are the greatest, the most brilliant people probably in the world,” he said.
“The job they’ve done is unbelievable. We have a very big lead, and we’re going to keep our lead, and it’s a very positive thing. It’s an amazing industry.”
“We’re leading, and we’re going to keep it that way,” Trump declared.
“It’s not artificial. We all agree on that, and we’re going to be renaming it super intelligence, officially renaming it.”

Trump also said that AI companies would make more of an effort to win over reluctant neighbors of massive new data centers springing up around the country.
“They’re going to do things for the community that will be really financially beneficial and otherwise beneficial,” he said.

“The one thing that we all have in common is we love our country, and we love the world, and we want to make sure it’s a safe place. And what we’re talking about today will make it a better place and a much safer place.”

The tech giants in attendance included Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su, who joined the head table as Trump hosted Xi for a state dinner last week, venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Broadcom CEO Hock Tan and Exiger CEO Brandon Daniels.

Trump announced the squad on Sunday after repeatedly blasting attempts to curb the booming technology over fears it could eventually threaten humanity. In another fiery Truth Social post, Trump compared fears of an AI apocalypse to “many Hoaxes, all generated by the Radical Left Dumocrats”. The President added: “AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25 per cent of our Country’s GDP.” Trump has now put Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton in charge of his new Super Intelligence Force. He will lead the powerful squad alongside Federal Trade Commission chairman Andrew Ferguson, Pentagon chief technology officer Emil Michael and Office of Personnel Management director Scott Kupor. White House officials have also stressed that US AI labs must continue pushing ahead despite mounting warnings about the risks. Democrat Senator Bernie Sanders has meanwhile called for a halt to further AI development amid fears over the impact on American jobs . China has also criticised calls to curb development as “fearmongering” designed to stunt its growth. The bitter AI rivalry is expected to be a major talking point when Trump meets Chinese President Xi Jinping next week. Trump has not said whether his new force will be military or civilian, although he has previously compared it to the creation of the US Space Force. His administration has also rolled out AI-powered America.gov to help Americans access federal information and services online. Trump said: “Anyone who has used Grok or Gemini or ChatGPT will understand instantly how to use America.gov.” The President also said tech bosses had signed what was “almost a Constitution, in a way” covering the rapidly advancing technology. Trump has said his new force will “cherish” and “watch over” the booming industry while also looking for wrongdoing. When first announcing plans for the task force, the President said he was screening candidates to lead it, adding that “only High I.Q. individuals need apply”. coreStoryFacts.text: President Donald Trump announced that he would name four top administration officials to a “Super Intelligence Force” that will coordinate the federal government’s response to artificial intelligence.

President Trump said Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor, and Emil Michael, undersecretary of war for research and engineering, will lead the task force.
Benton Institute for Broadband & Society 1041 Ridge Rd, Unit 214 Wilmette, IL 60091
President Donald Trump announced a new Super Intelligence Force (SIF) on Sunday and has already picked members who will lead the charge on AI in America.

"We’re going to be signing a document today at about 5 o’clock, renaming artificial intelligence, because it’s not artificial, we all agree on that," Trump said, "we're going to be renaming it super intelligence." Trump's full embrace of the use of artificial intelligence comes as Democrats have called for a halt to further developing the technology over fears it will put Americans out of work or at a disadvantage.
Trump made the announcement on Truth Social this morning, describing that the task force was created in response to his White House Accord on Super Intelligence that he hosted the previous week.

The site is designed to help citizens access federal information and services, such as filling out passport applications online and enrolling in Medicaid. 'Anyone who has used Grok or Gemini or ChatGPT will understand instantly how to use America.gov,' Trump said at an event unveiling the new website.

White House officials have stressed the importance of AI pushing ahead despite those concerns, explaining that American technologists must lead the AI boom to prevent China or other rivals from dominating the space.

WASHINGTON — President Trump called for “tremendous self-regulation” of artificial intelligence Tuesday at a White House lunch with tech billionaires — where they agreed to a “morally binding” set of principles for the technology.
At the meal, Trump and six of the CEOs signed a one-page document titled the “White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities.”
Amodei, who dined with Trump on Sunday night, this month called for a deliberate slowdown of AI — after doomsday warnings from his former employee Jacob Coxon sparked Democratic calls for regulation.
“The biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it really is a form of protection… I think it’s morally binding.”

Trump fended off questions about polling showing 71% of Americans think the feds are doing too little to regulate AI and about Microsoft founder Bill Gates’ claim Sunday that AI could cause “a billion deaths” if mismanaged.
Trump said there was nothing to fear because the firms would be “policing each other” and “if something goes wrong, their companies are at stake.”
“It’s almost like a constitution in a way,” Trump told a stunned pack of reporters crowded around him and the group of businessmen on the driveway.
The leaders of Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI and XAI signed alongside Trump.
Huang, whom Trump called a “very handsome guy,” said that AI was essential to economic growth and had created about a million jobs in the US.
Trump said the “extremely friendly” lunch, whose bigwigs included Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Palantir CEO Alex Karp, featured “a lot of commonality.”
“I think the technology has very real risks,” Amodei told reporters alongside Trump outside the West Wing.
“We’re leading, and we’re going to keep it that way,” Trump declared.

The tech giants in attendance included Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su, who joined the head table as Trump hosted Xi for a state dinner last week, venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Broadcom CEO Hock Tan and Exiger CEO Brandon Daniels.

WASHINGTON — President Trump called for “tremendous self-regulation” of artificial intelligence Tuesday at a White House lunch with tech billionaires — where they agreed to a “morally binding” set of principles for the technology. Trump hosted nearly two dozen business titans in the East Room before surprising journalists by walking his guests onto the driveway outside the West Wing for a 33-minute impromptu press conference. “There’s a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation,” Trump said during the lunch as he sat between Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang on his right and XAI’s Elon Musk and Google’s Sundar Pichai to his left. “We automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that. But the self-regulation is very important.” At the meal, Trump and six of the CEOs signed a one-page document titled the “White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities.” “It’s almost like a constitution in a way,” Trump told a stunned pack of reporters crowded around him and the group of businessmen on the driveway. “The biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it really is a form of protection… I think it’s morally binding.” The leaders of Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI and XAI signed alongside Trump. The accord commits the firms to “four layers” of safeguards, including establishing internal controls to monitor risks to “cybersecurity, biosecurity, and chemical threats, and to ensure that its models do not hack or access technical systems in unintended ways.” Companies will then designate internal teams to track compliance. External auditors will conduct independent reviews, with a committee of each company’s board of directors in charge of “ensur[ing] any issues identified are remediated.” The six companies “will meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems,” the document says, adding, “Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations.” Zuckerberg said the agreement would yield “multiple layers of auditing and controls, starting with internal risk review, external auditors and evaluators, and agreeing that we’re going to have all of our boards of directors independently review the reports that come from the auditors.” “The idea isn’t that this is the only thing that we will ever do. It is that this is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to,” Zuckerberg said. Huang, whom Trump called a “very handsome guy,” said that AI was essential to economic growth and had created about a million jobs in the US. “There’s no conflict between innovation, technology, and safety,” Huang said. “You see behind me just an incredible number of leaders in our industry moving together as one, and we’re going to advance this technology that is so consequential to humanity, so consequential to the future prosperity of our nation. We’re going to do it responsibly and safely.” Pichai, jokingly introduced by the president as a “monster,” said “we are signing up to a set of processes and controls, like we do in other areas like financial controls.” Trump fended off questions about polling showing 71% of Americans think the feds are doing too little to regulate AI and about Microsoft founder Bill Gates’ claim Sunday that AI could cause “a billion deaths” if mismanaged. Trump said there was nothing to fear because the firms would be “policing each other” and “if something goes wrong, their companies are at stake.” Trump said that if he learned of catastrophic threats, “I’d come out here, I’d hold a news conference, and I’d let the world know about it.” Trump hosted the unusual driveway press conference shortly before signing orders renaming the technology as “super intelligence ” — a term he pushed last week at the United Nations and during meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The new terminology will be used in official communications, but there’s no guarantee of wider adoption. Trump said the “extremely friendly” lunch, whose bigwigs included Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Palantir CEO Alex Karp, featured “a lot of commonality.” Amodei, who dined with Trump on Sunday night, this month called for a deliberate slowdown of AI — after doomsday warnings from his former employee Jacob Coxon sparked Democratic calls for regulation. “I think the technology has very real risks,” Amodei told reporters alongside Trump outside the West Wing. The president basked in the presence of the famous tech pioneers — many of whom were invited to his inauguration last year, despite some of the cohort censoring and deplatforming him following the 2021 Capitol riot. “These are the greatest, the most brilliant people probably in the world,” he said. “The job they’ve done is unbelievable. We have a very big lead, and we’re going to keep our lead, and it’s a very positive thing. It’s an amazing industry.” “We’re leading, and we’re going to keep it that way,” Trump declared. “It’s not artificial. We all agree on that, and we’re going to be renaming it super intelligence, officially renaming it.” Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more. Trump also said that AI companies would make more of an effort to win over reluctant neighbors of massive new data centers springing up around the country. “They’re going to do things for the community that will be really financially beneficial and otherwise beneficial,” he said. “The one thing that we all have in common is we love our country, and we love the world, and we want to make sure it’s a safe place. And what we’re talking about today will make it a better place and a much safer place.” The tech giants in attendance included Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su, who joined the head table as Trump hosted Xi for a state dinner last week, venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Broadcom CEO Hock Tan and Exiger CEO Brandon Daniels.

Trump announced the squad on Sunday after repeatedly blasting attempts to curb the booming technology over fears it could eventually threaten humanity. In a speech shared by the White House on X, the President declared: “I am announcing the formation of the Super Intelligence Force (SIF).” You'll now receive top stories, breaking news, and more, straight to your email. Trump vowed the new force would “ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence” and “protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans.” But his bullish AI push comes despite stark warnings from within the industry about the dangers posed by increasingly powerful systems. US withdraws all bomber jets from RAF Fairford a week after 'terror plot' But Trump has refused to slam the brakes on America’s AI revolution and previously branded opposition to its development a “sick conspiracy” that would benefit China. In another fiery Truth Social post, Trump compared fears of an AI apocalypse to “many Hoaxes, all generated by the Radical Left Dumocrats”. The President added: “AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25 per cent of our Country’s GDP.” Trump has now put Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton in charge of his new Super Intelligence Force. He will lead the powerful squad alongside Federal Trade Commission chairman Andrew Ferguson, Pentagon chief technology officer Emil Michael and Office of Personnel Management director Scott Kupor. The team will report directly to Trump and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles while coordinating the government’s dealings with AI companies and other groups. Trump revealed the force on Truth Social following his White House Accord on Super Intelligence last week. It comes after the President summoned some of the world’s most powerful tech bosses to the White House on Tuesday for crunch talks over the technology. OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, X boss Elon Musk , Google chief Sundar Pichai and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos were also present. Trump used the gathering to announce his administration would ditch the term “artificial intelligence” and instead call it “super intelligence”. The President said: “We’re going to be signing a document today at about 5 o’clock, renaming artificial intelligence, because it’s not artificial, we all agree on that.” Trump continued: “We’re going to be renaming it super intelligence.” Musk even corrected himself after mistakenly referring to the technology as “AI” while Trump was watching, prompting the President to laugh and thank him. Trump has insisted America must charge ahead with developing the technology or risk allowing China to seize the upper hand. White House officials have also stressed that US AI labs must continue pushing ahead despite mounting warnings about the risks. Democrat Senator Bernie Sanders has meanwhile called for a halt to further AI development amid fears over the impact on American jobs . But Trump has shown no appetite for slowing down as Washington and Beijing battle for technological supremacy. China has also criticised calls to curb development as “fearmongering” designed to stunt its growth. The bitter AI rivalry is expected to be a major talking point when Trump meets Chinese President Xi Jinping next week. Trump has not said whether his new force will be military or civilian, although he has previously compared it to the creation of the US Space Force. His administration has also rolled out AI-powered America.gov to help Americans access federal information and services online. Trump said: “Anyone who has used Grok or Gemini or ChatGPT will understand instantly how to use America.gov.” The President also said tech bosses had signed what was “almost a Constitution, in a way” covering the rapidly advancing technology. Trump has said his new force will “cherish” and “watch over” the booming industry while also looking for wrongdoing. When first announcing plans for the task force, the President said he was screening candidates to lead it, adding that “only High I.Q. individuals need apply”.
