Former leader Hashim Thaçi was convicted on a plethora of war crimes and sentenced to 25 years in prison.
Thaçi previously served as the state’s first prime minister, the political director of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), and as Kosovo's president at the time of his indictment in 2020.

While Thaçi and his three fellow defendants intend to appeal the judgment and believe they may yet walk free, its pronouncement provides a unique and useful opportunity to reflect on the social and political ramifications of yet another post-Yugoslav courtroom drama.

His role as a founding father of his country extended beyond the war, leading it to independence and later steering it to a pro-European course diplomatically engaged with non-recognizing neighbor Serbia before his arrest.
The prosecutor was Jack Smith, a man with a unique career path perhaps better known to readers for cases closer to home.

The meeting, which presented an unprecedented opportunity for high stakes talks between the leader of Serbia and that of its now-unrecognized former province, both with European inclinations, was scuttled, as Thaçi surrendered to face charges.
Kurti’s crusade evolved into his party, Vetëvendosje (LVV), or Self-Determination.
Gaughan is a first-year graduate student in the International Affairs program at The George Washington University.

While Euroscepticism has raged within EU member and candidate states for years and faith in U.S. reliability repeatedly shaken in the twenty-first century, Kosovo citizens’ support for the EU and the U.S. has traditionally polled around or above 90 percent.

Thaçi previously served as the state’s first prime minister, the political director of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), and as Kosovo's president at the time of his indictment in 2020. He is among the state’s most revered personas, and was long seen as one of the West’s most reliable partners. While Thaçi and his three fellow defendants intend to appeal the judgment and believe they may yet walk free, its pronouncement provides a unique and useful opportunity to reflect on the social and political ramifications of yet another post-Yugoslav courtroom drama. Kosovo is a unique state for many reasons. It was the site of mass crackdowns and repression by the Milošević regime in its latter days from 1998 to 1999 that triggered a war and ended with a 78-day bombing campaign of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia by NATO. Today, a lack of official UN and other recognition, stemming from continued disputes with and rejection by Serbia, the state from which it seceded in February 2008, have left it in a political void, with attempts to win entry into international organizations routinely obstructed. Hashim Thaçi served as the adored political director of the KLA during the war, winning the hearts of his countrymen and of the West. His role as a founding father of his country extended beyond the war, leading it to independence and later steering it to a pro-European course diplomatically engaged with non-recognizing neighbor Serbia before his arrest. In 2020, the chief prosecutor for the Kosovo Specialist Chamber – a court technically under Kosovar law but based in the Hague, staffed by international judges and lawyers, deeply unpopular within Kosovo but very popular among European governments – filed the charges. The prosecutor was Jack Smith, a man with a unique career path perhaps better known to readers for cases closer to home. These proceedings followed the 2019 friendly presentation of a national award to former President Clinton and came as Thaçi was en route to Washington for a meeting with then-President Trump and Serbian President (and Kosovo War-era FRY information minister ) Aleksandar Vučić. The meeting, which presented an unprecedented opportunity for high stakes talks between the leader of Serbia and that of its now-unrecognized former province, both with European inclinations, was scuttled, as Thaçi surrendered to face charges. Six years later, as Kosovar leaders predicted the acquittal of their ally or rival (depending on political camp), the small country was shaken to see him handed a quarter-century imprisonment for war crimes relating to alleged KLA kidnappings and extrajudicial killings. One unifier among Kosovar Albanian leadership, who represent the overwhelming majority ethnic background of the former Serbian province, was objection. Despite two inconclusive parliamentary elections since early 2025, Kosovo’s political leaders joined together in their public opposition to the judgment against one of their own. The Kosovar parliament voted 99-0 to condemn the judgment on September 28. One clear winner from this verdict will be Kosovo’s incumbent PM, Albin Kurti, whose populist party has successfully rivaled Thaçi’s more moderate, pro-European outlook. Thaçi and Kurti have been rivals since their shared days as rebels of the Kosovo war; while the former led the political sector of the KLA, the latter led a student movement more averse to dialogue and reconciliation. Kurti’s crusade evolved into his party, Vetëvendosje (LVV), or Self-Determination. From the war years to their tense days as president and prime minister together, Thaçi has routinely sought to ingratiate the EU and negotiate with Belgrade while Kurti has sought to underscore Prishtina’s independence and aversion to compromise on Kosovar sovereignty. The prevention of Thaçi’s return to the political scene must undoubtedly offer relief to the embattled PM, who has narrowly managed to maintain his office after two subsequent elections without a clear majority in the country’s 120-seat assembly. Parallel and seemingly detached from the dialogue among Kosovo’s angry domestic and diasporic population is that among Serbians. Serbian officials — who just weeks ago mourned the death of convicted genocidaire General Ratko Mladić, known for his brutality in the Bosnian War (and particularly, the Srebrenica massacre and siege of Sarajevo) — have criticized the sentences (ranging between 13 and 25 years) for being too lenient, compared to the prosecution’s requested 45. Serbia continues to play a major role in Kosovo’s affairs as its former home, wartime adversary, and current obstacle to international recognition. Meanwhile, the question may have been opened — for the first time — of whether Kosovar faith in the West can be shaken. While Euroscepticism has raged within EU member and candidate states for years and faith in U.S. reliability repeatedly shaken in the twenty-first century, Kosovo citizens’ support for the EU and the U.S. has traditionally polled around or above 90 percent. As Western judges weighed and continue to weigh the fate of Kosovo’s path-charting leader, it is worth watching whether such a significant new development can shake so strong a partnership. American leaders would do well to consider the extent to which they should involve themselves in the small Balkan nation where their country is perhaps most popular, as Trump administration ally Richard Grenell has regularly commented in defense of Thaçi, and opposition to Kurti. For now, policymakers and diplomats should treat such legacies of the conflict with the sensitivity they deserve while promoting what dialogue and diplomacy can be found in a deeply divided region. In a time of such political turmoil, the United States must be wary of forgetting or forsaking even its smallest allies, especially one so loyal. Despite political distractions at home and abroad, policymakers in the State Department, Congress, and the EU should at the very least project interest in the trial’s outcome, whether through reaffirmation of the court and for Kosovo’s other state institutions, its leaders, or both. They must express, and through diplomatic engagement, prove their continued motivation to assist Prishtina in its reforms, and its drive to gain recognition on the world stage. Stephen R. Israeli media has reported that the co-pilot intended to crash the aircraft on Israeli territory. Critics have focused on how a pilot from a country with no diplomatic relations with Israel was cleared to operate a flight bound for Tel Aviv. Transport Minister Miri Regev rejected responsibility for the failure, saying security oversight for flights operated by foreign airlines falls under the remit of the Mossad and Shin Bet, Israel’s foreign and domestic intelligence agencies. A 2024 report by the state comptroller found there was no clear division of responsibility for the security of foreign airlines operating in Israel, and recommended that the government address the issue. Israeli media have reported that pilots from countries hostile to Israel have repeatedly flown into the country in recent years. Keren Terner, who previously served as director-general of the transport ministry and is now running for Parliament for the opposition, blamed Regev for the security failure, noting that the Civil Aviation Authority was under the “direct subordination” of her ministry. “You are responsible for the security of foreign companies. Not the Shin Bet, not Mossad. You. That’s what the government decided, and that’s what the law stipulates,” Terner wrote on X. Opposition leader Yair Lapid dismissed Netanyahu’s announcement of a security review as a “sham investigation”. “The chain of failures that preceded the incident could have led to a disaster of historic proportions, and this is how an Israeli prime minister responds?” Lapid wrote on X. “Just as Netanyahu escaped an investigation into the October 7 massacre, he is now running away again,” he added. Gadi Eisenkot, a leading challenger to Netanyahu ahead of the Oct 27 election, wrote on X that “in a proper and functioning government, the minister of transportation would have submitted a letter of resignation last night”. (Sponsor) When it comes to investing in cryptocurrency, how much should you own at different ages—like 30, 55, or 70? Traditional investing guidelines, such as "100 minus your age," suggest that a 30-year-old should have 70% in stocks and a 70-year-old should have 30%. However, crypto like Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) challenges these rules, requiring a fresh approach. While stocks have decades of data to analyze past market crashes and recoveries, Bitcoin has only about 17 years of history and doesn't pay interest or dividends like bonds and stocks do. Its value can fluctuate wildly, leading to significant gains or severe losses. Therefore, a more practical question is how much you could afford to lose without impacting your lifestyle. This becomes particularly important as you approach retirement. Investors typically shift their portfolios from stocks to bonds and cash as they get older. This shift is predicated on a decreasing time frame before they start withdrawing funds. While age often signals that shrinking timeline, your time horizon should ultimately dictate how much crypto you can comfortably hold. For instance, a 30-year-old who sees their investment drop by 70% can afford to wait it out; their paycheck can still cover living expenses. They can hold onto their crypto, with plenty of time for the market to recover. Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. The saving is done, the portfolio is built, and the question quietly changes from how much can I grow this to how much can I take out? Get that second question wrong and decades of good investing can come apart in a handful of years. That is exactly what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps answer. It covers what your retirement could actually cost, which income sources are worth using, and the withdrawal math that decides whether the money lasts. It is free today from Fisher Investments. Read More Here › In contrast, a retiree counts on their savings to pay monthly bills regardless of market fluctuations. If this retiree has to sell during a market downturn to cover expenses, their temporary paper loss converts into a permanent one, as they miss out on any potential market recovery. This is known as sequence-of-returns risk, where the timing of returns plays a crucial role in long-term investment success. The volatility of crypto can make this risk even more pronounced. For example, Bitcoin fell about 77% from its peak of around $69,000 in November 2021 to about $15,500 a year later. As of October 4, 2026, Bitcoin trades near $85,000, but that remains roughly 33% below its record of around $126,000 in October 2025. The amount of crypto you hold significantly influences how much a downturn impacts your finances. For a retiree with an $800,000 portfolio, allocating 2% to crypto means holding $16,000. A 77% drop in value means they lose about $12,000—painful, but it leaves their monthly income largely untouched. However, if that same retiree has 20% in crypto, they stand to lose approximately $123,000, a loss that could force them to cut back on essentials like spending or housing. The timing of these downturns also worsens the situation. A market crash early in retirement is particularly harmful, as selling coins at low prices to cover immediate bills misses the chance to recover later. Major investment firms have laid out a framework for crypto allocation. For instance, Morgan Stanley's Global Investment Committee announced in October 2025 that aggressive growth portfolios might include up to 4% in crypto, while income-oriented portfolios should hold none. Similarly, BlackRock suggested that 1% to 2% in Bitcoin is a reasonable guideline. These recommendations correspond to three key stages of an investor's life: Young Investors (Early Career) : With many years of paychecks ahead, they can afford to take on more risk, often nearing the upper end of the 0% to 4% allocation range. Approaching Retirement : With fewer years to recover from volatility, this group should gradually reduce their crypto holdings as they near retirement. Retirees : Living off their savings requires a cautious approach, making it essential to limit crypto exposure to a level that insulates their income from drastic losses. Additionally, a crypto market rally can inadvertently push an allocation beyond recommended limits. For example, if Bitcoin rises from $15,500 to $85,000, a 2% holding could transform into 10% of a portfolio if other investments remain stable. This is why experts like Morgan Stanley emphasize the importance of regular rebalancing. Your ideal crypto investment is whatever amount you could afford to lose without affecting your lifestyle, typically between 0% and 4% of your overall portfolio. Younger investors can lean toward the higher end, while those nearing retirement should adjust downwards, and retirees should minimize exposure to ensure their monthly expenses won't be impacted. Keep in mind that this approach may limit potential gains. A retiree with just 1% in Bitcoin might miss out on significant profit if the coin appreciates rapidly. Major life changes, such as retiring early, losing a pension, or experiencing a crypto boom, can all affect this calculation. Regularly reassessing your crypto allocation is essential to stay aligned with your financial goals. So how much crypto should you own after a big life change? While stocks have decades of data to analyze past market crashes and recoveries, Bitcoin has only about 17 years of history and doesn't pay interest or dividends like bonds and stocks do. Its value can fluctuate wildly, leading to significant gains or severe losses. Therefore, a more practical question is how much you could afford to lose without impacting your lifestyle. This becomes particularly important as you approach retirement.

Investors typically shift their portfolios from stocks to bonds and cash as they get older. This shift is predicated on a decreasing time frame before they start withdrawing funds. While age often signals that shrinking timeline, your time horizon should ultimately dictate how much crypto you can comfortably hold.

For instance, a 30-year-old who sees their investment drop by 70% can afford to wait it out; their paycheck can still cover living expenses. They can hold onto their crypto, with plenty of time for the market to recover.

Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. The saving is done, the portfolio is built, and the question quietly changes from how much can I grow this to how much can I take out? Get that second question wrong and decades of good investing can come apart in a handful of years.

In contrast, a retiree counts on their savings to pay monthly bills regardless of market fluctuations. If this retiree has to sell during a market downturn to cover expenses, their temporary paper loss converts into a permanent one, as they miss out on any potential market recovery. This is known as sequence-of-returns risk, where the timing of returns plays a crucial role in long-term investment success.

The volatility of crypto can make this risk even more pronounced. For example, Bitcoin fell about 77% from its peak of around $69,000 in November 2021 to about $15,500 a year later. As of October 4, 2026, Bitcoin trades near $85,000, but that remains roughly 33% below its record of around $126,000 in October 2025.

The amount of crypto you hold significantly influences how much a downturn impacts your finances. For a retiree with an $800,000 portfolio, allocating 2% to crypto means holding $16,000. A 77% drop in value means they lose about $12,000—painful, but it leaves their monthly income largely untouched.
However, if that same retiree has 20% in crypto, they stand to lose approximately $123,000, a loss that could force them to cut back on essentials like spending or housing.

The timing of these downturns also worsens the situation. A market crash early in retirement is particularly harmful, as selling coins at low prices to cover immediate bills misses the chance to recover later.

Major investment firms have laid out a framework for crypto allocation. For instance, Morgan Stanley's Global Investment Committee announced in October 2025 that aggressive growth portfolios might include up to 4% in crypto, while income-oriented portfolios should hold none. Similarly, BlackRock suggested that 1% to 2% in Bitcoin is a reasonable guideline.
These recommendations correspond to three key stages of an investor's life:
Young Investors (Early Career) : With many years of paychecks ahead, they can afford to take on more risk, often nearing the upper end of the 0% to 4% allocation range.
Approaching Retirement : With fewer years to recover from volatility, this group should gradually reduce their crypto holdings as they near retirement.
Retirees : Living off their savings requires a cautious approach, making it essential to limit crypto exposure to a level that insulates their income from drastic losses.

Additionally, a crypto market rally can inadvertently push an allocation beyond recommended limits. For example, if Bitcoin rises from $15,500 to $85,000, a 2% holding could transform into 10% of a portfolio if other investments remain stable. This is why experts like Morgan Stanley emphasize the importance of regular rebalancing.

Your ideal crypto investment is whatever amount you could afford to lose without affecting your lifestyle, typically between 0% and 4% of your overall portfolio. Younger investors can lean toward the higher end, while those nearing retirement should adjust downwards, and retirees should minimize exposure to ensure their monthly expenses won't be impacted.

Keep in mind that this approach may limit potential gains. A retiree with just 1% in Bitcoin might miss out on significant profit if the coin appreciates rapidly. Major life changes, such as retiring early, losing a pension, or experiencing a crypto boom, can all affect this calculation. Regularly reassessing your crypto allocation is essential to stay aligned with your financial goals. So how much crypto should you own after a big life change?

passages: In our latest analysis, we asked AI models—ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini— to evaluate which cryptocurrency among Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC), Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH), and XRP (CRYPTO: XRP) is likely to bounce back to its all-time high first.
All three models gave the same ranking: Bitcoin led, followed by Ethereum, with XRP trailing.
ChatGPT predicts Bitcoin could close 2026 around $100,000, Ethereum at approximately $3,400, and XRP near $2.05.
Similarly, Gemini projects year-end prices of $108,500, $3,450, and $2.15, respectively.
ChatGPT assigned XRP only a 15% probability, while Gemini placed it at just 8%.
It has the smallest gap to cover, the largest amount of invested funds, and the smallest decline over the past year—down about 30%, compared with Ethereum's 38% and XRP's 50% drops.
The immediate critical test for Bitcoin is to surpass its recent high of $87,500, followed by the significant threshold of $100,000.
If Bitcoin falls below $80,000, it could hinder its progress and allow Ethereum to narrow its gap further.
If Ethereum exceeds $4,946 before Bitcoin returns to $126,080, it would suggest the AI models may have miscalculated the recovery order.
Grok noted that U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs), which hold Bitcoin and trade similarly to shares, have approximately $108 billion in assets.
In comparison, Ethereum funds have $17.8 billion, and XRP funds only $1.8 billion.
Grok mentioned that these funds hold nearly 6% of Bitcoin's total supply.
While the models agreed on the order, they differed in confidence.
This raises an interesting question: how much should we rely on these AI predictions when all three cryptocurrencies remain significantly below their previous peaks?
To reach their former highs, Bitcoin needs a gain of about 49%, Ethereum requires around 83%, and XRP must climb approximately 145%.
As a result, the ranking aligns almost perfectly with the size of the gap each cryptocurrency must close.
In terms of recent performance, Ethereum has shown more significant growth.
This shows Ethereum is closing the gap faster than Bitcoin and XRP.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Even optimistic year-end forecasts put Bitcoin near $100,000, which would still leave it about 21% short of its $126,080 record, with full recovery potentially extending into mid-2027.
Additionally, Gemini noted that new XRP supplies entering the market might dilute demand per token.
ChatGPT pointed out that Evernorth's 473 million XRP represents only a small fraction of XRP's $95 billion market value.
Grok observed that XRP's previous record in 2025 was more of a fleeting spike than a sustainable price level.

This raises an interesting question: how much should we rely on these AI predictions when all three cryptocurrencies remain significantly below their previous peaks?

ChatGPT assigned XRP only a 15% probability, while Gemini placed it at just 8%.

In our latest analysis, we asked AI models—ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini— to evaluate which cryptocurrency among Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ), Ethereum ( CRYPTO: ETH ), and XRP ( CRYPTO: XRP ) is likely to bounce back to its all-time high first. All three models gave the same ranking: Bitcoin led, followed by Ethereum, with XRP trailing.

While the models agreed on the order, they differed in confidence. ChatGPT estimated a 55% chance of Bitcoin reaching its record high first; Grok was slightly more optimistic at 58%, and Gemini was the most confident, giving Bitcoin a 70% probability. This raises an interesting question: how much should we rely on these AI predictions when all three cryptocurrencies remain significantly below their previous peaks?

Starting from their respective previous highs—$126,080 for Bitcoin, $4,946 for Ethereum , and $3.65 for XRP—we looked at the market as of October 1, 2026. At that time, Bitcoin was trading around $84,670, Ethereum at $2,699, and XRP at $1.49.

To reach their former highs, Bitcoin needs a gain of about 49%, Ethereum requires around 83%, and XRP must climb approximately 145%. As a result, the ranking aligns almost perfectly with the size of the gap each cryptocurrency must close.
Gemini highlighted the specific dollar amount Bitcoin needs to regain its past glory, saying it would require about $820 billion in market value to reach $126,080.

In terms of recent performance, Ethereum has shown more significant growth. Over the 90 days leading up to October 1, Ethereum climbed about 53%, while Bitcoin gained around 33% and XRP only 31%. This shows Ethereum is closing the gap faster than Bitcoin and XRP.

Despite this momentum, the AI models still favored Bitcoin. Grok noted that U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs), which hold Bitcoin and trade similarly to shares, have approximately $108 billion in assets. In comparison, Ethereum funds have $17.8 billion, and XRP funds only $1.8 billion. Grok mentioned that these funds hold nearly 6% of Bitcoin’s total supply.

ChatGPT added that financial forecasts support Bitcoin’s potential, citing Citi’s target of $113,000 for Bitcoin, which is only about 10% below its all-time high, while their target for Ethereum at $3,028 is 39% lower than its peak.

ChatGPT predicts Bitcoin could close 2026 around $100,000, Ethereum at approximately $3,400, and XRP near $2.05. Similarly, Gemini projects year-end prices of $108,500, $3,450, and $2.15, respectively. Although XRP shows the highest percentage gain potential—ranging from 38% to 44%—its chances of being the first to reach its all-time high are quite low. ChatGPT assigned XRP only a 15% probability, while Gemini placed it at just 8%.
This skepticism about XRP stems from the fact that even a 40% increase over three months would still leave it far short of its high at $3.65, requiring a 145% surge.

Additionally, Gemini noted that new XRP supplies entering the market might dilute demand per token. ChatGPT pointed out that Evernorth’s 473 million XRP represents only a small fraction of XRP’s $95 billion market value. Grok observed that XRP’s previous record in 2025 was more of a fleeting spike than a sustainable price level.

Overall, Bitcoin appears to have the strongest chance of regaining its all-time high first. It has the smallest gap to cover, the largest amount of invested funds, and the smallest decline over the past year—down about 30%, compared with Ethereum’s 38% and XRP’s 50% drops.

However, the timeline is crucial. ChatGPT’s prediction of $100,000 by year-end still leaves Bitcoin about 21% shy of its all-time high, and the models indicate potential recovery timelines extending into mid-2027.

The immediate critical test for Bitcoin is to surpass its recent high of $87,500, followed by the significant threshold of $100,000 . If Bitcoin falls below $80,000, it could hinder its progress and allow Ethereum to narrow its gap further. If Ethereum exceeds $4,946 before Bitcoin returns to $126,080, it would suggest the AI models may have miscalculated the recovery order.

In our latest analysis, we asked AI models—ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini— to evaluate which cryptocurrency among Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ), Ethereum ( CRYPTO: ETH ), and XRP ( CRYPTO: XRP ) is likely to bounce back to its all-time high first. All three models gave the same ranking: Bitcoin led, followed by Ethereum, with XRP trailing.

While the models agreed on the order, they differed in confidence. ChatGPT estimated a 55% chance of Bitcoin reaching its record high first; Grok was slightly more optimistic at 58%, and Gemini was the most confident, giving Bitcoin a 70% probability. This raises an interesting question: how much should we rely on these AI predictions when all three cryptocurrencies remain significantly below their previous peaks?

Starting from their respective previous highs—$126,080 for Bitcoin, $4,946 for Ethereum , and $3.65 for XRP—we looked at the market as of October 1, 2026. At that time, Bitcoin was trading around $84,670, Ethereum at $2,699, and XRP at $1.49.

To reach their former highs, Bitcoin needs a gain of about 49%, Ethereum requires around 83%, and XRP must climb approximately 145%. As a result, the ranking aligns almost perfectly with the size of the gap each cryptocurrency must close.
Gemini highlighted the specific dollar amount Bitcoin needs to regain its past glory, saying it would require about $820 billion in market value to reach $126,080.

In terms of recent performance, Ethereum has shown more significant growth. Over the 90 days leading up to October 1, Ethereum climbed about 53%, while Bitcoin gained around 33% and XRP only 31%. This shows Ethereum is closing the gap faster than Bitcoin and XRP.

Despite this momentum, the AI models still favored Bitcoin. Grok noted that U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs), which hold Bitcoin and trade similarly to shares, have approximately $108 billion in assets. In comparison, Ethereum funds have $17.8 billion, and XRP funds only $1.8 billion. Grok mentioned that these funds hold nearly 6% of Bitcoin’s total supply.

ChatGPT added that financial forecasts support Bitcoin’s potential, citing Citi’s target of $113,000 for Bitcoin, which is only about 10% below its all-time high, while their target for Ethereum at $3,028 is 39% lower than its peak.

ChatGPT predicts Bitcoin could close 2026 around $100,000, Ethereum at approximately $3,400, and XRP near $2.05. Similarly, Gemini projects year-end prices of $108,500, $3,450, and $2.15, respectively. Although XRP shows the highest percentage gain potential—ranging from 38% to 44%—its chances of being the first to reach its all-time high are quite low. ChatGPT assigned XRP only a 15% probability, while Gemini placed it at just 8%.
This skepticism about XRP stems from the fact that even a 40% increase over three months would still leave it far short of its high at $3.65, requiring a 145% surge.

Additionally, Gemini noted that new XRP supplies entering the market might dilute demand per token. ChatGPT pointed out that Evernorth’s 473 million XRP represents only a small fraction of XRP’s $95 billion market value. Grok observed that XRP’s previous record in 2025 was more of a fleeting spike than a sustainable price level.

Overall, Bitcoin appears to have the strongest chance of regaining its all-time high first. It has the smallest gap to cover, the largest amount of invested funds, and the smallest decline over the past year—down about 30%, compared with Ethereum’s 38% and XRP’s 50% drops.

However, the timeline is crucial. ChatGPT’s prediction of $100,000 by year-end still leaves Bitcoin about 21% shy of its all-time high, and the models indicate potential recovery timelines extending into mid-2027.

The immediate critical test for Bitcoin is to surpass its recent high of $87,500, followed by the significant threshold of $100,000 . If Bitcoin falls below $80,000, it could hinder its progress and allow Ethereum to narrow its gap further. If Ethereum exceeds $4,946 before Bitcoin returns to $126,080, it would suggest the AI models may have miscalculated the recovery order.

sources.title: Apple says it’s tightening macOS ‘Full Disk Access’ controls due to new risks from AI agents
passages: Days after a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app on Mac read their private messages — a claim that Meta disputed — Apple announced that it’s introducing additional controls around a setting called “Full Disk Access” on macOS.
The feature was designed to allow backups to function properly, but AI agents have now increased “the risks associated with this level of access,” Apple said.
This setting, Apple explains, gives an app permission to access files, mail, messages, and even browsing history.
The report raised questions about the level of security and trust users have in desktop-based AI, which can control things on their systems and read their files and messages.
We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy,” Apple wrote.
Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s inquiry about the feature change.
AI agents that run on the desktop allow users to provide their respective apps with greater access to the files, messages, and other personal content on their computers by adjusting macOS settings.
Correction: Due to an editorial error, the change was described as Apple “limiting” permissions.
After publication, the author of this article updated the wording to reflect their original intent: the change reflects informed consent, but is not a new limit.

extraction.body: Days after a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app on Mac read their private messages — a claim that Meta disputed — Apple announced that it’s introducing additional controls around a setting called “Full Disk Access” on macOS. The feature was designed to allow backups to function properly, but AI agents have now increased “the risks associated with this level of access,” Apple said. Apple’s statement comes shortly after Inc. columnist Jason Aten reported that Muse knew the content of his private messages — even though he claimed to have not given the AI agent permission. The report raised questions about the level of security and trust users have in desktop-based AI, which can control things on their systems and read their files and messages. The decision also comes after a Wired report cited that a flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac app could have allowed hackers to access sensitive data. AI agents that run on the desktop allow users to provide their respective apps with greater access to the files, messages, and other personal content on their computers by adjusting macOS settings. In Muse’s case, the AI optionally allows users to enable Full Disk Access. This setting, Apple explains, gives an app permission to access files, mail, messages, and even browsing history. “Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems…without users’ full knowledge and understanding,” Apple said in a new blog post aimed at developers. The company says that, going forward, it will introduce new controls aimed at ensuring that users who “genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access” can do so only with “very explicit user action.” “Addressing this is critical. As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy,” Apple wrote. Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s inquiry about the feature change. Correction: Due to an editorial error, the change was described as Apple “limiting” permissions. extraction.body: Days after a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app on Mac read their private messages — a claim that Meta disputed — Apple announced that it’s introducing additional controls around a setting called “Full Disk Access” on macOS. The feature was designed to allow backups to function properly, but AI agents have now increased “the risks associated with this level of access,” Apple said. Apple’s statement comes shortly after Inc. columnist Jason Aten reported that Muse knew the content of his private messages — even though he claimed to have not given the AI agent permission. The report raised questions about the level of security and trust users have in desktop-based AI, which can control things on their systems and read their files and messages. The decision also comes after a Wired report cited that a flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac app could have allowed hackers to access sensitive data. AI agents that run on the desktop allow users to provide their respective apps with greater access to the files, messages, and other personal content on their computers by adjusting macOS settings. In Muse’s case, the AI optionally allows users to enable Full Disk Access. This setting, Apple explains, gives an app permission to access files, mail, messages, and even browsing history. “Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems…without users’ full knowledge and understanding,” Apple said in a new blog post aimed at developers. The company says that, going forward, it will introduce new controls aimed at ensuring that users who “genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access” can do so only with “very explicit user action.” “Addressing this is critical. As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy,” Apple wrote. Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s inquiry about the feature change. Correction: Due to an editorial error, the change was described as Apple “limiting” permissions. sources.title: It’s not AI anymore, it’s ‘super intelligence’ (according to the White House)
passages: This week, the White House got nearly every major tech CEO in one room — Zuckerberg, Bezos, Musk, and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei among them — to sign an AI safety pledge that President Donald Trump called “morally binding.” Trump also signed an executive order officially rebranding AI as “super intelligence,” and meanwhile, Meta and OpenAI are putting friendlier faces on their AI products , even as the biggest money in AI still appears to be coming from the enterprise.

On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Anthony Ha, and Sean O’Kane dig into this week’s AI moves, the ugly economics of consumer AI , plus the shifting IPO market and a handful of startup deals.

sources.title: The MacBook Air M5 is $200 off for the first time in months

extraction.body: Amazon’s October Prime Day has effectively chopped off Apple’s June price increases. Usually $1,299, the 13-inch MacBook Air with the M5 chip and 512GB of storage is on sale for $1,099 at Amazon. That’s a more palatable price for a machine that’s significantly faster than Apple’s $699 MacBook Neo. The 15-inch version, also with 512GB of storage, is $1,299 at Amazon (was $1,499). Even without flashy new features compared to the last-gen model, it’s still one of our favorite laptops, thanks to its long battery life, bright screen, and excellent speakers. Read our Apple MacBook Air (2026, M5) review.

passages: So it’s only natural that Trump’s new task force is named in accordance with this new branding.

The Wall Street Journal reports that Clayton will chair the Super Intelligence Force, effectively making him the new AI/SI czar, with Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Undersecretary of War for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor serving as vice chairs.

“The Super Intelligence Force is tasked with coordinating the effort of the Federal Government to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Trump said in a Sunday morning post on his social network Truth Social.

Since then, Trump signed an executive order seeking to rebrand AI as “super intelligence,” a term seemingly embraced, with some stumbles , by the tech executives who gathered at the White House this week to sign a non-binding safety pledge. (The pledge included an impressive typo .)

Back in September, in response to an AI safety debate that the president has largely dismissed as a hoax created by “Radical Left Dumocrats,” Trump said he would nevertheless form an AI Force and appoint an AI czar (“Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!”).

Back in September, in response to an AI safety debate that the president has largely dismissed as a hoax created by “Radical Left Dumocrats,” Trump said he would nevertheless form an AI Force and appoint an AI czar (“Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!”). Since then, Trump signed an executive order seeking to rebrand AI as “super intelligence,” a term seemingly embraced, with some stumbles , by the tech executives who gathered at the White House this week to sign a non-binding safety pledge. (The pledge included an impressive typo .) So it’s only natural that Trump’s new task force is named in accordance with this new branding. The Wall Street Journal reports that Clayton will chair the Super Intelligence Force, effectively making him the new AI/SI czar, with Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Undersecretary of War for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor serving as vice chairs. The task force will reportedly have 120 days to create a report on the risks and opportunities presented by AI. sources.title: Trump Unveils Super Intelligence Force for AI Safety
passages: Former President Trump announced the creation of a "Super Intelligence Force" today, marking his administration's most significant response to escalating debates over artificial intelligence safety and regulation.

The real test will be whether this task force can strike the delicate balance between ensuring AI safety and maintaining America's competitive edge in what many consider the most important technology race of our time.

extraction.body: Former President Trump announced the creation of a "Super Intelligence Force" today, marking his administration's most significant response to escalating debates over artificial intelligence safety and regulation. The new government task force signals a major shift in how political leaders are approaching the rapidly evolving AI landscape, potentially reshaping the regulatory framework that tech giants like Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI operate within. The political landscape around artificial intelligence just got a major shake-up. Trump's announcement of a "Super Intelligence Force" represents the most concrete government action we've seen yet in response to mounting concerns about AI safety and the breakneck pace of development across the tech industry. Over the past year, we've watched OpenAI push the boundaries with increasingly powerful models, while Google and Microsoft race to integrate AI across their entire product ecosystems. Meanwhile, safety researchers have grown increasingly vocal about the need for stronger oversight and regulation. This new task force appears designed to bridge that gap between rapid innovation and responsible governance. Unlike previous government AI initiatives that focused primarily on research and development, the Super Intelligence Force seems positioned to tackle the thornier questions around safety protocols, ethical deployment, and potential national security implications. But beneath the surface, there's growing unease about whether the current pace of development is sustainable or safe. Trump's Super Intelligence Force could be the mechanism that finally addresses this balance. What makes this particularly significant is the bipartisan nature of AI safety concerns. While political parties disagree on many tech policy issues, the potential risks of advanced AI systems have created unusual consensus around the need for some form of government involvement. The task force's exact mandate remains unclear, but the name itself suggests a focus on the most advanced AI systems - the kind of "superintelligent" artificial general intelligence that researchers believe could emerge in the coming years. For tech companies, this development likely means increased scrutiny of their AI research and deployment practices. We're probably looking at new compliance requirements, safety audits, and potentially restrictions on certain types of AI development. The U.S. has largely relied on industry self-regulation up to this point. Trump's Super Intelligence Force suggests that era might be ending. Trump's Super Intelligence Force announcement marks a pivotal moment in AI governance, signaling that the era of industry self-regulation may be coming to an end. For tech companies racing to develop increasingly powerful AI systems, this means navigating a new landscape of government oversight and compliance requirements. The real test will be whether this task force can strike the delicate balance between ensuring AI safety and maintaining America's competitive edge in what many consider the most important technology race of our time.

Last month, Trump said he would create an AI task force amid rising concerns about the technology.

Trump's announcement was thin on details, with the president not outlining any specific action or oversight the task force will have on AI development -- an issue about which some tech CEOs have raised concerns and called for federal regulation.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump formally announced the creation of what he called a “Super Intelligence Force,” an artificial intelligence task force that he says will work to promote AI dominance while also protecting American lives and interests. "The Super Intelligence Force is tasked with coordinating the effort of the Federal Government to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Trump wrote on his social media platform Sunday. Trump's announcement was thin on details, with the president not outlining any specific action or oversight the task force will have on AI development -- an issue about which some tech CEOs have raised concerns and called for federal regulation. "The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump added. An ABC News request sent to the White House for more information about the task force's objectives did not immediately receive a response. Last month, Trump said he would create an AI task force amid rising concerns about the technology. Sunday's formal announcement comes after the president met with top tech CEOs at the White House last week, where he said he and six companies signed a "constitution" establishing standards on how to self-police their technology. Trump said the task force will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, as well as Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor. Clayton, who is expected to serve as the White House's new AI czar, told The Wall Street Journal in an interview published Saturday that global dominance in AI makes the U.S. more equipped to address risks from adversaries, echoing the president’s support for the technology's continued growth. "The risk of not being first is high," Clayton told The Wall Street Journal. “Not being first increases the identified, and unidentified, risks, particularly from our adversaries. Being first will better enable us to address those risks on behalf of the American people." Clayton said of the AI task force, "I expect there will be mechanisms developed in dialogue, just like there are in other industries." According to The Wall Street Journal, Clayton cited risk models for the financial industry that have been developed in conjunction with the Federal Reserve and Securities and Exchange Commission. He told the newspaper that the task force would examine current law and discuss possible actions that Congress could take. Clayton also expressed confidence in the group that the president has appointed to run the AI task force, citing the "diverse skill sets" and "common commitment" of its members. "These are all serious people who have addressed opportunities and risks in the past and are committed to doing this so that America wins the AI race and we win it through the benefit of the American people," he added. 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events President Donald Trump formally announced the creation of what he called a “Super Intelligence Force,” an artificial intelligence task force that he says will work to promote AI dominance while also protecting American lives and interests. \"The Super Intelligence Force is tasked with coordinating the effort of the Federal Government to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Trump wrote on his social media platform Sunday. coreStoryFacts.text: So it’s only natural that Trump’s new task force is named in accordance with this new branding.

The Wall Street Journal reports that Clayton will chair the Super Intelligence Force, effectively making him the new AI/SI czar, with Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Undersecretary of War for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor serving as vice chairs.

“The Super Intelligence Force is tasked with coordinating the effort of the Federal Government to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Trump said in a Sunday morning post on his social network Truth Social.

Since then, Trump signed an executive order seeking to rebrand AI as “super intelligence,” a term seemingly embraced, with some stumbles , by the tech executives who gathered at the White House this week to sign a non-binding safety pledge. (The pledge included an impressive typo .)

Back in September, in response to an AI safety debate that the president has largely dismissed as a hoax created by “Radical Left Dumocrats,” Trump said he would nevertheless form an AI Force and appoint an AI czar (“Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!”).

Former President Trump announced the creation of a "Super Intelligence Force" today, marking his administration's most significant response to escalating debates over artificial intelligence safety and regulation.

The real test will be whether this task force can strike the delicate balance between ensuring AI safety and maintaining America's competitive edge in what many consider the most important technology race of our time.
President Donald Trump unveiled the formation of the Super Intelligence Force (SIF) to ensure America’s supremacy in the realm of “Super Intelligence” (SI).
At the @DeptofWar we have seen what is possible when red tape is removed and America’s best technology is rapidly put into action.
Working alongside America’s leading technology companies, we are…
In a Sunday Truth Social post, Trump announced the creation of the task force, which will be led by officials reporting to himself.
The SIF is designed to coordinate the federal government with groups when it comes to “SI” in order to improve the lives of Americans.

extraction.body: Former President Trump announced the creation of a "Super Intelligence Force" today, marking his administration's most significant response to escalating debates over artificial intelligence safety and regulation. The new government task force signals a major shift in how political leaders are approaching the rapidly evolving AI landscape, potentially reshaping the regulatory framework that tech giants like Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI operate within. The political landscape around artificial intelligence just got a major shake-up. Trump's announcement of a "Super Intelligence Force" represents the most concrete government action we've seen yet in response to mounting concerns about AI safety and the breakneck pace of development across the tech industry. Over the past year, we've watched OpenAI push the boundaries with increasingly powerful models, while Google and Microsoft race to integrate AI across their entire product ecosystems. Meanwhile, safety researchers have grown increasingly vocal about the need for stronger oversight and regulation. This new task force appears designed to bridge that gap between rapid innovation and responsible governance. extraction.body: President Donald Trump formally announced the creation of what he called a “Super Intelligence Force,” an artificial intelligence task force that he says will work to promote AI dominance while also protecting American lives and interests. "The Super Intelligence Force is tasked with coordinating the effort of the Federal Government to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Trump wrote on his social media platform Sunday. Trump's announcement was thin on details, with the president not outlining any specific action or oversight the task force will have on AI development -- an issue about which some tech CEOs have raised concerns and called for federal regulation. "The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump added. An ABC News request sent to the White House for more information about the task force's objectives did not immediately receive a response. Last month, Trump said he would create an AI task force amid rising concerns about the technology. Sunday's formal announcement comes after the president met with top tech CEOs at the White House last week, where he said he and six companies signed a "constitution" establishing standards on how to self-police their technology. Trump said the task force will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, as well as Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor. Clayton, who is expected to serve as the White House's new AI czar, told The Wall Street Journal in an interview published Saturday that global dominance in AI makes the U.S. more equipped to address risks from adversaries, echoing the president’s support for the technology's continued growth. "The risk of not being first is high," Clayton told The Wall Street Journal. “Not being first increases the identified, and unidentified, risks, particularly from our adversaries. Being first will better enable us to address those risks on behalf of the American people." Clayton said of the AI task force, "I expect there will be mechanisms developed in dialogue, just like there are in other industries." According to The Wall Street Journal, Clayton cited risk models for the financial industry that have been developed in conjunction with the Federal Reserve and Securities and Exchange Commission. He told the newspaper that the task force would examine current law and discuss possible actions that Congress could take. Clayton also expressed confidence in the group that the president has appointed to run the AI task force, citing the "diverse skill sets" and "common commitment" of its members. However, he argues the company has lost the issuance channel that funded its Bitcoin purchases. Schiff said that rally may have restored some confidence in the stock or triggered short covering. The preferred stock had sunk to about $75 earlier this year, which CEO Phong Le blamed on unexpected leverage. Referring to Executive Chairman Michael Saylor, Schiff argued that the rebound has not reopened Strategy's key funding route. "There's no way that he's going to be able to start selling more Stretch; that means he's not going to be able to raise money to really start buying more Bitcoin," Schiff said. He added that Strategy has raised enough cash to keep paying STRC dividends a little longer before it runs out. However, he said the company no longer has the machinery to buy more Bitcoin. Saylor, for his part, pointed to calmer trading in the stock. He said STRC's 30-day historical volatility stood at 9% as of October 2. The company last sold STRC through its at-the-market program between May 11 and 17, raising about $1.95 billion. Its remaining STRC capacity has held at about $17.51 billion in every filing since, meaning no further shares were sold. Strategy then paused Bitcoin buying for 10 weeks over the summer, selling coins instead to fund dividends and STRC buybacks. When it resumed in late August, it relied on other funding sources. It sold class A common stock (MSTR) to fund 4,603 BTC that week and 1,665 BTC in late September. In between, it spent $75.7 million from its USD Cash account on 950 BTC. Common stock proceeds also flow back into STRC. Between September 21 and 27, Strategy used $103.5 million from MSTR sales to repurchase STRC shares. Strategy also held a $5.02 billion USD Reserve as of September 27. The company says the pool is meant to support preferred dividends and debt interest. Schiff expects Bitcoin to roll over once tech stocks pull back. Strategy usually reports purchases on Mondays, so its next filing will show whether common stock sales keep funding its buys. Since leaving the White House, Sacks has "maintained close ties with the president," according to the Guardian, and "in May, he successfully urged Trump to scrap an executive order that would've subjected AI models to government review."
Clayton, 60, is a registered independent with degrees from the University of Pennsylvania (engineering, law) and the University of Cambridge (economics).
As a lawyer in private practice, he focused mostly on Wall Street: mergers and acquisitions, market offerings and regulatory proceedings.

From March 2021 to April 2025, Clayton served as chair and "lead independent director" of the board of Apollo Global Management . (Apollo has owned a 90% majority stake in Yahoo since September 2021.)

In a post on Truth Social , Trump said Clayton will lead a newly formed "Super Intelligence Force" alongside Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor.
The group will report directly to Trump and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.

Its goal, Trump wrote, is "to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans."

Despite new polls showing that 86% of Americans want AI companies to meet independent safety standards even if doing so slows development — with 74% largely mistrusting the leaders of those companies — Trump insisted in recent days that federal regulations are unnecessary and that those who say otherwise are " Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers ."
But Clayton sidestepped questions over who won the 2020 election during his July confirmation hearings, and he was confirmed without Democratic support.

"I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force , which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term," Trump wrote in his September social media post about naming an AI czar.

Clayton, it seems, will now be in charge of cherishing, helping and watching over the AI industry as it grows.
He's "a good man," Trump told Axios when the outlet asked last week if Clayton was being considered for the job .
According to Axios , Trump's AI Force idea "caught advisers by surprise," setting off "a mad dash" within the administration "to imagine what AI Force would look like."

Trump had initially created the AI and cryptocurrency czar position when he returned to the White House in January 2025.
Trump previously floated Clayton’s name as a potential AI czar, telling Axios in September that Clayton was “a good man” and the prospect of appointing him was “a good idea”.
In a social media post on Sunday, Trump announced that Clayton would lead what the US president called “the Super Intelligence Force (SIF)”.
Musk said on his social media platform X that SI was “better” than AI – and that he was renaming his aerospace company’s AI unit from SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI.
Clayton, who leads the US’s 18 intelligence agencies , previously served as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and led the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term.
In September, Trump announced he was creating an “AI Force” and a czar to oversee the technology’s growth and monitor for “bad” development.
The announcement came after tech industry leaders warned that AI was developing too rapidly to control and that it could harm humans.

Trump’s post also said the SIF would “coordinate the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and super intelligence companies”.
But to address concerns, the president created an advisory committee in addition to the czar – whom he previously promised would be led by a “high IQ” individual.
Trump also recently met with AI industry leaders to discuss concerns.
Trump has insisted continued development is paramount to defeating China in the global AI race.

Trump previously floated Clayton’s name as a potential AI czar, telling Axios in September that Clayton was “a good man” and the prospect of appointing him was “a good idea”.
In a social media post on Sunday, Trump announced that Clayton would lead what the US president called “the Super Intelligence Force (SIF)”.
Musk said on his social media platform X that SI was “better” than AI – and that he was renaming his aerospace company’s AI unit from SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI.
Clayton, who leads the US’s 18 intelligence agencies , previously served as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and led the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term.
In September, Trump announced he was creating an “AI Force” and a czar to oversee the technology’s growth and monitor for “bad” development.
The announcement came after tech industry leaders warned that AI was developing too rapidly to control and that it could harm humans.

Trump’s post also said the SIF would “coordinate the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and super intelligence companies”.
But to address concerns, the president created an advisory committee in addition to the czar – whom he previously promised would be led by a “high IQ” individual.
Trump also recently met with AI industry leaders to discuss concerns.
Trump has insisted continued development is paramount to defeating China in the global AI race.

Mariam Zuhaib/AP hide caption Director of national intelligence Jay Clayton is the new White House AI czar, President Trump said on Sunday. Trump wrote on Truth Social that Clayton will lead the White House's new "Super Intelligence Force," a group that will "ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence." Trump prefers the term "super intelligence" to "artificial intelligence." He said his "Super Intelligence Force" will "coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies." Before being confirmed earlier this year to lead national intelligence, Clayton was United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York, and chairman of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Trump's announcement follows various statements of alarm from tech leaders over risks in the rapid development of AI, including that it could go rogue. Trump has largely brushed aside the warnings and attempted to reframe concerns around AI. On Tuesday, Trump met with AI executives at the White House, and said afterwards that leaders of several artificial intelligence companies had signed a voluntary accord that will include internal and external reviews of their work. Meanwhile, the White House also launched a revamped government website this week, America.gov , which says it is sourced via artificial intelligence from "official government sources." In his social media post, Trump also named other members of his "Super Intelligence Force". He said it will include: Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor, and Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael. It is unclear what Clayton's appointment as AI czar means for the AI industry, as current artificial intelligence regulation by the U.S. government is limited. Congress has not passed federal law broadly regulating the use or development of AI. Some states, including California, have enacted measures about AI, including requiring entities to be transparent when it is used . During an interview with CNBC last month, Clayton called super intelligence a "national security issue." He also pushed back against calls for a "pause" in developing the technology, pointing out that other countries around the world are continuing to develop AI. "I don't think any American should think that that's a good strategy," he said. In December 2024, president-elect Trump announced he would appoint David Sacks, a Silicon Valley investor, as an AI and crypto czar , with a brief to advise the administration on policies surrounding AI. Earlier this year, Sacks stepped down from his role and became co-chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. He has backed AI leaders Sam Altman and Dario Amodei's warnings about the technology, and the idea of a "slow down" in AI development. Last month, Sacks wrote on social media that the tech leaders should "stop pretending you need anyone else's permission" to make such moves. sources.title: Trump names intelligence chief Clayton as AI czar, to head task force, WSJ reports - bdnews24.com
passages: US President Donald Trump has appointed Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as the administration's AI czar, the Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday, citing an interview with Clayton.
Clayton, who was appointed intelligence chief in August, will lead a new White House panel tasked with reporting within 120 days on the risks and opportunities posed by AI, the newspaper said.

Clayton's panel will review AI-related risks and current government reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks and other incidents, and recommend ways to strengthen federal-response capabilities under existing authorities, the Journal said, citing the task force's charter.
Venture capitalist David Sacks held the AI czar role at the beginning of Trump's second term.
Trump has appeared to take a light touch toward AI regulation, arguing that excessive oversight could weaken competitiveness against China.
He said on Tuesday that he does not want to work with Chinese President Xi Jinping on governing AI technology.

Clayton, who was appointed intelligence chief in August, will lead a new White House panel tasked with reporting within 120 days on the risks and opportunities posed by AI, the newspaper said. "The president asked that a group be put together," which the administration refers to as the "Super Intelligence Force," to ensure the US remains a leader in advanced AI while protecting Americans' interests, Clayton told the Journal, adding that "the risk of not being first is high." The safety of AI has become a major issue in recent weeks, with some researchers warning that people building the technology believe it could kill humans within a decade. Several Democratic and Republican lawmakers have responded with alarm and calls for more action. Trump has appeared to take a light touch toward AI regulation, arguing that excessive oversight could weaken competitiveness against China. He said on Tuesday that he does not want to work with Chinese President Xi Jinping on governing AI technology. Clayton's panel will review AI-related risks and current government reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks and other incidents, and recommend ways to strengthen federal-response capabilities under existing authorities, the Journal said, citing the task force's charter. This is the second time Trump has named an adviser to oversee AI-related decisions across the administration. Venture capitalist David Sacks held the AI czar role at the beginning of Trump's second term. The task force's vice chairs will be Emil Michael, Scott Kupor and Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, while members will include Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, according to the report. External advisers will also include Sacks and former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, the Journal said. coreStoryFacts.text: President Trump on Sunday named Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as his new "AI czar," adding a different category of intelligence, the "artificial" kind, to the U.S. spy chief's portfolio.

Since leaving the White House, Sacks has "maintained close ties with the president," according to the Guardian, and "in May, he successfully urged Trump to scrap an executive order that would've subjected AI models to government review."
Clayton, 60, is a registered independent with degrees from the University of Pennsylvania (engineering, law) and the University of Cambridge (economics).
As a lawyer in private practice, he focused mostly on Wall Street: mergers and acquisitions, market offerings and regulatory proceedings.

From March 2021 to April 2025, Clayton served as chair and "lead independent director" of the board of Apollo Global Management . (Apollo has owned a 90% majority stake in Yahoo since September 2021.)

In a post on Truth Social , Trump said Clayton will lead a newly formed "Super Intelligence Force" alongside Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor.
The group will report directly to Trump and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.

Its goal, Trump wrote, is "to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans."

Despite new polls showing that 86% of Americans want AI companies to meet independent safety standards even if doing so slows development — with 74% largely mistrusting the leaders of those companies — Trump insisted in recent days that federal regulations are unnecessary and that those who say otherwise are " Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers ."
But Clayton sidestepped questions over who won the 2020 election during his July confirmation hearings, and he was confirmed without Democratic support.
In late 2024, Trump nominated Clayton to serve as U.S.
In November 2025, Trump ordered the Department of Justice to investigate Democrats associated with Jeffrey Epstein, and U.S.
On Tuesday, Clayton attended Trump's White House meeting with top AI executives.
Speaking afterward to CNBC, he used the president's new preferred term for AI — i.e., "superintelligence " — while pushing back against lawmakers who have called for regulating or pausing U.S.
"I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force , which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term," Trump wrote in his September social media post about naming an AI czar.
Asked to respond to criticism from Democratic Sen.
Clayton, it seems, will now be in charge of cherishing, helping and watching over the AI industry as it grows.
He's "a good man," Trump told Axios when the outlet asked last week if Clayton was being considered for the job .
According to Axios , Trump's AI Force idea "caught advisers by surprise," setting off "a mad dash" within the administration "to imagine what AI Force would look like."
"Whoever wins AI ... that's the group that wins," Trump told the United Nations General Assembly last month .
"We're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way."
As for reining in "bad" actors, he wrote, "we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System."

In the same post, the president again dismissed concerns about AI safety as a "hoax" perpetrated by "Radical Left Democrats." He also wrote that going forward, his administration would not "in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," which he described as "the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet" — only "even larger and more impactful."

The group will report directly to Trump and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles. Its goal, Trump wrote, is "to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans." Clayton will keep his job as DNI, which oversees the nation's 18 intelligence agencies. Trump's announcement follows meeting last Tuesday at the White House where top AI executives signed what he called a " morally binding " agreement to police themselves in order to prevent their increasingly powerful models from going rogue and harming humanity . "There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation," the president said at the meeting. "This is going to be all for the good, and we're going to have it be nice and safe." Despite new polls showing that 86% of Americans want AI companies to meet independent safety standards even if doing so slows development — with 74% largely mistrusting the leaders of those companies — Trump insisted in recent days that federal regulations are unnecessary and that those who say otherwise are " Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers ." "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" he wrote on social media . Elsewhere, Trump has said that regulation would handicap the U.S. in its race to "win" AI. "Whoever wins AI ... that's the group that wins," Trump told the United Nations General Assembly last month . "We're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way." According to the Guardian , Trump's previous AI and crypto czar, billionaire tech investor David Sacks, consistently "counseled the president to give a soft touch to AI regulation, helping push executive orders and other measures aimed at loosening restrictions on the technology." Sacks also "maintains direct financial stakes in multiple AI companies," the paper reported, though he took steps to divest some of his holdings last year while serving in the administration. Chuck Schumer blocked his appointment. Reports suggest Clayton was also considered for roles as secretary of the treasury, attorney general and director of the Central Intelligence Agency. In November 2025, Trump ordered the Department of Justice to investigate Democrats associated with Jeffrey Epstein, and U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi assigned Clayton to lead the probe . After former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard resigned in May 2026, Trump tapped Clayton to replace her. "He's very qualified," Democratic Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia said at the time . But Clayton sidestepped questions over who won the 2020 election during his July confirmation hearings, and he was confirmed without Democratic support. "I'm not an election denier," Clayton told the Senate. "He went through our processes, and Joe Biden became the president of the United States." "When something is both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it." On Tuesday, Clayton attended Trump's White House meeting with top AI executives. Speaking afterward to CNBC, he used the president's new preferred term for AI — i.e., "superintelligence " — while pushing back against lawmakers who have called for regulating or pausing U.S. AI development. "Super intelligence is a national security issue, and that was something that was recognized yesterday by not just the industry leaders but everybody in the room," Clayton said. "But to, in some way, not try to drive forward inside the United States, with companies that are regulated in the United States ... to somehow say we should back away from this and let the rest of the world develop these models and implement these models? I don't think anybody in that room, and I don't think any American, should think that that's a good strategy." Asked to respond to criticism from Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts that Trump's current policy of letting AI companies police themselves will prove to be "a recipe for disaster," Clayton suggested that the U.S. government's existing regulatory framework could also help keep AI in check. "My response to the American people on that front is we have a Federal Trade Commission, we have a Department of Justice," Clayton said. "I know the leaders of both those organizations, and they're committed to protecting the American people in this regard." As for reining in "bad" actors, he wrote, "we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System." He's "a good man," Trump told Axios when the outlet asked last week if Clayton was being considered for the job . "He's right here. That's a good idea." It's unclear what happened to a separate idea Trump floated last month, which he called "the AI Force." It is unclear what Clayton's appointment as AI czar means for the AI industry, as current artificial intelligence regulation by the U.S. government is limited. Congress has not passed federal law broadly regulating the use or development of AI. Some states, including California, have enacted measures about AI, including requiring entities to be transparent when it is used . During an interview with CNBC last month, Clayton called super intelligence a "national security issue." He also pushed back against calls for a "pause" in developing the technology, pointing out that other countries around the world are continuing to develop AI. Clayton, who was appointed intelligence chief in August, will lead a new White House panel tasked with reporting within 120 days on the risks and opportunities posed by AI, the newspaper said.

Clayton's panel will review AI-related risks and current government reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks and other incidents, and recommend ways to strengthen federal-response capabilities under existing authorities, the Journal said, citing the task force's charter.
Venture capitalist David Sacks held the AI czar role at the beginning of Trump's second term.
Trump has appeared to take a light touch toward AI regulation, arguing that excessive oversight could weaken competitiveness against China.
