extraction.body: TEL AVIV — Early indications suggest the Flydubai co-pilot accused of attacking his captain and trying to seize control of an Israel-bound plane acted alone, rather than as part of a larger organization or on behalf of a foreign government, multiple U.S. officials briefed on the investigation and a former Israeli security official told NBC News. The U.S. officials cautioned that the investigation into Wednesday’s midair attack remains at an early stage. “The assessment is that he operated alone. Right now, it looks like a case of ‘lone wolf’ terrorism inspired by content found online,” said Shalom Ben Hanan, a former official in the Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency. “We still need to wait for the final investigation results to determine whether an organization or a state is behind it,” he added. Emirati authorities, who are leading the investigation, said Saturday that the co-pilot attacked the captain with a crash ax and attempted to take control of the aircraft’s flight controls in an attempted terrorist attack. The flight was carrying 174 mostly Israeli passengers from Dubai to Tel Aviv. A crash was averted when crew members and passengers entered the cockpit and subdued the attacker, according to eyewitnesses and Israeli officials. NBC News has identified the suspect as Omani citizen Hamam al-Hammami, based on information from multiple sources from three agencies briefed on the investigation and a diplomat in the Middle East. Authorities have not released his identity. UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said Saturday that investigators were working to establish the incident’s “full circumstances, motives, and any links.” The preliminary assessment comes after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday that investigators were examining whether the attacker had been sent by someone. President Donald Trump also raised the possibility of Iranian involvement Thursday, threatening renewed strikes against Iran if it was behind the attack. A senior U.S. official briefed on the Israeli investigation previously told NBC News there were no indications that Iran directed or was involved in the attack. The flight captain, Indian national Smit Machchhar , said Friday from a hospital in Abu Dhabi that he had been severely injured and could sense the aircraft descending before he managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to intervene. “I was acting for my own life, but at the same time, I knew I couldn’t let all of them die,” he said on a video call released by India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Raf Sanchez and Paul Goldman reported from Tel Aviv and Tom Winter from New York.

Australian security agencies have launched an investigation after it emerged that the flydubai co-pilot who allegedly tried to hijack an Israel-bound flight spent about two years in the country as a student.

Disaster was narrowly averted on Wednesday when passengers and crew intervened to stop the co-pilot’s attempt to take control of the flydubai flight to Tel Aviv, which had 182 people onboard and plunged 16,625 feet (5,067 metres) in just over 30 seconds.

The United ⁠Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general has said the co-pilot had used a crash axe in the attempted “terrorist attack”, in which the pilot was stabbed mid-air. Numerous media outlets have named the co-pilot as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national.

A source familiar with the case, but not authorised to speak publicly, said the man was granted an Australian student visa in 2014, before arriving in the country to commence a university course the following year.
He left Australia in 2017, and his visa was cancelled in 2019 after authorities confirmed he was no longer enrolled in the course, the source said.
The Australian federal police (AFP) on Sunday said multiple agencies – including the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (Asio) – were probing the man’s connections to the country.
“The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team (VIC JCTT), comprising the AFP, Victoria Police and ASIO, can confirm it is investigating the man’s links to Australia,” an AFP spokesperson said.
“An update will be provided at an appropriate time.”

US media outlets, including CNN, reported that a now-deleted LinkedIn profile said al-Hammami had studied engineering at an Australian university. Guardian Australia has not verified which university the co-pilot attended.

It came after a British university, Buckinghamshire New University, said a student named Hamam al-Hammami had “previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management” at the institution. It added: “He did not undertake any pilot training at the university.”
A flydubai spokesperson on Saturday said the circumstances surrounding the incident were still ‌under investigation and the airline was not in a position to comment further.

The airline’s flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv have been suspended until further notice after the attack. The Omani co-pilot and the flight’s Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, were taken to the UAE, as it leads the investigation. Officials have said a number of countries including Israel are participating.

The Wall Street Journal has reported that the co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views. He was then moved to an administrative job at Oman Air, according to the official, before being hired by the UAE-based budget airline flydubai.

Authorities have identified the accused co-pilot as Hamam al Hammami, an Omani national who was born in the UAE and has a Syrian mother. (Photo: Social Media) Flydubai Attack Live Update: A routine international flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv has turned into a major security investigation after Australian authorities began examining the background and connections of the co-pilot accused of attacking the captain in the cockpit. Australian authorities confirmed that the Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team, involving the Australian Federal Police (AFP), Victoria Police and the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (ASIO), is investigating Hamam al Hammami’s "links to Australia". The Omani national reportedly studied in Melbourne, with local reports identifying RMIT University as the institution he attended. The investigation adds a new international dimension to the September 30 incident involving flydubai Flight 1073. The Boeing 737 was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv when al Hammami allegedly attacked Indian Captain Smit Machchhar inside the cockpit. Australia has emerged as a key part of the investigation into flydubai co-pilot Hamam al Hammami after authorities confirmed they are examining his links to the country. The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team, which includes the Australian Federal Police, Victoria Police and ASIO, is looking into his time in Australia, including reports that he studied at RMIT University in Melbourne. Investigators are also examining allegations about his activities and possible extremist links while he was in the country. Authorities have identified the accused co-pilot as Hamam al Hammami, an Omani national who was born in the UAE and has a Syrian mother. Reports indicate that his background stretches across several countries. He reportedly studied in Melbourne before completing a distance-learning aviation management course at Buckinghamshire New University in the UK. Australian media reports have also raised questions about his activities while he was in the country. The Financial Times reported that al Hammami allegedly visited radical mosques and extremist websites during his time in Australia, citing people familiar with the investigation. The report also said Australian intelligence agencies had previously held a file on him. Reuters said it could not independently verify those claims. "The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team (VIC JCTT), comprising the AFP, Victoria Police and ASIO, can confirm it is investigating the man's links to Australia. An update will be provided at an appropriate time," an Australian Federal Police spokesperson said. The flight left Dubai on Wednesday carrying 182 people and was heading toward Tel Aviv when the situation inside the cockpit suddenly escalated. According to UAE authorities, al Hammami attacked the captain using an emergency crash axe and attempted to take control of the aircraft. The incident sent the aircraft into a steep descent, with reports indicating that it dropped from around 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet in roughly a minute. Passengers and members of the crew eventually overpowered the co-pilot. The aircraft diverted to Saudi Arabia, where it made an emergency landing in Tabuk. Captain Smit Machchhar, who was injured during the attack, has since been praised for his actions. Reports say he managed to open the cockpit door despite his injuries, allowing others to intervene and help regain control of the aircraft. The UAE prosecutor general described the incident as a "terrorist attack" and said investigators were examining the circumstances, motive, possible connections and both physical and digital evidence. UAE senior diplomatic adviser Anwar Gargash also described the incident as a "dangerous terrorist act" and praised the captain for preventing a much larger catastrophe. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu separately said the co-pilot had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination", adding that it appeared "very likely that he was going to down the plane". Authorities have not yet publicly established whether al Hammami acted alone or had support from an extremist organisation. A Gulf diplomat told the Associated Press that investigators were trying to determine whether he was a "lone wolf, or has any connection with any extremist groups". The investigation is also examining al Hammami's history before he joined flydubai. Sources cited by the Associated Press said Oman had previously banned him from flying because of concerns that he had adopted extremist views. That has raised questions about how he later obtained employment with a UAE-based airline and was assigned to an international passenger flight. The case has therefore expanded beyond the actions on Flight 1073. Investigators are now examining his education, travel history, online activity, previous aviation employment and any possible extremist connections. While investigators focus on the co-pilot, Captain Smit Machchhar has received widespread praise for his response during the attack. The Indian pilot fought to regain control of the cockpit after being attacked and helped create an opportunity for passengers and other crew members to intervene. He was later treated for his injuries. Israeli officials have praised Machchhar's actions, while reports said he was visited in hospital by senior UAE officials. The incident has also taken on a wider geopolitical dimension. US President Donald Trump said early information he had received suggested possible links between the attack and Iran. He warned that if Iranian agents were found responsible, the United States would "hit them very hard". No evidence establishing Iranian involvement has been publicly presented, and investigations into the incident remain underway. For now, Australian, Emirati and other authorities are focusing on reconstructing al Hammami's movements and background and determining whether the attack was the work of an individual or part of a wider extremist network.

Sources cited by the Associated Press said Oman had previously banned him from flying because of concerns that he had adopted extremist views. That has raised questions about how he later obtained employment with a UAE-based airline and was assigned to an international passenger flight.

The case has therefore expanded beyond the actions on Flight 1073. Investigators are now examining his education, travel history, online activity, previous aviation employment and any possible extremist connections.
While investigators focus on the co-pilot, Captain Smit Machchhar has received widespread praise for his response during the attack.

The Indian pilot fought to regain control of the cockpit after being attacked and helped create an opportunity for passengers and other crew members to intervene. He was later treated for his injuries.
Israeli officials have praised Machchhar's actions, while reports said he was visited in hospital by senior UAE officials.
The incident has also taken on a wider geopolitical dimension.

US President Donald Trump said early information he had received suggested possible links between the attack and Iran. He warned that if Iranian agents were found responsible, the United States would "hit them very hard".
No evidence establishing Iranian involvement has been publicly presented, and investigations into the incident remain underway.

For now, Australian, Emirati and other authorities are focusing on reconstructing al Hammami's movements and background and determining whether the attack was the work of an individual or part of a wider extremist network.

According to The Guardian, a source familiar with the case, but not authorised to speak publicly, said the man was granted an Australian student visa in 2014 before travelling to Australia the following year to begin a university course. He remained in the country until 2017, when he left Australia. The source said the man’s Australian student visa was subsequently cancelled in 2019 after authorities confirmed that he was no longer enrolled in the course. Australian Agencies Probe Links The Australian Federal Police (AFP) said on Sunday that multiple agencies, including the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (ASIO), were investigating the co-pilot’s connections to Australia, according to The Guardian. The development adds an international dimension to an investigation already involving authorities in the UAE, Israel and Saudi Arabia. The alleged attack took place on September 30 aboard flydubai flight FZ1073 while the aircraft was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The co-pilot allegedly stabbed the captain and attempted to take control of the aircraft. Passengers and crew members managed to subdue the co-pilot, averting what Israeli officials have described as an apparent attempt to crash the plane. A reserve flydubai pilot crew travelling on the aircraft subsequently landed it at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, where Saudi authorities detained the co-pilot. The co-pilot was transferred to the UAE on Thursday. Reuters reported, citing a source briefed on the investigation, that Israeli officials were expected to question him as part of the wider probe. An Israeli government official told Reuters that Israeli investigators would participate in the UAE-led investigation alongside Emirati authorities. Co-Pilot’s Motive Still Under Investigation The UAE has opened an investigation into the incident, with state media reporting that authorities were seeking to establish its circumstances and motives and determine whether it was linked to terrorist activity or purpose, or involved prior planning or direction. Flydubai Chief Executive Ghaith Al Ghaith said in his first public comments on the incident that an official investigation was underway with the airline’s support. “It is important that we allow this process to establish the facts,” Al Ghaith said in a written statement, while acknowledging that there were “many questions” surrounding what happened on flight FZ1073. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Friday that Israel was investigating whether the co-pilot had acted under anyone’s direction.

extraction.body: TEL AVIV — Early indications suggest the Flydubai co-pilot accused of attacking his captain and trying to seize control of an Israel-bound plane acted alone, rather than as part of a larger organization or on behalf of a foreign government, multiple U.S. officials briefed on the investigation and a former Israeli security official told NBC News. The U.S. officials cautioned that the investigation into Wednesday’s midair attack remains at an early stage. “The assessment is that he operated alone. Right now, it looks like a case of ‘lone wolf’ terrorism inspired by content found online,” said Shalom Ben Hanan, a former official in the Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency. “We still need to wait for the final investigation results to determine whether an organization or a state is behind it,” he added. Emirati authorities, who are leading the investigation, said Saturday that the co-pilot attacked the captain with a crash ax and attempted to take control of the aircraft’s flight controls in an attempted terrorist attack. The flight was carrying 174 mostly Israeli passengers from Dubai to Tel Aviv. A crash was averted when crew members and passengers entered the cockpit and subdued the attacker, according to eyewitnesses and Israeli officials. NBC News has identified the suspect as Omani citizen Hamam al-Hammami, based on information from multiple sources from three agencies briefed on the investigation and a diplomat in the Middle East. Authorities have not released his identity. UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said Saturday that investigators were working to establish the incident’s “full circumstances, motives, and any links.” The preliminary assessment comes after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday that investigators were examining whether the attacker had been sent by someone. President Donald Trump also raised the possibility of Iranian involvement Thursday, threatening renewed strikes against Iran if it was behind the attack. A senior U.S. official briefed on the Israeli investigation previously told NBC News there were no indications that Iran directed or was involved in the attack. The flight captain, Indian national Smit Machchhar , said Friday from a hospital in Abu Dhabi that he had been severely injured and could sense the aircraft descending before he managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to intervene. “I was acting for my own life, but at the same time, I knew I couldn’t let all of them die,” he said on a video call released by India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Raf Sanchez and Paul Goldman reported from Tel Aviv and Tom Winter from New York.

passages: President Donald Trump announced a new "Super Intelligence Force" in a post on Truth Social Sunday, just days after signing an executive order renaming Artificial Intelligence.
Trump says the force will "ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence," by coordinating the federal government's efforts.

Trump says the force will "ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence," by coordinating the federal government's efforts.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump announced a new "Super Intelligence Force" in a post on Truth Social Sunday, just days after signing an executive order renaming Artificial Intelligence. Trump says the force will "ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence," by coordinating the federal government's efforts. "The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump said on Truth Social. He said the force will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering and Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael, and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor will all serve as vice chairs. Clayton spoke with The Wall Street Journal about the force, saying, "The president asked that a group be put together." He said the panel has been tasked with reporting on the risks and opportunities AI poses within 120 days, and emphasized the U.S. government's desire to lead the industry, saying "the risk of not being first is high." According to The Journal, the force will review AI-related risks and current government reporting mechanisms, checking them for breaches, hacks and other incidents and issues. The Journal says in addition to Clayton and the vice chairs, Super Intelligence Force members will include Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. Super Intelligence vs AI The force is just the latest effort Trump has made, using the term superintelligence rather than artificial intelligence. During a UN General Assembly meeting last month, Trump said the word artificial "makes it sound fake, and it is not fake, it's actually amazing." Since then, he's signed an executive order directing the U.S. government to officially rebrand AI as "super intelligence" in federal communications.

(CNN) — President Donald Trump on Sunday announced the leadership and duties of a “Super Intelligence Force,” which he said will “ensure that America continues to lead the world” when it comes to artificial intelligence.
Trump announced last month that he was planning to create an “AI Force” and name an AI czar as the government faces growing calls to impose guardrails on the technology’s rapid development.
“I’m seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police,” Trump told reporters.
“These models are very complex and, again, I believe they’re going to be used for the good.”

The group signed a new commitment aimed at better “self-policing” their companies’ AI models, arguing that the light-touch approach represents the best way to balance safety concerns with the president’s desire to accelerate a technology he’s dubbed “Super Intelligence.”

The president said in his announcement on Truth Social that the task force will “protect the interests” and “improve the lives” of Americans. He said it will coordinate the government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, infrastructure providers and AI companies. The group will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor. The task force will report to Trump and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, the president said. Trump announced last month that he was planning to create an “AI Force” and name an AI czar as the government faces growing calls to impose guardrails on the technology’s rapid development. CNN reported Friday that Trump was expected to tap Clayton to lead the group. The announcement detailing the task force comes in the wake of episodes that have raised widespread safety concerns tied to AI, including AI agents going rogue and attempting to hack into federal databases. The president has made clear that he considers outpacing China and preserving AI-driven economic gains a higher priority than addressing growing public concerns, and previously referred to fears over AI as being a “hoax.” His support for the technology comes amid widespread frustrations over the data centers used to support it, which are shaking up midterm races. The president hosted top AI executives at the White House last week. The group signed a new commitment aimed at better “self-policing” their companies’ AI models, arguing that the light-touch approach represents the best way to balance safety concerns with the president’s desire to accelerate a technology he’s dubbed “Super Intelligence.” “I’m seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police,” Trump told reporters. “These models are very complex and, again, I believe they’re going to be used for the good.” When asked about AI during his confirmation hearing to lead the US intelligence community, Clayton said the technology is a “game changer.” “When something’s both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it,” Clayton said. extraction.body: President Donald Trump announced a new "Super Intelligence Force" in a post on Truth Social Sunday, just days after signing an executive order renaming Artificial Intelligence. Trump says the force will "ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence," by coordinating the federal government's efforts. "The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump said on Truth Social. He said the force will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering and Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael, and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor will all serve as vice chairs. Clayton spoke with The Wall Street Journal about the force, saying, "The president asked that a group be put together." He said the panel has been tasked with reporting on the risks and opportunities AI poses within 120 days, and emphasized the U.S. government's desire to lead the industry, saying "the risk of not being first is high." According to The Journal, the force will review AI-related risks and current government reporting mechanisms, checking them for breaches, hacks and other incidents and issues. The Journal says in addition to Clayton and the vice chairs, Super Intelligence Force members will include Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. Super Intelligence vs AI The force is just the latest effort Trump has made, using the term superintelligence rather than artificial intelligence. During a UN General Assembly meeting last month, Trump said the word artificial "makes it sound fake, and it is not fake, it's actually amazing." Since then, he's signed an executive order directing the U.S. government to officially rebrand AI as "super intelligence" in federal communications.

sources.title: Trump Creates 'Super Intelligence Force' for AI Oversight
passages: The White House dropped a bombshell today with Trump's announcement of a dedicated 'Super Intelligence Force' - a new federal taskforce that will tackle the growing complexities of AI policy and oversight.

extraction.body: President Trump just announced the creation of a 'Super Intelligence Force' to oversee AI policy, naming his national intelligence chief to head the new taskforce. The move comes as Washington grapples with mounting concerns over artificial intelligence's rapid development and potential national security implications. This represents the most significant federal AI oversight initiative since the technology exploded into mainstream use. The White House dropped a bombshell today with Trump's announcement of a dedicated 'Super Intelligence Force' - a new federal taskforce that will tackle the growing complexities of AI policy and oversight. The president has tapped his national intelligence chief to spearhead this initiative, signaling just how seriously the administration views AI's potential impact on national security and economic competitiveness. The decision to place this under intelligence leadership rather than a tech-focused agency like the FTC speaks volumes about how the administration views AI - primarily through a national security lens. This mirrors similar moves by allies, where governments are treating advanced AI capabilities as strategic assets that need careful oversight and protection. The taskforce will likely focus on several key areas: preventing AI technology transfer to adversaries, establishing safety standards for advanced AI systems, and coordinating between federal agencies that are already working on AI initiatives. The Pentagon, Commerce Department, and NSF have all launched their own AI programs, creating a patchwork of oversight that this new force could help streamline. What makes this particularly interesting is the 'Super Intelligence' branding - a term that typically refers to AI systems that surpass human intelligence across all domains. The announcement comes as Nvidia's latest chips continue enabling more powerful AI training, while startups and established tech giants alike pour billions into developing increasingly sophisticated models. The question isn't whether more advanced AI is coming - it's how quickly, and whether government oversight can keep pace. For the tech industry, this could mean new compliance requirements, security clearances for certain AI research, and potentially restrictions on international collaborations. Trump's Super Intelligence Force represents a watershed moment in AI governance - the first time a U.S. administration has created a dedicated, high-level taskforce specifically for AI oversight. With intelligence leadership at the helm, this signals that AI policy will be driven primarily by national security considerations rather than innovation-first approaches. The tech industry should expect new regulations, compliance requirements, and a much more hands-on federal approach to AI development in the months ahead.

Australia in the World: 2025 Snapshot focuses on a key element of our national power: our foreign policy. It explains how we can protect Australia’s security, stability and prosperity at this time of growing uncertainty: focusing on our region, where our interests are most at stake; investing not only in traditional but also in more diverse relationships; and upholding international rules that protect us all. The starting point of my work as Australia's Minister for Foreign Affairs has always been who we are and what we want - because these are the overriding national interests that our foreign policy projects and protects. We are one of the world's great and enduring democracies. Our people have an abiding tradition of respect for the dignity, rights and freedoms of every individual, founded upon the rule of law. Our national power comes from our people, our economic strength, our military and strategic capabilities, our development assistance and our diplomatic engagement with other countries. This 2025 Snapshot focuses on a key element of our national power: our foreign policy. It explains how we can protect our security, stability and prosperity at this time of growing uncertainty: focusing on our region, where our interests are most at stake; investing not only in traditional but also in more diverse relationships; and upholding international rules that protect us all. In my first year as Foreign Minister, I emphasised our commitment by travelling to every Pacific Islands Forum member and all of the countries of ASEAN, other than Myanmar - engagement we continue to build on. By combining all arms of our national power - including economic, strategic, diplomatic, development and military - as well as by working with our partners, we can advance our interests and values, and create a credible deterrent for any potential adversary. In our region, Australia is progressing Pacific partnerships in unprecedented ways, turbocharging our economic ties with Southeast Asia, and upgrading and diversifying key relationships. In the world, we are defending and upholding global rules, protecting Australian citizens, and promoting Australia's interests in peace, security and trade. We live in an interconnected world, but what matters most to Australia's future is our own region, the Indo-Pacific. Over 50,000 Australian students have participated in New Colombo Plan study programs, language training, internships, and research across 40 locations in our region. Recent reforms to the New Colombo Plan will ensure the program supports Australia's strategic objectives to deepen engagement in our region and lift the capability of our people. These reforms include a greater emphasis on students learning languages and undertaking longer-term study experiences in the Indo-Pacific, and augment our reputation for world-class international education. Nowhere better encapsulates Australia's opportunities and challenges than the region to our north: Southeast Asia. Navigating these dynamics requires deeper engagement, fostering alignment, and building the Asia capability of the Australian population. This includes increasing people-to-people links with the region, through the ASEAN-Australia Centre and the reformed New Colombo Plan - as well as more trade and investment through Invested: Australia's Southeast Asia Economic Strategy to 2040. For the same reasons, Australia has formally upgraded our diplomatic relationships with Vietnam, Philippines, Brunei and Laos. We have signed a Defence Cooperation Agreement with Indonesia and we continue to deepen our longstanding ties with Malaysia and Singapore, where our cooperation is underpinned by Comprehensive Strategic Partnerships. We are working to support Timor-Leste's long-term economic growth and advance our shared interest in a peaceful, stable and prosperous region. In 2024, Prime Minister Albanese hosted leaders of ASEAN and Timor-Leste for the ASEAN-Australia Special Summit in Melbourne to celebrate 50 years since Australia became ASEAN's first formal Dialogue Partner. During the Summit, the Australian Government announced over $500 million in new and expanded initiatives to deepen our economic and cultural ties, further our people-to-people engagement and strengthen our educational and environmental cooperation, reinforcing Australia's deep commitment to Southeast Asia and ASEAN. Indonesia stands as a major and growing power in our region and beyond, and is one of Australia's closest friends and partners. Indonesia is the world's largest Muslim-majority country, the world's third largest democracy, and over the next fifteen years, it is projected to become the world's fifth largest economy. Indonesia's success has always been central to Australia's success, which is why Australia was one of the earliest supporters of a sovereign and independent Indonesia. We will continue to deepen our trade and investment, development, security and defence ties, including through our landmark Defence Cooperation Agreement, the Indonesia-Australia Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, and Invested: Australia's Southeast Asia Economic Strategy to 2040. We are working closely with regional partners to uphold international law in the South China Sea, including through the cooperative maritime activity between Australia, the Philippines, Japan and the United States held in 2024. At the ASEAN-Australia Special Summit in March 2024, the Australian Government committed a further $64 million to enhance Australia's Southeast Asia Maritime Partnerships. In December 2024, Australia launched the Southeast Asia Maritime Institute in Malaysia, led by the University of Wollongong's Australian National Centre for Ocean Resources and Security. The Prime Minister launched Invested: Australia's Southeast Asia Economic Strategy to 2040 in Jakarta in September 2023. As part of that Strategy, initiatives are now being implemented to help more Australian businesses seize the opportunities in one of the world's fastest growing regions. This includes the establishment of the $2 billion Southeast Asia Investment Financing Facility (SEAIFF). The SEAIFF will provide loans, guarantees, equity and insurance for projects that will boost Australian trade and investment in Southeast Asia, particularly in support of the region's clean energy transition and infrastructure development. The Australian Prime Minister visited China in 2023, and the Chinese Premier visited Australia in 2024, with both visits taking place for the first time in seven years. Through direct dialogue, as well as advocacy at the World Trade Organization, Australia has secured China's agreement to lift all trade impediments that it had placed on $20 billion of Australian exports. Australia and China continue to have different systems and values. Australia is clear about our concerns with China's human rights record or when China's actions run counter to the region's interests in peace and stability - including in the South China Sea and the Taiwan Strait. We seek to address our concerns through dialogue and by upholding rules, while working with our partners to do the same. Japan's status as an Indo-Pacific power makes it central to Australia's security and prosperity. As democracies and middle powers, we share perspectives on responding to challenges in our region. Together, we are modernising our substantial trade, investment, defence and security links. We have agreed a Joint Declaration on Security Cooperation and a Reciprocal Access Agreement, enabling closer cooperation in peacetime and in conflict. Australia and Japan are also pooling our resources and capabilities to support joint projects, such as Telstra's acquisition of Digicel Pacific and the East Micronesia Cable. Our history of investment and scientific research collaboration are helping us both decarbonise our economies and achieve net zero. The new Australia-Japan Critical Minerals Partnership will contribute to building secure and trusted supply chains for these important resources. While sanctions are rarely our first choice in sending a strong message, targeted sanctions are one of the key tools for Australia to respond to situations of international concern, including to deter and disrupt breaches of international law, egregious human rights abuses and other threats to our national interest. Where it is in our national interest to do so, Australia coordinates with international partners to apply sanctions, and is investing $26.4 million in monitoring and enforcement. Australia has taken its strongest action ever on Iran, with sanctions on hundreds of Iranian-linked individuals and entities, including with links to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Australia’s diplomatic network spans 171 overseas posts and consulates in more than 90 countries around the world. This presence enables us to promote Australia’s interests in peace, security, trade, investment and other areas of cooperation. Australia's efforts in the world keep Australians more secure at home, but as the world becomes more uncertain and unstable, the Australian Government's support for Australians overseas is increasingly important. There are more than one million Australians overseas at any time. Following disasters and conflicts in recent years, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade assisted the departure of over 3,400 Australians and their families from Lebanon, more than 850 from Israel and the Occupied Palestinian Territories, over 680 from Vanuatu, more than 450 from New Caledonia and over 200 from Sudan.

extraction.body: Foreign Minister Penny Wong (Daniel Walding/DFAT) Shifting more funds to infrastructure makes sense but implementation is the real test. Australia doubles down on Pacific infrastructure The Australian government announced last week it would invest an additional $550 million in its infrastructure facility for the Pacific Islands. This is a welcome development and in line with a Lowy Institute policy brief we wrote last year. As we noted then, the Australian Infrastructure Financing Facility for the Pacific (AIFFP) has been a gamechanger for Australia’s role in the Pacific. Before this, we estimate Australia was investing about $115 million a year in climate-resilient infrastructure. With the AIFFP and its $2 billion pipeline of projects approved thus far, we estimated that Australia will be providing around $270 million in annual investment. The facility was however quickly running out of financing firepower. It still had about $2 billion in lending capacity. But it had largely exhausted its $1 billion allocation of grants. The ability to mix grants with loans is crucial to ensure overall AIFFP financing terms are concessional enough for fragile Pacific economies that cannot sustainably borrow at normal market rates. Pure grant financed projects are also needed, especially for climate adaptation in the most vulnerable countries. The announcement itself came with few specifics, but AIFFP has confirmed to us that the increased funding will take the form of additional grants. More grants will allow Australia to continue building out its pipeline of infrastructure projects in the Pacific without disruption. Given the AIFFP’s track record to date of a 1:1 ratio in loan-to-grant financing and assuming it is disbursed over ten years, this could result in up to $110 million in additional annual investment. Though Australia should aim to rely less on loans and more on grants, meaning the increase in financing would be lower than this. For one, the AIFFP should do more pure grant financing for climate adaptation projects in the most vulnerable countries. Secondly, even Papua New Guinea and Fiji that have some capacity to borrow still likely require more concessional financing terms than what the AIFFP has historically provided. AIFFP lending terms are also generally more expensive than China’s or the multilateral development banks, making the facility more reliant on mixing in grants to be competitive. Finally, to the extent that Australia prioritises projects based on their “strategic” rather economic merit, this again is likely to necessitate more concessional financing. Government officials in the Pacific might appreciate the technical support they receive but it is largely invisible to political elites and the public more broadly. Even so, a $550 million infusion of grants will have a big impact. We estimate it should be enough to take total Australian investment in climate-resilient Pacific infrastructure to around $325–380 million annually. This would be around twice the $180 million China provided for all its infrastructure projects in 2023. More grants for AIFFP will likely come from reduced spending elsewhere in the aid budget. As we argued last year, while it would be better to increase Australia’s aggregate aid spend, redirecting more to the AIFFP within a fixed total aid budget is still a good idea. Climate adaptation and traditional development spending in areas such as health, education and poverty reduction need to go hand in hand. And currently Pacific climate adaptation is woefully under-funded, with infrastructure the biggest funding gap. It is also the case that, by our estimate, some 40-50% of Australia’s aid to the Pacific tends to be spent on technical assistance, mostly expatriate advisors. Hence, redirecting more aid to infrastructure does not necessarily mean less spending on health or education services, but rather less on technical advice and capacity building. Advisors definitely play an important role. Better governance is arguably the holy grail of development. But improving governance is rarely about how many advisors are provided. Australia spends far more on this than other donors and it remains a longstanding source of concern over the effectiveness of the aid program. Shifting from governance to infrastructure also makes diplomatic sense. Government officials in the Pacific might appreciate the technical support they receive but it is largely invisible to political elites and the public more broadly. In the soft power contest, providing advisors cannot compete with the tangibility of hard infrastructure investments . This is one reason why Australia finds itself battling with China for influence in the Pacific despite outspending China by almost seven-fold in total development support. It is not clear what the focus of the additional funding will be. The AIFFP has tended to prioritise large scale projects in ports, airports and undersea cables. But there are many other important priorities that need funding such as community level capital works, ongoing infrastructure maintenance, and retrofitting existing assets for greater climate resilience. The effectiveness of AIFFP investments will also ultimately depend on partner government policies, but it is not clear how Australia is trying to address this beyond providing technical assistance. In our policy brief we suggested linking AIFFP funding to the quality of partner government policies as a way of channelling investments to where they will be most effective and incentivising partner governments to undertake reforms that would improve the benefit and sustainability of AIFFP investments. Most important is the issue of Australia’s capacity to deliver. Building infrastructure in the Pacific is hard. The last publicly released review in 2022 found the facility was performing well but raised questions about staffing and operating models. The AIFFP has since amassed around $2 billion in signed projects, most still under implementation. Delivery will be much harder than signing deals. Yet, more money also means having to develop more high-quality projects, which will become more difficult as the lowest hanging fruit has already been plucked. Australia doubling down on Pacific infrastructure makes sense. With new funding in place, the next part is making sure Australia can deliver. Roland Rajah is Lead Economist and Director of the Indo-Pacific Development Centre at the Lowy Institute, focusing on economic development challenges across Southeast Asia, the Pacific Islands, and South Asia. His research spans macroeconomics, aid and development finance, geoeconomics, and regional integration. Riley Duke is a Research Fellow at the Lowy Institute and lead author of the Institute's Pacific Aid Map . Georgia Hammersley was a Research Associate in the Lowy Institute’s Indo-Pacific Development Centre . passages: Foreign Minister Penny Wong (Daniel Walding/DFAT)
Shifting more funds to infrastructure makes sense but implementation is the real test.
Australia doubles down on Pacific infrastructure

The Australian government announced last week it would invest an additional $550 million in its infrastructure facility for the Pacific Islands. This is a welcome development and in line with a Lowy Institute policy brief we wrote last year.

As we noted then, the Australian Infrastructure Financing Facility for the Pacific (AIFFP) has been a gamechanger for Australia’s role in the Pacific. Before this, we estimate Australia was investing about $115 million a year in climate-resilient infrastructure. With the AIFFP and its $2 billion pipeline of projects approved thus far, we estimated that Australia will be providing around $270 million in annual investment.

The facility was however quickly running out of financing firepower. It still had about $2 billion in lending capacity. But it had largely exhausted its $1 billion allocation of grants. The ability to mix grants with loans is crucial to ensure overall AIFFP financing terms are concessional enough for fragile Pacific economies that cannot sustainably borrow at normal market rates. Pure grant financed projects are also needed, especially for climate adaptation in the most vulnerable countries.
The announcement itself came with few specifics, but AIFFP has confirmed to us that the increased funding will take the form of additional grants.

More grants will allow Australia to continue building out its pipeline of infrastructure projects in the Pacific without disruption. Given the AIFFP’s track record to date of a 1:1 ratio in loan-to-grant financing and assuming it is disbursed over ten years, this could result in up to $110 million in additional annual investment. Though Australia should aim to rely less on loans and more on grants, meaning the increase in financing would be lower than this.

For one, the AIFFP should do more pure grant financing for climate adaptation projects in the most vulnerable countries. Secondly, even Papua New Guinea and Fiji that have some capacity to borrow still likely require more concessional financing terms than what the AIFFP has historically provided. AIFFP lending terms are also generally more expensive than China’s or the multilateral development banks, making the facility more reliant on mixing in grants to be competitive. Finally, to the extent that Australia prioritises projects based on their “strategic” rather economic merit, this again is likely to necessitate more concessional financing.
Government officials in the Pacific might appreciate the technical support they receive but it is largely invisible to political elites and the public more broadly.

Even so, a $550 million infusion of grants will have a big impact. We estimate it should be enough to take total Australian investment in climate-resilient Pacific infrastructure to around $325–380 million annually. This would be around twice the $180 million China provided for all its infrastructure projects in 2023.

More grants for AIFFP will likely come from reduced spending elsewhere in the aid budget. As we argued last year, while it would be better to increase Australia’s aggregate aid spend, redirecting more to the AIFFP within a fixed total aid budget is still a good idea. Climate adaptation and traditional development spending in areas such as health, education and poverty reduction need to go hand in hand. And currently Pacific climate adaptation is woefully under-funded, with infrastructure the biggest funding gap.

It is also the case that, by our estimate, some 40-50% of Australia’s aid to the Pacific tends to be spent on technical assistance, mostly expatriate advisors. Hence, redirecting more aid to infrastructure does not necessarily mean less spending on health or education services, but rather less on technical advice and capacity building.

Advisors definitely play an important role. Better governance is arguably the holy grail of development. But improving governance is rarely about how many advisors are provided. Australia spends far more on this than other donors and it remains a longstanding source of concern over the effectiveness of the aid program.

Shifting from governance to infrastructure also makes diplomatic sense. Government officials in the Pacific might appreciate the technical support they receive but it is largely invisible to political elites and the public more broadly. In the soft power contest, providing advisors cannot compete with the tangibility of hard infrastructure investments . This is one reason why Australia finds itself battling with China for influence in the Pacific despite outspending China by almost seven-fold in total development support.

It is not clear what the focus of the additional funding will be. The AIFFP has tended to prioritise large scale projects in ports, airports and undersea cables. But there are many other important priorities that need funding such as community level capital works, ongoing infrastructure maintenance, and retrofitting existing assets for greater climate resilience.

The effectiveness of AIFFP investments will also ultimately depend on partner government policies, but it is not clear how Australia is trying to address this beyond providing technical assistance. In our policy brief we suggested linking AIFFP funding to the quality of partner government policies as a way of channelling investments to where they will be most effective and incentivising partner governments to undertake reforms that would improve the benefit and sustainability of AIFFP investments.

Most important is the issue of Australia’s capacity to deliver. Building infrastructure in the Pacific is hard. The last publicly released review in 2022 found the facility was performing well but raised questions about staffing and operating models. The AIFFP has since amassed around $2 billion in signed projects, most still under implementation. Delivery will be much harder than signing deals. Yet, more money also means having to develop more high-quality projects, which will become more difficult as the lowest hanging fruit has already been plucked.
Australia doubling down on Pacific infrastructure makes sense. With new funding in place, the next part is making sure Australia can deliver.

Roland Rajah is Lead Economist and Director of the Indo-Pacific Development Centre at the Lowy Institute, focusing on economic development challenges across Southeast Asia, the Pacific Islands, and South Asia. His research spans macroeconomics, aid and development finance, geoeconomics, and regional integration.
Riley Duke is a Research Fellow at the Lowy Institute and lead author of the Institute's Pacific Aid Map .
Georgia Hammersley was a Research Associate in the Lowy Institute’s Indo-Pacific Development Centre .

extraction.body: Home Australian Outlook Blog Posts Fresh perspectives Australia Cannot Buy Pacific Influence with More Aid With Chinese development finance flowing into the Pacific and Western aid in record retreat, Canberra can’t outspend Beijing. Australia’s best bet for lasting influence is to hand Pacific partners real control over how aid is designed and delivered. With a 43 per cent increase in Chinese development finance to the Pacific , alongside Beijing’s broader geopolitical push into a region Australia has traditionally considered central to its strategic interests, Canberra’s geostrategic position is coming under increasing pressure. At the same time, the Western aid system is retreating. Official Development Assistance (ODA) fell by 23.1 per cent in 2025 , the largest annual contraction on record, with Germany, the United States, United Kingdom, Japan and France accounting for almost all of the decline. US aid alone fell by 56.9 per cent. Australia’s aid effort has followed the same broader decline over the longer term, falling substantially relative to national income and losing political salience at home . The problem for Australia is clear: China is expanding its development presence in the Pacific at a time when much of Western aid is retreating and Australia’s overall aid effort remains historically low relative to national income. In this environment, Canberra cannot assume that throwing more money at the region will in turn generate more loyalty. Pacific states have their own interests and priorities, and aid does not automatically generate influence. On the other hand, Canberra cannot afford to think this way. Australia cannot win a competition for Pacific influence simply by trying to match China dollar for dollar. It must compete differently. That means changing not only the scope of the aid Australia provides, but who has power over how it is designed and delivered. Giving Pacific governments, civil society and local organisations greater authority can strengthen local agency, build trust and legitimacy, and ultimately strengthen Australia’s long-term relationships in the region. If Australia wants influence in the Pacific, it needs to earn it. Pacific governments are deliberate when it comes to choosing foreign development programs, weighing up how well they serve their own interests, and perhaps more importantly, what kind of partnerships they come attached to. Research into Pacific perceptions of Beijing demonstrates this clearly, with many Pacific actors welcoming Chinese development opportunities whilst remaining cautious about the debt, transparency and sovereignty concerns that accompany them. However, there is also research to suggest that this scepticism extends to Australian engagement as well. What stands out is Pacific nations do not automatically accept foreign influence simply because assistance is on offer, regardless of the geopolitical affiliations. This offers an important lesson for Australia. By accepting aid, Pacific nations are not necessarily signalling political alignment, unconditional trust or a lack of awareness for the geopolitical competition driving development initiatives. In fact, it is quite the opposite. This does not mean geopolitics should be removed from Australian aid. That would be unrealistic. Geopolitical competition can help explain where Australia directs its aid and why particular programs are prioritised. But it cannot, by itself, determine what makes aid effective. In any case, if Canberra wants to genuinely strengthen its influence over the long term, Australia needs to become a more effective, trusted and locally legitimate development partner. In earning that legitimacy, however, lies somewhat of a paradox: Australia may strengthen its regional position not by controlling more, but by giving Pacific partners greater control. Strategic competition may tempt Canberra to tighten its grip on aid. But in actuality too much control risks weakening the very relationships Australian aid hopes to strengthen. Pacific aid has become increasingly “politici[s]ed, privati[s]ed and contested” . Much of Australia’s assistance is concentrated among just four major contractors – Abt Global, DT Global, Tetra Tech and Palladium – while Pacific firms and institutions can remain marginalised from the very programs designed to support them. The issue is not simply who funds development. It is who gets to control it. Large contractors are not inherently the problem. Complex programs require technical expertise, financial oversight and the capacity to deliver major projects. The problem emerges when Canberra identifies the problem, determines the priorities, designs the program and controls implementation, leaving Pacific passive actors as recipients instead of genuine development partners. Aid may deliver projects, reports and funding without delivering genuine local agency. A 2025 independent evaluation of the Australian Humanitarian Partnership found that funding to local partners had risen from around 20 per cent in 2018 to more than 40 per cent by 2024. More importantly, locally co-chaired coordination arrangements were found to improve trust and transparency. That matters. Localisation is not simply about fairness or representation. It can strengthen the trust and relationships on which effective aid, and ultimately Australian influence, depend. Localisation cannot simply involve consulting Pacific communities after Canberra has already identified the problem, designed the program and decided how the money will be spent. It must mean giving Pacific actors greater authority over those decisions in the first place. That requires shifting more funding, decision-making and implementation power towards Pacific governments, civil society organisations and local firms. There is also no single set of “Pacific priorities”. While Papua New Guinea faces major challengers in turning economic growth into jobs and extending infrastructure and basic services to a large, dispersed population, Fiji places particular a stronger emphasis on climate and disaster resilience. A few kilometres away, Solomon Islands faces its own pressures around job creation, public finances and economic diversification. These differences strengthen the case for greater context-specific and local decision-making, rather than attempting to design development priorities predominantly from Canberra. Again, this does not mean Australia should abandon its own national interests. Canberra is entitled to care about regional security, the development outcomes of its neighbours and the responsible use of Australian public money helping to support those initiatives. Nor should localisation mean abandoning Australian channels for accountability, financial oversight or evaluation. But accountability should not become an excuse for permanent donor control. The challenge is to build these accountability measures with Pacific partners, while giving them a greater role in determining what development should look like in their own communities. This is where development policy and strategic policy can support one another. More transparent, locally led and trusted aid can strengthen Australia’s strategic position indirectly because influence ultimately depends on relationships, credibility and legitimacy, not simply how much money Canberra spends. Australia does not need to reinvent its aid system. What it needs is practical, incremental, and pragmatic reform within the system it already has. Canberra should do fewer things better: simplify fragmented programs, concentrate resources on initiatives with a strong evidence base, and shift greater funding and implementation authority towards Pacific governments, civil society and local firms. External expertise will still be necessary, but it should support Pacific capability instead of substitute for it. Australia has already committed itself to this direction. At the 55 th Pacific Islands Forum Leaders’ Meeting in Palau from 31 August to 3 September 2026 , Prime Minister Anthony Albanese argued that the region’s major challenges require solutions “designed and delivered for the Pacific, by the Pacific” . That emphasis on partnership has since appeared more broadly in Australia’s foreign policy, with the government’s September 2026 UN Security Council campaign pledging to “listen with respect” and “partner as equals”. DFAT similarly describes its approach as “Pacific-led, Australian-backed” and places locally led development at the centre of its development policy. The real test is whether that language produces a genuine shift in who controls funding, implementation and decision-making. That shift does not require Australia to abandon its strategic interests. Competition with China will continue to shape where and why Canberra spends development funding. But Pacific agency, trust and legitimacy will increasingly determine whether that spending truly produces lasting influence. Done properly, Australia’s strategic interests and locally led development in the Pacific are not competing goals but mutually reinforcing ones. Championing Pacific-led development sits firmly within Australia’s interests. If Canberra wants to remain a trusted and influential Pacific partner, out-competing Beijing or simply spending more will not be enough. Australia must build relationships in which Pacific states have greater power to shape the development programs intended for them. Aid can assist Australia in expanding its regional influence, but Canberra would do well to remember that it cannot buy Pacific loyalty. passages: Home Australian Outlook Blog Posts Fresh perspectives Australia Cannot Buy Pacific Influence with More Aid

With Chinese development finance flowing into the Pacific and Western aid in record retreat, Canberra can’t outspend Beijing. Australia’s best bet for lasting influence is to hand Pacific partners real control over how aid is designed and delivered.

With a 43 per cent increase in Chinese development finance to the Pacific , alongside Beijing’s broader geopolitical push into a region Australia has traditionally considered central to its strategic interests, Canberra’s geostrategic position is coming under increasing pressure.

At the same time, the Western aid system is retreating. Official Development Assistance (ODA) fell by 23.1 per cent in 2025 , the largest annual contraction on record, with Germany, the United States, United Kingdom, Japan and France accounting for almost all of the decline. US aid alone fell by 56.9 per cent. Australia’s aid effort has followed the same broader decline over the longer term, falling substantially relative to national income and losing political salience at home .

The problem for Australia is clear: China is expanding its development presence in the Pacific at a time when much of Western aid is retreating and Australia’s overall aid effort remains historically low relative to national income.

In this environment, Canberra cannot assume that throwing more money at the region will in turn generate more loyalty. Pacific states have their own interests and priorities, and aid does not automatically generate influence. On the other hand, Canberra cannot afford to think this way.
Australia cannot win a competition for Pacific influence simply by trying to match China dollar for dollar. It must compete differently.

That means changing not only the scope of the aid Australia provides, but who has power over how it is designed and delivered. Giving Pacific governments, civil society and local organisations greater authority can strengthen local agency, build trust and legitimacy, and ultimately strengthen Australia’s long-term relationships in the region.
If Australia wants influence in the Pacific, it needs to earn it.

Pacific governments are deliberate when it comes to choosing foreign development programs, weighing up how well they serve their own interests, and perhaps more importantly, what kind of partnerships they come attached to. Research into Pacific perceptions of Beijing demonstrates this clearly, with many Pacific actors welcoming Chinese development opportunities whilst remaining cautious about the debt, transparency and sovereignty concerns that accompany them. However, there is also research to suggest that this scepticism extends to Australian engagement as well. What stands out is Pacific nations do not automatically accept foreign influence simply because assistance is on offer, regardless of the geopolitical affiliations.

This offers an important lesson for Australia. By accepting aid, Pacific nations are not necessarily signalling political alignment, unconditional trust or a lack of awareness for the geopolitical competition driving development initiatives. In fact, it is quite the opposite.

This does not mean geopolitics should be removed from Australian aid. That would be unrealistic. Geopolitical competition can help explain where Australia directs its aid and why particular programs are prioritised. But it cannot, by itself, determine what makes aid effective. In any case, if Canberra wants to genuinely strengthen its influence over the long term, Australia needs to become a more effective, trusted and locally legitimate development partner.

In earning that legitimacy, however, lies somewhat of a paradox: Australia may strengthen its regional position not by controlling more, but by giving Pacific partners greater control. Strategic competition may tempt Canberra to tighten its grip on aid. But in actuality too much control risks weakening the very relationships Australian aid hopes to strengthen.

Pacific aid has become increasingly “politici[s]ed, privati[s]ed and contested” . Much of Australia’s assistance is concentrated among just four major contractors – Abt Global, DT Global, Tetra Tech and Palladium – while Pacific firms and institutions can remain marginalised from the very programs designed to support them. The issue is not simply who funds development. It is who gets to control it.

Large contractors are not inherently the problem. Complex programs require technical expertise, financial oversight and the capacity to deliver major projects. The problem emerges when Canberra identifies the problem, determines the priorities, designs the program and controls implementation, leaving Pacific passive actors as recipients instead of genuine development partners.
Aid may deliver projects, reports and funding without delivering genuine local agency.

A 2025 independent evaluation of the Australian Humanitarian Partnership found that funding to local partners had risen from around 20 per cent in 2018 to more than 40 per cent by 2024. More importantly, locally co-chaired coordination arrangements were found to improve trust and transparency.
That matters. Localisation is not simply about fairness or representation. It can strengthen the trust and relationships on which effective aid, and ultimately Australian influence, depend.

Localisation cannot simply involve consulting Pacific communities after Canberra has already identified the problem, designed the program and decided how the money will be spent. It must mean giving Pacific actors greater authority over those decisions in the first place.
That requires shifting more funding, decision-making and implementation power towards Pacific governments, civil society organisations and local firms.

There is also no single set of “Pacific priorities”. While Papua New Guinea faces major challengers in turning economic growth into jobs and extending infrastructure and basic services to a large, dispersed population, Fiji places particular a stronger emphasis on climate and disaster resilience. A few kilometres away, Solomon Islands faces its own pressures around job creation, public finances and economic diversification. These differences strengthen the case for greater context-specific and local decision-making, rather than attempting to design development priorities predominantly from Canberra.

Again, this does not mean Australia should abandon its own national interests. Canberra is entitled to care about regional security, the development outcomes of its neighbours and the responsible use of Australian public money helping to support those initiatives. Nor should localisation mean abandoning Australian channels for accountability, financial oversight or evaluation. But accountability should not become an excuse for permanent donor control. The challenge is to build these accountability measures with Pacific partners, while giving them a greater role in determining what development should look like in their own communities.

This is where development policy and strategic policy can support one another. More transparent, locally led and trusted aid can strengthen Australia’s strategic position indirectly because influence ultimately depends on relationships, credibility and legitimacy, not simply how much money Canberra spends.
Australia does not need to reinvent its aid system. What it needs is practical, incremental, and pragmatic reform within the system it already has.

Canberra should do fewer things better: simplify fragmented programs, concentrate resources on initiatives with a strong evidence base, and shift greater funding and implementation authority towards Pacific governments, civil society and local firms. External expertise will still be necessary, but it should support Pacific capability instead of substitute for it.

Australia has already committed itself to this direction. At the 55 th Pacific Islands Forum Leaders’ Meeting in Palau from 31 August to 3 September 2026 , Prime Minister Anthony Albanese argued that the region’s major challenges require solutions “designed and delivered for the Pacific, by the Pacific” . That emphasis on partnership has since appeared more broadly in Australia’s foreign policy, with the government’s September 2026 UN Security Council campaign pledging to “listen with respect” and “partner as equals”. DFAT similarly describes its approach as “Pacific-led, Australian-backed” and places locally led development at the centre of its development policy. The real test is whether that language produces a genuine shift in who controls funding, implementation and decision-making.

That shift does not require Australia to abandon its strategic interests. Competition with China will continue to shape where and why Canberra spends development funding. But Pacific agency, trust and legitimacy will increasingly determine whether that spending truly produces lasting influence.

Done properly, Australia’s strategic interests and locally led development in the Pacific are not competing goals but mutually reinforcing ones. Championing Pacific-led development sits firmly within Australia’s interests. If Canberra wants to remain a trusted and influential Pacific partner, out-competing Beijing or simply spending more will not be enough. Australia must build relationships in which Pacific states have greater power to shape the development programs intended for them.

Aid can assist Australia in expanding its regional influence, but Canberra would do well to remember that it cannot buy Pacific loyalty. It must earn it, by supporting Pacific plans and priorities on Pacific terms.

His research interests include Australian foreign policy, development, diplomacy and Asia-Pacific security.

coreStoryFacts.text: Australia in the World: 2025 Snapshot focuses on a key element of our national power: our foreign policy.

It explains how we can protect Australia’s security, stability and prosperity at this time of growing uncertainty: focusing on our region, where our interests are most at stake; investing not only in traditional but also in more diverse relationships; and upholding international rules that protect us all.
There are more than one million Australians overseas at any time.

Following disasters and conflicts in recent years, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade assisted the departure of over 3,400 Australians and their families from Lebanon, more than 850 from Israel and the Occupied Palestinian Territories, over 680 from Vanuatu, more than 450 from New Caledonia and over 200 from Sudan.
In our region, Australia is progressing Pacific partnerships in unprecedented ways, turbocharging our economic ties with Southeast Asia, and upgrading and diversifying key relationships.

Through direct dialogue, as well as advocacy at the World Trade Organization, Australia has secured China's agreement to lift all trade impediments that it had placed on $20 billion of Australian exports.

In 2024, Prime Minister Albanese hosted leaders of ASEAN and Timor-Leste for the ASEAN-Australia Special Summit in Melbourne to celebrate 50 years since Australia became ASEAN's first formal Dialogue Partner.
The Prime Minister launched Invested: Australia's Southeast Asia Economic Strategy to 2040 in Jakarta in September 2023.
As part of that Strategy, initiatives are now being implemented to help more Australian businesses seize the opportunities in one of the world's fastest growing regions.
This includes the establishment of the $2 billion Southeast Asia Investment Financing Facility (SEAIFF).
This presence enables us to promote Australia’s interests in peace, security, trade, investment and other areas of cooperation.

These reforms include a greater emphasis on students learning languages and undertaking longer-term study experiences in the Indo-Pacific, and augment our reputation for world-class international education.
In December 2024, Australia launched the Southeast Asia Maritime Institute in Malaysia, led by the University of Wollongong's Australian National Centre for Ocean Resources and Security.
The Australian Passport Office and its agents are committed to providing a secure, efficient and responsive passport service for Australia.

We are working closely with regional partners to uphold international law in the South China Sea, including through the cooperative maritime activity between Australia, the Philippines, Japan and the United States held in 2024.
Together, we are modernising our substantial trade, investment, defence and security links.
We have agreed a Joint Declaration on Security Cooperation and a Reciprocal Access Agreement, enabling closer cooperation in peacetime and in conflict.
Australia and Japan are also pooling our resources and capabilities to support joint projects, such as Telstra's acquisition of Digicel Pacific and the East Micronesia Cable.
Australia and China continue to have different systems and values.
We seek to address our concerns through dialogue and by upholding rules, while working with our partners to do the same.
For the same reasons, Australia has formally upgraded our diplomatic relationships with Vietnam, Philippines, Brunei and Laos.

We have signed a Defence Cooperation Agreement with Indonesia and we continue to deepen our longstanding ties with Malaysia and Singapore, where our cooperation is underpinned by Comprehensive Strategic Partnerships.
Australia has taken its strongest action ever on Iran, with sanctions on hundreds of Iranian-linked individuals and entities, including with links to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Australia doubles down on Pacific infrastructure

Australia doubles down on Pacific infrastructure
With new funding in place, the next part is making sure Australia can deliver.
Copyright © 2026 Lowy Institute, 31 Bligh Street, Sydney NSW 2000, Australia
The Australian government announced last week it would invest an additional $550 million in its infrastructure facility for the Pacific Islands.
This is a welcome development and in line with a Lowy Institute policy brief we wrote last year.
Before this, we estimate Australia was investing about $115 million a year in climate-resilient infrastructure.
With the AIFFP and its $2 billion pipeline of projects approved thus far, we estimated that Australia will be providing around $270 million in annual investment.
More grants will allow Australia to continue building out its pipeline of infrastructure projects in the Pacific without disruption.
Though Australia should aim to rely less on loans and more on grants, meaning the increase in financing would be lower than this.
Most important is the issue of Australia’s capacity to deliver.
The last publicly released review in 2022 found the facility was performing well but raised questions about staffing and operating models.
Delivery will be much harder than signing deals.
Yet, more money also means having to develop more high-quality projects, which will become more difficult as the lowest hanging fruit has already been plucked.
Hence, redirecting more aid to infrastructure does not necessarily mean less spending on health or education services, but rather less on technical advice and capacity building.
As we argued last year, while it would be better to increase Australia’s aggregate aid spend, redirecting more to the AIFFP within a fixed total aid budget is still a good idea.
Climate adaptation and traditional development spending in areas such as health, education and poverty reduction need to go hand in hand.
And currently Pacific climate adaptation is woefully under-funded, with infrastructure the biggest funding gap.
Even so, a $550 million infusion of grants will have a big impact.
Shifting from governance to infrastructure also makes diplomatic sense.
In the soft power contest, providing advisors cannot compete with the tangibility of hard infrastructure investments .

It still had about $2 billion in lending capacity.
But it had largely exhausted its $1 billion allocation of grants.
