coreStoryFacts.text: Finally, the case has elements of a domestic US political drama which—regardless of objective reality—has altered perceptions about the integrity of the process in a Balkans region that is already prone to viewing war-crimes tribunals as politically controlled by Western powers.
Thaçi’s indictment in 2020 was controversially announced while he was en route to the White House to meet with US President Donald Trump to sign a peace deal with Serbia.
Agon Maliqi is a nonresident senior fellow with the Atlantic Council’s Europe Center.
He is a political and foreign policy analyst from Pristina, Kosovo.
Rubin’s testimony was reinforced by Paul Williams, an international law expert who advised Kosovo’s delegation.

On September 22, John Stewart Duncan, then a British adviser to NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe who drafted and negotiated the KLA’s demilitarization deal, further corroborated this portrayal of the KLA’s command structure, adding that the guerilla army’s real power rested with regional commanders.

Washington’s reputation is involved because Thaçi, as Rubin noted in his testimony, worked closely with successive US administrations to lead Kosovo toward peace and independence and promote ethnic reconciliation.
For two decades, he was essentially seen as Washington’s man.
On September 15, the defense opened its case, announcing just fifteen witnesses— mostly senior Western officials with direct knowledge of events.
The strategy is not to deny the alleged crimes, which do not implicate Thaçi directly.

This reflects a longstanding US commitment—starting with the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in 1993—to pair Balkan peace deals with justice and accountability for war crimes.

Since November 2020, Thaçi has been in detention at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, a hybrid Kosovar–international court in The Hague, alongside three other members of the Kosovo Liberation Army’s (KLA) General Staff.
Their trial began in April 2023, and the prosecution took two years, concluding in April of this year.
Did a political representative of a guerrilla army have command responsibility for alleged crimes committed by its members during the Kosovo war?

It also comes at a time when caretaker Prime Minister Albin Kurti is increasingly at odds with Washington and Brussels over what US and EU officials see as destabilizing moves regarding relations with Serbia and the rights of Kosovo Serbs.

The indictment against Thaçi and the three others alleges that during 1998-1999—while the KLA waged a rural insurgency against the Yugoslav army and police, whose top leadership was found guilty of massacres and the ethnic cleansing of at least 700,000 Albanians—the KLA engaged in a number of illegal detentions, disappearances, mistreatment, and murders of civilians seen as political rivals and collaborators, both Albanian and Serb.

Drawing on his Kosovo experience and his recent stint as the head of the State Department’s Global Engagement Center under former President Joe Biden, Rubin also expressed his belief that many allegations against KLA leaders stemmed from Russian and Serbian propaganda.
A weekly column by Atlantic Council President and CEO Frederick Kempe, Inflection Points focuses on the global challenges facing the United States and how to best address them.
The first defense witness carried the weight of the US government of that era.
Rubin, former assistant secretary of state, testified for three days , accompanied by current State Department officials as observers.
That camp has favored closer cooperation with the West and has shown a greater willingness to pursue a final settlement with Serbia.
Rama’s relations with Kurti have arguably deteriorated beyond repair.

On September 16, a long-awaited verdict in the Hague shocked the small Balkan state of Kosovo, the youngest country in Europe.
Former leader Hashim Thaçi was convicted on a plethora of war crimes and sentenced to 25 years in prison.
Thaçi previously served as the state’s first prime minister, the political director of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), and as Kosovo's president at the time of his indictment in 2020.

His role as a founding father of his country extended beyond the war, leading it to independence and later steering it to a pro-European course diplomatically engaged with non-recognizing neighbor Serbia before his arrest.

As Western judges weighed and continue to weigh the fate of Kosovo’s path-charting leader, it is worth watching whether such a significant new development can shake so strong a partnership.
Serbia continues to play a major role in Kosovo’s affairs as its former home, wartime adversary, and current obstacle to international recognition.

The strategy is not to deny the alleged crimes, which do not implicate Thaçi directly. Instead, the defense is arguing that the KLA lacked a proper command structure and that Thaçi, often outside Kosovo and serving in a political role, had no authority over operations. The first defense witness carried the weight of the US government of that era. James P. Rubin, former assistant secretary of state, testified for three days , accompanied by current State Department officials as observers. He rejected the prosecution’s portrayal of Thaçi’s power at the time and disputed the notion that the KLA had anything resembling a “military structure.” According to Rubin, this was one reason why the United States refused to arm the KLA even while it was bombing Slobodan Milosevic’s Yugoslavia. Rubin was well placed to know. Tasked by then Secretary of State Madeleine Albright to work with Thaçi during peace talks in France (February–March 1999) and later to secure KLA demilitarization after NATO’s intervention, he said that Thaçi’s signatory role reflected representation, not authority. Having spent time with Thaçi both in France and for three days in a KLA mountain hideout, Rubin testified that the then twenty-nine-year-old “had superiors from whom he had to get approval,” and he was “more of a public face to present to the West.” Rubin’s testimony was reinforced by Paul Williams, an international law expert who advised Kosovo’s delegation. Williams said that Thaçi faced “extraordinary pressure from local commanders” not to sign the peace accords, and that he had to travel back to Kosovo to seek their approval. On September 22, John Stewart Duncan, then a British adviser to NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe who drafted and negotiated the KLA’s demilitarization deal, further corroborated this portrayal of the KLA’s command structure, adding that the guerilla army’s real power rested with regional commanders. Media reports suggest that more high-ranking Western officials—from the United States, NATO, the United Kingdom, and France—will testify in the coming days. The defense is expected to conclude by mid-November, with a ruling anticipated around March of next year. The outcome of the case will likely have political implications for Kosovo and the Balkans, as well as for the United States. Washington’s reputation is involved because Thaçi, as Rubin noted in his testimony, worked closely with successive US administrations to lead Kosovo toward peace and independence and promote ethnic reconciliation. For two decades, he was essentially seen as Washington’s man. Thaçi is also being tried in a court sponsored by the United States and the European Union (EU), and the court’s chief prosecutor and presiding judge in the case are both American. This reflects a longstanding US commitment—starting with the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in 1993—to pair Balkan peace deals with justice and accountability for war crimes. Finally, the case has elements of a domestic US political drama which—regardless of objective reality—has altered perceptions about the integrity of the process in a Balkans region that is already prone to viewing war-crimes tribunals as politically controlled by Western powers. Thaçi’s indictment in 2020 was controversially announced while he was en route to the White House to meet with US President Donald Trump to sign a peace deal with Serbia. The announcement came from Jack Smith, then chief prosecutor of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers and later special prosecutor against Trump, which fueled speculation among Trump’s allies in Washington about possible domestic US political motivations behind the case. Rubin’s testimony also frequently shifted from KLA command-and-control dynamics to these broader political issues. He accused the prosecution of distorting justice, calling the tribunal “an example of international justice that has gotten out of control.” On Thaçi’s indictment, he said that “politics had interfered in the rule of law” and sought to alter the Kosovo war narrative. Drawing on his Kosovo experience and his recent stint as the head of the State Department’s Global Engagement Center under former President Joe Biden, Rubin also expressed his belief that many allegations against KLA leaders stemmed from Russian and Serbian propaganda. Rubin’s political narratives inside the courtroom and the decision of Western governments to allow officials to support the defense have created a perception in Kosovo, particularly among Thaçi’s supporters, that an acquittal may be on the way. So much so that an opposite outcome would likely fuel a sense of betrayal and skepticism toward the West, which has been steadily on the rise in Kosovo even before Thaçi’s indictment. Yet if he is acquitted, Thaçi’s return to Kosovo would almost certainly shake up the political scene, which has been mired in deadlock due to an inability to form a government. It also comes at a time when caretaker Prime Minister Albin Kurti is increasingly at odds with Washington and Brussels over what US and EU officials see as destabilizing moves regarding relations with Serbia and the rights of Kosovo Serbs. It remains unclear what political role Thaçi might play if an acquittal comes in the spring, but snap elections are looming. Yet Thaçi’s return would very likely boost Kurti’s rival camp, whatever his role may be. That camp has favored closer cooperation with the West and has shown a greater willingness to pursue a final settlement with Serbia. An acquittal would also likely please Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama, a vocal supporter of Thaçi’s defense who sees him as the preferred ethnic-Albanian partner across the border. Rama’s relations with Kurti have arguably deteriorated beyond repair. At the same time, an acquittal would likely anger Belgrade, which has supplied the prosecution with evidence against Thaçi and would likely use an acquittal to reinforce its standard narrative of Western bias against Serbs. Some, if not all, of the countries of the region may soon join the European Union and shape the bloc’s ability to become a more effective geopolitical player. At the same time, longstanding disputes in the region, coupled with institutional weaknesses, will continue to pose problems and present a security vulnerability for NATO that could be exploited by Russia or China. Thaçi previously served as the state’s first prime minister, the political director of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), and as Kosovo's president at the time of his indictment in 2020. He is among the state’s most revered personas, and was long seen as one of the West’s most reliable partners. While Thaçi and his three fellow defendants intend to appeal the judgment and believe they may yet walk free, its pronouncement provides a unique and useful opportunity to reflect on the social and political ramifications of yet another post-Yugoslav courtroom drama. Kosovo is a unique state for many reasons. It was the site of mass crackdowns and repression by the Milošević regime in its latter days from 1998 to 1999 that triggered a war and ended with a 78-day bombing campaign of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia by NATO. Today, a lack of official UN and other recognition, stemming from continued disputes with and rejection by Serbia, the state from which it seceded in February 2008, have left it in a political void, with attempts to win entry into international organizations routinely obstructed. Hashim Thaçi served as the adored political director of the KLA during the war, winning the hearts of his countrymen and of the West. His role as a founding father of his country extended beyond the war, leading it to independence and later steering it to a pro-European course diplomatically engaged with non-recognizing neighbor Serbia before his arrest. In 2020, the chief prosecutor for the Kosovo Specialist Chamber – a court technically under Kosovar law but based in the Hague, staffed by international judges and lawyers, deeply unpopular within Kosovo but very popular among European governments – filed the charges. The prosecutor was Jack Smith, a man with a unique career path perhaps better known to readers for cases closer to home. These proceedings followed the 2019 friendly presentation of a national award to former President Clinton and came as Thaçi was en route to Washington for a meeting with then-President Trump and Serbian President (and Kosovo War-era FRY information minister ) Aleksandar Vučić. The meeting, which presented an unprecedented opportunity for high stakes talks between the leader of Serbia and that of its now-unrecognized former province, both with European inclinations, was scuttled, as Thaçi surrendered to face charges. Six years later, as Kosovar leaders predicted the acquittal of their ally or rival (depending on political camp), the small country was shaken to see him handed a quarter-century imprisonment for war crimes relating to alleged KLA kidnappings and extrajudicial killings. One unifier among Kosovar Albanian leadership, who represent the overwhelming majority ethnic background of the former Serbian province, was objection. Despite two inconclusive parliamentary elections since early 2025, Kosovo’s political leaders joined together in their public opposition to the judgment against one of their own. The Kosovar parliament voted 99-0 to condemn the judgment on September 28. One clear winner from this verdict will be Kosovo’s incumbent PM, Albin Kurti, whose populist party has successfully rivaled Thaçi’s more moderate, pro-European outlook. Thaçi and Kurti have been rivals since their shared days as rebels of the Kosovo war; while the former led the political sector of the KLA, the latter led a student movement more averse to dialogue and reconciliation. Kurti’s crusade evolved into his party, Vetëvendosje (LVV), or Self-Determination. From the war years to their tense days as president and prime minister together, Thaçi has routinely sought to ingratiate the EU and negotiate with Belgrade while Kurti has sought to underscore Prishtina’s independence and aversion to compromise on Kosovar sovereignty. The prevention of Thaçi’s return to the political scene must undoubtedly offer relief to the embattled PM, who has narrowly managed to maintain his office after two subsequent elections without a clear majority in the country’s 120-seat assembly. Parallel and seemingly detached from the dialogue among Kosovo’s angry domestic and diasporic population is that among Serbians. Serbian officials — who just weeks ago mourned the death of convicted genocidaire General Ratko Mladić, known for his brutality in the Bosnian War (and particularly, the Srebrenica massacre and siege of Sarajevo) — have criticized the sentences (ranging between 13 and 25 years) for being too lenient, compared to the prosecution’s requested 45. Serbia continues to play a major role in Kosovo’s affairs as its former home, wartime adversary, and current obstacle to international recognition. Meanwhile, the question may have been opened — for the first time — of whether Kosovar faith in the West can be shaken. While Euroscepticism has raged within EU member and candidate states for years and faith in U.S. reliability repeatedly shaken in the twenty-first century, Kosovo citizens’ support for the EU and the U.S. has traditionally polled around or above 90 percent. As Western judges weighed and continue to weigh the fate of Kosovo’s path-charting leader, it is worth watching whether such a significant new development can shake so strong a partnership. American leaders would do well to consider the extent to which they should involve themselves in the small Balkan nation where their country is perhaps most popular, as Trump administration ally Richard Grenell has regularly commented in defense of Thaçi, and opposition to Kurti. For now, policymakers and diplomats should treat such legacies of the conflict with the sensitivity they deserve while promoting what dialogue and diplomacy can be found in a deeply divided region. In a time of such political turmoil, the United States must be wary of forgetting or forsaking even its smallest allies, especially one so loyal. Despite political distractions at home and abroad, policymakers in the State Department, Congress, and the EU should at the very least project interest in the trial’s outcome, whether through reaffirmation of the court and for Kosovo’s other state institutions, its leaders, or both. They must express, and through diplomatic engagement, prove their continued motivation to assist Prishtina in its reforms, and its drive to gain recognition on the world stage. Stephen R. facts.text: Finally, the case has elements of a domestic US political drama which—regardless of objective reality—has altered perceptions about the integrity of the process in a Balkans region that is already prone to viewing war-crimes tribunals as politically controlled by Western powers.
Thaçi’s indictment in 2020 was controversially announced while he was en route to the White House to meet with US President Donald Trump to sign a peace deal with Serbia.
Agon Maliqi is a nonresident senior fellow with the Atlantic Council’s Europe Center.
He is a political and foreign policy analyst from Pristina, Kosovo.
Rubin’s testimony was reinforced by Paul Williams, an international law expert who advised Kosovo’s delegation.

On September 22, John Stewart Duncan, then a British adviser to NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe who drafted and negotiated the KLA’s demilitarization deal, further corroborated this portrayal of the KLA’s command structure, adding that the guerilla army’s real power rested with regional commanders.

Washington’s reputation is involved because Thaçi, as Rubin noted in his testimony, worked closely with successive US administrations to lead Kosovo toward peace and independence and promote ethnic reconciliation.
For two decades, he was essentially seen as Washington’s man.
On September 15, the defense opened its case, announcing just fifteen witnesses— mostly senior Western officials with direct knowledge of events.
The strategy is not to deny the alleged crimes, which do not implicate Thaçi directly.

This reflects a longstanding US commitment—starting with the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in 1993—to pair Balkan peace deals with justice and accountability for war crimes.

Since November 2020, Thaçi has been in detention at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, a hybrid Kosovar–international court in The Hague, alongside three other members of the Kosovo Liberation Army’s (KLA) General Staff.
Their trial began in April 2023, and the prosecution took two years, concluding in April of this year.
Did a political representative of a guerrilla army have command responsibility for alleged crimes committed by its members during the Kosovo war?

It also comes at a time when caretaker Prime Minister Albin Kurti is increasingly at odds with Washington and Brussels over what US and EU officials see as destabilizing moves regarding relations with Serbia and the rights of Kosovo Serbs.

The indictment against Thaçi and the three others alleges that during 1998-1999—while the KLA waged a rural insurgency against the Yugoslav army and police, whose top leadership was found guilty of massacres and the ethnic cleansing of at least 700,000 Albanians—the KLA engaged in a number of illegal detentions, disappearances, mistreatment, and murders of civilians seen as political rivals and collaborators, both Albanian and Serb.

Drawing on his Kosovo experience and his recent stint as the head of the State Department’s Global Engagement Center under former President Joe Biden, Rubin also expressed his belief that many allegations against KLA leaders stemmed from Russian and Serbian propaganda.
A weekly column by Atlantic Council President and CEO Frederick Kempe, Inflection Points focuses on the global challenges facing the United States and how to best address them.
The first defense witness carried the weight of the US government of that era.
Rubin, former assistant secretary of state, testified for three days , accompanied by current State Department officials as observers.
That camp has favored closer cooperation with the West and has shown a greater willingness to pursue a final settlement with Serbia.
Rama’s relations with Kurti have arguably deteriorated beyond repair.

JERUSALEM - Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered a security review of international flights to Israel on Oct 4, after an attempt by an Omani co-pilot to crash an Israel-bound plane from Dubai. Netanyahu “has instructed the head of the National Security Council, Shmuel Ben Ezra, to appoint an examiner to conduct a thorough review of all security aspects of foreign civil aviation to Israel”, a statement from the premier’s office said. Calls have mounted in Israel for an investigation into the security lapse that allowed the Omani co-pilot of a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Sept 30 to attempt to bring down the aircraft after stabbing the Indian captain . Israeli media has reported that the co-pilot intended to crash the aircraft on Israeli territory. Critics have focused on how a pilot from a country with no diplomatic relations with Israel was cleared to operate a flight bound for Tel Aviv. Transport Minister Miri Regev rejected responsibility for the failure, saying security oversight for flights operated by foreign airlines falls under the remit of the Mossad and Shin Bet, Israel’s foreign and domestic intelligence agencies. A 2024 report by the state comptroller found there was no clear division of responsibility for the security of foreign airlines operating in Israel, and recommended that the government address the issue. Israeli media have reported that pilots from countries hostile to Israel have repeatedly flown into the country in recent years. Keren Terner, who previously served as director-general of the transport ministry and is now running for Parliament for the opposition, blamed Regev for the security failure, noting that the Civil Aviation Authority was under the “direct subordination” of her ministry. “You are responsible for the security of foreign companies. Not the Shin Bet, not Mossad. You. That’s what the government decided, and that’s what the law stipulates,” Terner wrote on X. Opposition leader Yair Lapid dismissed Netanyahu’s announcement of a security review as a “sham investigation”. “The chain of failures that preceded the incident could have led to a disaster of historic proportions, and this is how an Israeli prime minister responds?” Lapid wrote on X. “Just as Netanyahu escaped an investigation into the October 7 massacre, he is now running away again,” he added. Gadi Eisenkot, a leading challenger to Netanyahu ahead of the Oct 27 election, wrote on X that “in a proper and functioning government, the minister of transportation would have submitted a letter of resignation last night”. JERUSALEM - Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered a security review of international flights to Israel on Oct 4, after an attempt by an Omani co-pilot to crash an Israel-bound plane from Dubai.

Netanyahu “has instructed the head of the National Security Council, Shmuel Ben Ezra, to appoint an examiner to conduct a thorough review of all security aspects of foreign civil aviation to Israel”, a statement from the premier’s office said.

Calls have mounted in Israel for an investigation into the security lapse that allowed the Omani co-pilot of a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Sept 30 to attempt to bring down the aircraft after stabbing the Indian captain .
Israeli media has reported that the co-pilot intended to crash the aircraft on Israeli territory.
Critics have focused on how a pilot from a country with no diplomatic relations with Israel was cleared to operate a flight bound for Tel Aviv.

Transport Minister Miri Regev rejected responsibility for the failure, saying security oversight for flights operated by foreign airlines falls under the remit of the Mossad and Shin Bet, Israel’s foreign and domestic intelligence agencies.

A 2024 report by the state comptroller found there was no clear division of responsibility for the security of foreign airlines operating in Israel, and recommended that the government address the issue.
Israeli media have reported that pilots from countries hostile to Israel have repeatedly flown into the country in recent years.

Keren Terner, who previously served as director-general of the transport ministry and is now running for Parliament for the opposition, blamed Regev for the security failure, noting that the Civil Aviation Authority was under the “direct subordination” of her ministry.
“You are responsible for the security of foreign companies. Not the Shin Bet, not Mossad. You. That’s what the government decided, and that’s what the law stipulates,” Terner wrote on X.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid dismissed Netanyahu’s announcement of a security review as a “sham investigation”.
“The chain of failures that preceded the incident could have led to a disaster of historic proportions, and this is how an Israeli prime minister responds?” Lapid wrote on X.
“Just as Netanyahu escaped an investigation into the October 7 massacre, he is now running away again,” he added.

Gadi Eisenkot, a leading challenger to Netanyahu ahead of the Oct 27 election, wrote on X that “in a proper and functioning government, the minister of transportation would have submitted a letter of resignation last night”. AFP

Morgan Stanley and BlackRock cap crypto at somewhere between 0% and 4%, pushing young investors toward the higher end while urging retirees to minimize exposure. Bitcoin's 77% crash shows a 20% crypto allocation in an $800,000 portfolio could mean a $123,000 loss, forcing retirees to cut essentials. Time horizon matters more than age for crypto decisions, since retirees who sell during downturns permanently lock in losses and miss any recovery. Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor) When it comes to investing in cryptocurrency, how much should you own at different ages—like 30, 55, or 70? Traditional investing guidelines, such as "100 minus your age," suggest that a 30-year-old should have 70% in stocks and a 70-year-old should have 30%. However, crypto like Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) challenges these rules, requiring a fresh approach. While stocks have decades of data to analyze past market crashes and recoveries, Bitcoin has only about 17 years of history and doesn't pay interest or dividends like bonds and stocks do. Its value can fluctuate wildly, leading to significant gains or severe losses. Therefore, a more practical question is how much you could afford to lose without impacting your lifestyle. This becomes particularly important as you approach retirement. Investors typically shift their portfolios from stocks to bonds and cash as they get older. This shift is predicated on a decreasing time frame before they start withdrawing funds. While age often signals that shrinking timeline, your time horizon should ultimately dictate how much crypto you can comfortably hold. For instance, a 30-year-old who sees their investment drop by 70% can afford to wait it out; their paycheck can still cover living expenses. They can hold onto their crypto, with plenty of time for the market to recover. Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. The saving is done, the portfolio is built, and the question quietly changes from how much can I grow this to how much can I take out? Get that second question wrong and decades of good investing can come apart in a handful of years. That is exactly what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps answer. It covers what your retirement could actually cost, which income sources are worth using, and the withdrawal math that decides whether the money lasts. It is free today from Fisher Investments. Read More Here › In contrast, a retiree counts on their savings to pay monthly bills regardless of market fluctuations. If this retiree has to sell during a market downturn to cover expenses, their temporary paper loss converts into a permanent one, as they miss out on any potential market recovery. This is known as sequence-of-returns risk, where the timing of returns plays a crucial role in long-term investment success. The volatility of crypto can make this risk even more pronounced. For example, Bitcoin fell about 77% from its peak of around $69,000 in November 2021 to about $15,500 a year later. As of October 4, 2026, Bitcoin trades near $85,000, but that remains roughly 33% below its record of around $126,000 in October 2025. The amount of crypto you hold significantly influences how much a downturn impacts your finances. For a retiree with an $800,000 portfolio, allocating 2% to crypto means holding $16,000. A 77% drop in value means they lose about $12,000—painful, but it leaves their monthly income largely untouched. However, if that same retiree has 20% in crypto, they stand to lose approximately $123,000, a loss that could force them to cut back on essentials like spending or housing. The timing of these downturns also worsens the situation. A market crash early in retirement is particularly harmful, as selling coins at low prices to cover immediate bills misses the chance to recover later. Major investment firms have laid out a framework for crypto allocation. For instance, Morgan Stanley's Global Investment Committee announced in October 2025 that aggressive growth portfolios might include up to 4% in crypto, while income-oriented portfolios should hold none. Similarly, BlackRock suggested that 1% to 2% in Bitcoin is a reasonable guideline. These recommendations correspond to three key stages of an investor's life: Young Investors (Early Career) : With many years of paychecks ahead, they can afford to take on more risk, often nearing the upper end of the 0% to 4% allocation range. Approaching Retirement : With fewer years to recover from volatility, this group should gradually reduce their crypto holdings as they near retirement. Retirees : Living off their savings requires a cautious approach, making it essential to limit crypto exposure to a level that insulates their income from drastic losses. Additionally, a crypto market rally can inadvertently push an allocation beyond recommended limits. For example, if Bitcoin rises from $15,500 to $85,000, a 2% holding could transform into 10% of a portfolio if other investments remain stable. This is why experts like Morgan Stanley emphasize the importance of regular rebalancing. Your ideal crypto investment is whatever amount you could afford to lose without affecting your lifestyle, typically between 0% and 4% of your overall portfolio. Younger investors can lean toward the higher end, while those nearing retirement should adjust downwards, and retirees should minimize exposure to ensure their monthly expenses won't be impacted. Keep in mind that this approach may limit potential gains. A retiree with just 1% in Bitcoin might miss out on significant profit if the coin appreciates rapidly. Major life changes, such as retiring early, losing a pension, or experiencing a crypto boom, can all affect this calculation. Regularly reassessing your crypto allocation is essential to stay aligned with your financial goals. So how much crypto should you own after a big life change? (Sponsor) Most people spend their entire working lives focusing on one thing: growing a pile of money. Then they retire and discover the skill they actually need is close to the opposite. Turning that pile into steady income, year after year, through good markets and bad, without ever running out.

When it comes to investing in cryptocurrency, how much should you own at different ages—like 30, 55, or 70? Traditional investing guidelines, such as “100 minus your age,” suggest that a 30-year-old should have 70% in stocks and a 70-year-old should have 30%. However, crypto like Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) challenges these rules, requiring a fresh approach. While stocks have decades of data to analyze past market crashes and recoveries, Bitcoin has only about 17 years of history and doesn’t pay interest or dividends like bonds and stocks do. Its value can fluctuate wildly, leading to significant gains or severe losses. Therefore, a more practical question is how much you could afford to lose without impacting your lifestyle. This becomes particularly important as you approach retirement. Investors typically shift their portfolios from stocks to bonds and cash as they get older. This shift is predicated on a decreasing time frame before they start withdrawing funds. While age often signals that shrinking timeline, your time horizon should ultimately dictate how much crypto you can comfortably hold. For instance, a 30-year-old who sees their investment drop by 70% can afford to wait it out; their paycheck can still cover living expenses. They can hold onto their crypto, with plenty of time for the market to recover. In contrast, a retiree counts on their savings to pay monthly bills regardless of market fluctuations. If this retiree has to sell during a market downturn to cover expenses, their temporary paper loss converts into a permanent one, as they miss out on any potential market recovery. This is known as sequence-of-returns risk , where the timing of returns plays a crucial role in long-term investment success. The volatility of crypto can make this risk even more pronounced. For example, Bitcoin fell about 77% from its peak of around $69,000 in November 2021 to about $15,500 a year later. As of October 4, 2026, Bitcoin trades near $85,000, but that remains roughly 33% below its record of around $126,000 in October 2025. The amount of crypto you hold significantly influences how much a downturn impacts your finances. For a retiree with an $800,000 portfolio, allocating 2% to crypto means holding $16,000. A 77% drop in value means they lose about $12,000—painful, but it leaves their monthly income largely untouched. However, if that same retiree has 20% in crypto, they stand to lose approximately $123,000, a loss that could force them to cut back on essentials like spending or housing. The timing of these downturns also worsens the situation. A market crash early in retirement is particularly harmful, as selling coins at low prices to cover immediate bills misses the chance to recover later. Major investment firms have laid out a framework for crypto allocation. For instance, Morgan Stanley’s Global Investment Committee announced in October 2025 that aggressive growth portfolios might include up to 4% in crypto, while income-oriented portfolios should hold none. Similarly, BlackRock suggested that 1% to 2% in Bitcoin is a reasonable guideline. These recommendations correspond to three key stages of an investor’s life: Additionally, a crypto market rally can inadvertently push an allocation beyond recommended limits. For example, if Bitcoin rises from $15,500 to $85,000, a 2% holding could transform into 10% of a portfolio if other investments remain stable. This is why experts like Morgan Stanley emphasize the importance of regular rebalancing. Your ideal crypto investment is whatever amount you could afford to lose without affecting your lifestyle, typically between 0% and 4% of your overall portfolio. Younger investors can lean toward the higher end, while those nearing retirement should adjust downwards, and retirees should minimize exposure to ensure their monthly expenses won’t be impacted. Keep in mind that this approach may limit potential gains. A retiree with just 1% in Bitcoin might miss out on significant profit if the coin appreciates rapidly. Major life changes, such as retiring early, losing a pension, or experiencing a crypto boom, can all affect this calculation. Regularly reassessing your crypto allocation is essential to stay aligned with your financial goals. So how much crypto should you own after a big life change? Its value can fluctuate wildly, leading to significant gains or severe losses. Therefore, a more practical question is how much you could afford to lose without impacting your lifestyle. This becomes particularly important as you approach retirement.

Investors typically shift their portfolios from stocks to bonds and cash as they get older. This shift is predicated on a decreasing time frame before they start withdrawing funds. While age often signals that shrinking timeline, your time horizon should ultimately dictate how much crypto you can comfortably hold.

passages: In our latest analysis, we asked AI models—ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini— to evaluate which cryptocurrency among Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC), Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH), and XRP (CRYPTO: XRP) is likely to bounce back to its all-time high first.
All three models gave the same ranking: Bitcoin led, followed by Ethereum, with XRP trailing.
ChatGPT predicts Bitcoin could close 2026 around $100,000, Ethereum at approximately $3,400, and XRP near $2.05.
Similarly, Gemini projects year-end prices of $108,500, $3,450, and $2.15, respectively.
ChatGPT assigned XRP only a 15% probability, while Gemini placed it at just 8%.
It has the smallest gap to cover, the largest amount of invested funds, and the smallest decline over the past year—down about 30%, compared with Ethereum's 38% and XRP's 50% drops.
The immediate critical test for Bitcoin is to surpass its recent high of $87,500, followed by the significant threshold of $100,000.

In our latest analysis, we asked AI models—ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini— to evaluate which cryptocurrency among Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ), Ethereum ( CRYPTO: ETH ), and XRP ( CRYPTO: XRP ) is likely to bounce back to its all-time high first. All three models gave the same ranking: Bitcoin led, followed by Ethereum, with XRP trailing.

While the models agreed on the order, they differed in confidence. ChatGPT estimated a 55% chance of Bitcoin reaching its record high first; Grok was slightly more optimistic at 58%, and Gemini was the most confident, giving Bitcoin a 70% probability. This raises an interesting question: how much should we rely on these AI predictions when all three cryptocurrencies remain significantly below their previous peaks?

Starting from their respective previous highs—$126,080 for Bitcoin, $4,946 for Ethereum , and $3.65 for XRP—we looked at the market as of October 1, 2026. At that time, Bitcoin was trading around $84,670, Ethereum at $2,699, and XRP at $1.49.

To reach their former highs, Bitcoin needs a gain of about 49%, Ethereum requires around 83%, and XRP must climb approximately 145%. As a result, the ranking aligns almost perfectly with the size of the gap each cryptocurrency must close.
Gemini highlighted the specific dollar amount Bitcoin needs to regain its past glory, saying it would require about $820 billion in market value to reach $126,080.

In terms of recent performance, Ethereum has shown more significant growth. Over the 90 days leading up to October 1, Ethereum climbed about 53%, while Bitcoin gained around 33% and XRP only 31%. This shows Ethereum is closing the gap faster than Bitcoin and XRP.

Despite this momentum, the AI models still favored Bitcoin. Grok noted that U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs), which hold Bitcoin and trade similarly to shares, have approximately $108 billion in assets. In comparison, Ethereum funds have $17.8 billion, and XRP funds only $1.8 billion. Grok mentioned that these funds hold nearly 6% of Bitcoin’s total supply.

ChatGPT added that financial forecasts support Bitcoin’s potential, citing Citi’s target of $113,000 for Bitcoin, which is only about 10% below its all-time high, while their target for Ethereum at $3,028 is 39% lower than its peak.

ChatGPT predicts Bitcoin could close 2026 around $100,000, Ethereum at approximately $3,400, and XRP near $2.05. Similarly, Gemini projects year-end prices of $108,500, $3,450, and $2.15, respectively. Although XRP shows the highest percentage gain potential—ranging from 38% to 44%—its chances of being the first to reach its all-time high are quite low. ChatGPT assigned XRP only a 15% probability, while Gemini placed it at just 8%.
This skepticism about XRP stems from the fact that even a 40% increase over three months would still leave it far short of its high at $3.65, requiring a 145% surge.

Additionally, Gemini noted that new XRP supplies entering the market might dilute demand per token. ChatGPT pointed out that Evernorth’s 473 million XRP represents only a small fraction of XRP’s $95 billion market value. Grok observed that XRP’s previous record in 2025 was more of a fleeting spike than a sustainable price level.

Overall, Bitcoin appears to have the strongest chance of regaining its all-time high first. It has the smallest gap to cover, the largest amount of invested funds, and the smallest decline over the past year—down about 30%, compared with Ethereum’s 38% and XRP’s 50% drops.

However, the timeline is crucial. ChatGPT’s prediction of $100,000 by year-end still leaves Bitcoin about 21% shy of its all-time high, and the models indicate potential recovery timelines extending into mid-2027.

The immediate critical test for Bitcoin is to surpass its recent high of $87,500, followed by the significant threshold of $100,000 . If Bitcoin falls below $80,000, it could hinder its progress and allow Ethereum to narrow its gap further. If Ethereum exceeds $4,946 before Bitcoin returns to $126,080, it would suggest the AI models may have miscalculated the recovery order.

In our latest analysis, we asked AI models—ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini— to evaluate which cryptocurrency among Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ), Ethereum ( CRYPTO: ETH ), and XRP ( CRYPTO: XRP ) is likely to bounce back to its all-time high first. All three models gave the same ranking: Bitcoin led, followed by Ethereum, with XRP trailing.

While the models agreed on the order, they differed in confidence. ChatGPT estimated a 55% chance of Bitcoin reaching its record high first; Grok was slightly more optimistic at 58%, and Gemini was the most confident, giving Bitcoin a 70% probability. This raises an interesting question: how much should we rely on these AI predictions when all three cryptocurrencies remain significantly below their previous peaks?

Starting from their respective previous highs—$126,080 for Bitcoin, $4,946 for Ethereum , and $3.65 for XRP—we looked at the market as of October 1, 2026. At that time, Bitcoin was trading around $84,670, Ethereum at $2,699, and XRP at $1.49.

To reach their former highs, Bitcoin needs a gain of about 49%, Ethereum requires around 83%, and XRP must climb approximately 145%. As a result, the ranking aligns almost perfectly with the size of the gap each cryptocurrency must close.
Gemini highlighted the specific dollar amount Bitcoin needs to regain its past glory, saying it would require about $820 billion in market value to reach $126,080.

In terms of recent performance, Ethereum has shown more significant growth. Over the 90 days leading up to October 1, Ethereum climbed about 53%, while Bitcoin gained around 33% and XRP only 31%. This shows Ethereum is closing the gap faster than Bitcoin and XRP.

Despite this momentum, the AI models still favored Bitcoin. Grok noted that U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs), which hold Bitcoin and trade similarly to shares, have approximately $108 billion in assets. In comparison, Ethereum funds have $17.8 billion, and XRP funds only $1.8 billion. Grok mentioned that these funds hold nearly 6% of Bitcoin’s total supply.

ChatGPT added that financial forecasts support Bitcoin’s potential, citing Citi’s target of $113,000 for Bitcoin, which is only about 10% below its all-time high, while their target for Ethereum at $3,028 is 39% lower than its peak.

ChatGPT predicts Bitcoin could close 2026 around $100,000, Ethereum at approximately $3,400, and XRP near $2.05. Similarly, Gemini projects year-end prices of $108,500, $3,450, and $2.15, respectively. Although XRP shows the highest percentage gain potential—ranging from 38% to 44%—its chances of being the first to reach its all-time high are quite low. ChatGPT assigned XRP only a 15% probability, while Gemini placed it at just 8%.
This skepticism about XRP stems from the fact that even a 40% increase over three months would still leave it far short of its high at $3.65, requiring a 145% surge.

Additionally, Gemini noted that new XRP supplies entering the market might dilute demand per token. ChatGPT pointed out that Evernorth’s 473 million XRP represents only a small fraction of XRP’s $95 billion market value. Grok observed that XRP’s previous record in 2025 was more of a fleeting spike than a sustainable price level.

Overall, Bitcoin appears to have the strongest chance of regaining its all-time high first. It has the smallest gap to cover, the largest amount of invested funds, and the smallest decline over the past year—down about 30%, compared with Ethereum’s 38% and XRP’s 50% drops.

However, the timeline is crucial. ChatGPT’s prediction of $100,000 by year-end still leaves Bitcoin about 21% shy of its all-time high, and the models indicate potential recovery timelines extending into mid-2027.

The immediate critical test for Bitcoin is to surpass its recent high of $87,500, followed by the significant threshold of $100,000 . If Bitcoin falls below $80,000, it could hinder its progress and allow Ethereum to narrow its gap further. If Ethereum exceeds $4,946 before Bitcoin returns to $126,080, it would suggest the AI models may have miscalculated the recovery order.

extraction.body: Aviation security protocols under scrutiny after co-pilot accused of attempted axe attack aboard Flydubai flight. A Flydubai co-pilot accused of attacking his captain with an emergency axe and attempting to seize control of the flight bound for Israel had previously been barred from flying over concerns about alleged “extremist” views, raising questions about how he was allowed to fly to Tel Aviv. The co-pilot has been identified as Hamam al-Hammami, an Omani national, according to multiple media reports. The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has described the September 30 incident aboard Flight FZ1073 as an attempted “terrorist” operation . But investigators are still working to establish the motive and whether anyone else was connected to the attack, which has raised concerns about pilot vetting and aviation security. So, what security checks do pilots have to go through and how al-Hammami may have evaded background checks? That is now one of the central questions facing investigators. Al-Hammami had previously been barred from flying in Oman because of concerns that he had adopted “extremist” views and was instead moved to an administrative role at Oman Air, according to sources who spoke to the AP news agency. A Gulf diplomat told AP that al-Hammami had undergone standard security checks before being hired. It wasn’t immediately clear to what extent the co-pilot was vetted. The US-based network CNN reported that a LinkedIn profile bearing al-Hammami’s name said he had spent seven years at Oman Air before leaving in February 2025. The profile said he joined Royal Air Maroc in June 2025 and left in January this year. It is unclear what those alleged views were or whether Oman informed other countries or airlines about its concerns. Background checks for commercial pilots vary by airline and country, with no single global standard governing the process, an airline pilot and instructor told Al Jazeera. The captain with an international airline who chose to remain anonymous said pilots are generally required to obtain aviation medical certification from the regulator in the country where they are licensed to fly. In the UAE, that is overseen by the General Civil Aviation Authority (GCAA), he said. Some airlines also require prospective pilots to provide police clearance certificates from their country of residence as part of pre-employment screening, the pilot added. One type of check is a Class 1 medical assessment, which typically examines areas including vision, hearing, cardiovascular and neurological health, as well as conditions that could cause sudden incapacitation. When it comes to security checks, aviation rules require background checks for personnel who have unescorted access to security-restricted areas. Psychological assessments, drug and alcohol testing and other evaluations may be required depending on the jurisdiction. Israel has some of the world’s toughest aviation security measures. As a result, questions have been raised over how the alleged attacker was allowed to operate a flight to Israel, despite reportedly being an Omani national and Oman having no diplomatic relations with Israel. According to the Haaretz newspaper, Israeli authorities received the Flydubai flight’s crew and passenger lists before it departed. Under a law passed in 2023, airlines are required to provide information about passengers and crew members, including their names and nationalities, to Israel up to 48 hours before a flight. The Israel Tax Authority confirmed to Haaretz that it had received the lists for the Flydubai flight. The media outlet reported that the information is also supposed to be available to Israeli security bodies, including the Mossad, police and Shin Bet, to identify people who may pose a security risk. According to security sources who spoke to Haaretz, the Transportation Ministry’s Security Department and the Mossad are responsible for checking foreign flight crews and issuing alerts if concerns arise. However, two security sources told Haaretz that while the Transportation Ministry holds responsibility “on paper”, it does not have its own intelligence capacity. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said that Israel has longstanding arrangements with foreign airlines aimed at preventing pilots who are nationals of countries without diplomatic relations with Israel from flying there. Netanyahu has described what happened as a “loophole” and Israel says it will now strengthen its checks. The UAE has not yet publicly established a motive or announced whether investigators believe al-Hammami acted alone. UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said on Saturday that the latest ‘terrorist’ attack is a new warning that the region’s fight against “extremism” is not over. “This underscores the importance of the UAE’s early and firm stance: no tolerance for extremism and no leniency towards its rhetoric. Security begins with confronting hatred and drying up the sources of extremism,” he posted on X.

sources.title: Apple says it’s tightening macOS ‘Full Disk Access’ controls due to new risks from AI agents
passages: Days after a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app on Mac read their private messages — a claim that Meta disputed — Apple announced that it’s introducing additional controls around a setting called “Full Disk Access” on macOS.
The feature was designed to allow backups to function properly, but AI agents have now increased “the risks associated with this level of access,” Apple said.
This setting, Apple explains, gives an app permission to access files, mail, messages, and even browsing history.
The report raised questions about the level of security and trust users have in desktop-based AI, which can control things on their systems and read their files and messages.
We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy,” Apple wrote.
Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s inquiry about the feature change.
AI agents that run on the desktop allow users to provide their respective apps with greater access to the files, messages, and other personal content on their computers by adjusting macOS settings.
Correction: Due to an editorial error, the change was described as Apple “limiting” permissions.
After publication, the author of this article updated the wording to reflect their original intent: the change reflects informed consent, but is not a new limit.

passages: So it’s only natural that Trump’s new task force is named in accordance with this new branding.

The Wall Street Journal reports that Clayton will chair the Super Intelligence Force, effectively making him the new AI/SI czar, with Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Undersecretary of War for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor serving as vice chairs.

“The Super Intelligence Force is tasked with coordinating the effort of the Federal Government to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Trump said in a Sunday morning post on his social network Truth Social.

Since then, Trump signed an executive order seeking to rebrand AI as “super intelligence,” a term seemingly embraced, with some stumbles , by the tech executives who gathered at the White House this week to sign a non-binding safety pledge. (The pledge included an impressive typo .)

Back in September, in response to an AI safety debate that the president has largely dismissed as a hoax created by “Radical Left Dumocrats,” Trump said he would nevertheless form an AI Force and appoint an AI czar (“Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!”).

sources.title: Trump Unveils Super Intelligence Force for AI Safety
passages: Former President Trump announced the creation of a "Super Intelligence Force" today, marking his administration's most significant response to escalating debates over artificial intelligence safety and regulation.

The real test will be whether this task force can strike the delicate balance between ensuring AI safety and maintaining America's competitive edge in what many consider the most important technology race of our time.

extraction.body: Former President Trump announced the creation of a "Super Intelligence Force" today, marking his administration's most significant response to escalating debates over artificial intelligence safety and regulation. The new government task force signals a major shift in how political leaders are approaching the rapidly evolving AI landscape, potentially reshaping the regulatory framework that tech giants like Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI operate within. The political landscape around artificial intelligence just got a major shake-up. Trump's announcement of a "Super Intelligence Force" represents the most concrete government action we've seen yet in response to mounting concerns about AI safety and the breakneck pace of development across the tech industry. Over the past year, we've watched OpenAI push the boundaries with increasingly powerful models, while Google and Microsoft race to integrate AI across their entire product ecosystems. Meanwhile, safety researchers have grown increasingly vocal about the need for stronger oversight and regulation. This new task force appears designed to bridge that gap between rapid innovation and responsible governance. Unlike previous government AI initiatives that focused primarily on research and development, the Super Intelligence Force seems positioned to tackle the thornier questions around safety protocols, ethical deployment, and potential national security implications. But beneath the surface, there's growing unease about whether the current pace of development is sustainable or safe. Trump's Super Intelligence Force could be the mechanism that finally addresses this balance. What makes this particularly significant is the bipartisan nature of AI safety concerns. While political parties disagree on many tech policy issues, the potential risks of advanced AI systems have created unusual consensus around the need for some form of government involvement. The task force's exact mandate remains unclear, but the name itself suggests a focus on the most advanced AI systems - the kind of "superintelligent" artificial general intelligence that researchers believe could emerge in the coming years. For tech companies, this development likely means increased scrutiny of their AI research and deployment practices. We're probably looking at new compliance requirements, safety audits, and potentially restrictions on certain types of AI development. The U.S. has largely relied on industry self-regulation up to this point. Trump's Super Intelligence Force suggests that era might be ending. Trump's Super Intelligence Force announcement marks a pivotal moment in AI governance, signaling that the era of industry self-regulation may be coming to an end. For tech companies racing to develop increasingly powerful AI systems, this means navigating a new landscape of government oversight and compliance requirements. The real test will be whether this task force can strike the delicate balance between ensuring AI safety and maintaining America's competitive edge in what many consider the most important technology race of our time.

passages: President Donald Trump formally announced the creation of what he called a “Super Intelligence Force,” an artificial intelligence task force that he says will work to promote AI dominance while also protecting American lives and interests.
Last month, Trump said he would create an AI task force amid rising concerns about the technology.

Trump's announcement was thin on details, with the president not outlining any specific action or oversight the task force will have on AI development -- an issue about which some tech CEOs have raised concerns and called for federal regulation.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump formally announced the creation of what he called a “Super Intelligence Force,” an artificial intelligence task force that he says will work to promote AI dominance while also protecting American lives and interests. "The Super Intelligence Force is tasked with coordinating the effort of the Federal Government to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Trump wrote on his social media platform Sunday. Trump's announcement was thin on details, with the president not outlining any specific action or oversight the task force will have on AI development -- an issue about which some tech CEOs have raised concerns and called for federal regulation. "The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump added. An ABC News request sent to the White House for more information about the task force's objectives did not immediately receive a response. Last month, Trump said he would create an AI task force amid rising concerns about the technology. Sunday's formal announcement comes after the president met with top tech CEOs at the White House last week, where he said he and six companies signed a "constitution" establishing standards on how to self-police their technology. Trump said the task force will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, as well as Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor. Clayton, who is expected to serve as the White House's new AI czar, told The Wall Street Journal in an interview published Saturday that global dominance in AI makes the U.S. more equipped to address risks from adversaries, echoing the president’s support for the technology's continued growth. "The risk of not being first is high," Clayton told The Wall Street Journal. “Not being first increases the identified, and unidentified, risks, particularly from our adversaries. Being first will better enable us to address those risks on behalf of the American people." Clayton said of the AI task force, "I expect there will be mechanisms developed in dialogue, just like there are in other industries." According to The Wall Street Journal, Clayton cited risk models for the financial industry that have been developed in conjunction with the Federal Reserve and Securities and Exchange Commission. He told the newspaper that the task force would examine current law and discuss possible actions that Congress could take. Clayton also expressed confidence in the group that the president has appointed to run the AI task force, citing the "diverse skill sets" and "common commitment" of its members. extraction.body: Former President Trump announced the creation of a "Super Intelligence Force" today, marking his administration's most significant response to escalating debates over artificial intelligence safety and regulation. The new government task force signals a major shift in how political leaders are approaching the rapidly evolving AI landscape, potentially reshaping the regulatory framework that tech giants like Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI operate within. The political landscape around artificial intelligence just got a major shake-up. Trump's announcement of a "Super Intelligence Force" represents the most concrete government action we've seen yet in response to mounting concerns about AI safety and the breakneck pace of development across the tech industry. Over the past year, we've watched OpenAI push the boundaries with increasingly powerful models, while Google and Microsoft race to integrate AI across their entire product ecosystems. Meanwhile, safety researchers have grown increasingly vocal about the need for stronger oversight and regulation. This new task force appears designed to bridge that gap between rapid innovation and responsible governance. Unlike previous government AI initiatives that focused primarily on research and development, the Super Intelligence Force seems positioned to tackle the thornier questions around safety protocols, ethical deployment, and potential national security implications. But beneath the surface, there's growing unease about whether the current pace of development is sustainable or safe. Trump's Super Intelligence Force could be the mechanism that finally addresses this balance. What makes this particularly significant is the bipartisan nature of AI safety concerns. While political parties disagree on many tech policy issues, the potential risks of advanced AI systems have created unusual consensus around the need for some form of government involvement. The task force's exact mandate remains unclear, but the name itself suggests a focus on the most advanced AI systems - the kind of "superintelligent" artificial general intelligence that researchers believe could emerge in the coming years. For tech companies, this development likely means increased scrutiny of their AI research and deployment practices. We're probably looking at new compliance requirements, safety audits, and potentially restrictions on certain types of AI development. The U.S. has largely relied on industry self-regulation up to this point. Trump's Super Intelligence Force suggests that era might be ending. Trump's Super Intelligence Force announcement marks a pivotal moment in AI governance, signaling that the era of industry self-regulation may be coming to an end. For tech companies racing to develop increasingly powerful AI systems, this means navigating a new landscape of government oversight and compliance requirements. The real test will be whether this task force can strike the delicate balance between ensuring AI safety and maintaining America's competitive edge in what many consider the most important technology race of our time.

facts.text: So it’s only natural that Trump’s new task force is named in accordance with this new branding.

The Wall Street Journal reports that Clayton will chair the Super Intelligence Force, effectively making him the new AI/SI czar, with Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Undersecretary of War for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor serving as vice chairs.

Since then, Trump signed an executive order seeking to rebrand AI as “super intelligence,” a term seemingly embraced, with some stumbles , by the tech executives who gathered at the White House this week to sign a non-binding safety pledge. (The pledge included an impressive typo .)

Back in September, in response to an AI safety debate that the president has largely dismissed as a hoax created by “Radical Left Dumocrats,” Trump said he would nevertheless form an AI Force and appoint an AI czar (“Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!”).

Former President Trump announced the creation of a "Super Intelligence Force" today, marking his administration's most significant response to escalating debates over artificial intelligence safety and regulation.

The real test will be whether this task force can strike the delicate balance between ensuring AI safety and maintaining America's competitive edge in what many consider the most important technology race of our time.
President Donald Trump unveiled the formation of the Super Intelligence Force (SIF) to ensure America’s supremacy in the realm of “Super Intelligence” (SI).
At the @DeptofWar we have seen what is possible when red tape is removed and America’s best technology is rapidly put into action.

The SIF is designed to coordinate the federal government with groups when it comes to “SI” in order to improve the lives of Americans.
